It is sourced from UPU's PREDES messaging standards that contains electronic advance information initiated by the origin economy office of exchange (OE) destined for destination economy office of exchange. PREDES protocol is a widely accepted and used standard that is a recommended dataset for volume related network analysis and for the quality-of-service assessments conducted by the UPU. Postal items are usually classified into three categories: letter-post items (documents and small parcels up to 2 kilograms), parcel-post items (larger parcels of at least 2 kilograms), and express mail service (EMS). Records associated with parcel-post and EMS mail classes were categorized as business-to-business (B2B) postal activities. B2B postal connectivity is the average of the two numbers: the number of unique origin partner economies from which B2B postal items are received throughout a year, and the number of unique destination partner economies to which B2B postal items are shipped during the same time period. More details on the methodology can be found here: https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099042226142027181 Loading... × Indicator Container import dwell time 2023-2024 | 163 Economies | Updated Annual (about 1 month ago) Source: World Bank (WB) ID: CT_DT_M License: CC-BY-4.0 Aggregation Method: Economy group aggregates are based on World Bank income and regional groups using simple averages. Development Relevance: Trade logistics performance Statistical Concept and Methodology: Indicator is derived from a container-tracking dataset provided to the World Bank by a major global shipping line under confidentiality arrangements. Observations are recorded at the container level and include container status (full or empty), location, and timestamps for discrete event types. Each timestamp captures the date and time of one of 70-plus tracking events occurring across locations—such as seaports, inland terminals, depots, quays, and rail ramps—identified by UN/LOCODEs. Container voyages (sequences of events attributed to a particular consignment in a container) are segmented into five phases of movement: empty container positioning, export, shipping/transshipment, import, and empty container return. Phases are constructed by slicing individual container voyages into legs comprising sequences of steps: either dwell time at a single location or lead time between distinct locations. The container import dwell time is calculated as the time between the discharge of a full container from the vessel at the port of arrival (port of entry) until the time the container exits port's premises by truck or rail. More details on the methodology can be found here: https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099042226142027181 Loading... × Indicator Aviation import dwell time 2023-2024 | 135 Economies | Updated Annual (about 1 month ago) Source: Cargo iQ ; World Bank (WB) ID: AV_DT License: CC BY 4.0 Aggregation Method: Economy group aggregates are based on World Bank income and regional groups using simple averages. Development Relevance: Trade logistics performance Statistical Concept and Methodology: Data for this indicator was provided to the World Bank by Cargo iQ, a nonprofit group affiliated with the International Air Transport Association (IATA). Cargo iQ’s event recording follows an electronic data interchange protocol, adhering to a logical sequence of supply chain events. An air freight shipment, typically identified through an electronic airway bill (e-AWB), is tracked from the departure of the flight with cargo from origin airport to its arrival and subsequent check-in at a warehouse at the destination airport. This is followed by the notification to the consignee of the freight’s arrival (event NFD) and the forwarder or consignee’s collection of the freight from the carrier facility at the destination airport (event DLV). Aviation import dwell time is the time difference between the events NFD and DLV. The time elapsed between the NFD and DLV events was calculated for each e-AWB recorded at the destination economy, assuming the validity of the time difference (both timestamps had to exist, and the time difference between them had to be positive). To protect commercially sensitive information, only economies that have at least three airlines reporting and the two largest airlines (measured by the number of e-AWBs recorded per year) account for no more than 90 percent of the total number of e-AWBs recorded for that economy each year were included. More details on the methodology can be found here: https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099042226142027181 Loading... × Indicator Business-to-business postal delivery time 2023-2024 | 191 Economies | Updated Annual (about 1 month ago) Source: Universal Postal Union (UPU) ; World Bank (WB) ID: PO_B2B License: CC BY 4.0 Aggregation Method: Economy group aggregates are based on World Bank income and regional groups using simple averages. Development Relevance: Trade logistics performance Statistical Concept and Methodology: The indicator is calculated using dataset supplied by the Universal Postal Union (UPU). It is sourced from UPU's EMSEVT messaging standard that contains electronic data interchanges for individual tracked postal items enabling granular visibility over their progress along the supply chain. Postal items are usually classified into three categories: letter-post items (documents and small parcels up to 2 kilograms), parcel-post items (larger parcels of at least 2 kilograms), and express mail service (EMS). Records associated with parcel-post and EMS mail classes were categorized as business-to-business (B2B) postal activities. B2B postal delivery time is the time difference between the time a postal item arrives at the destination economy and the time the item is either delivered to the customer or an unsuccessful first delivery is attempted. The mean, median, and interquartile range (20th–80th percentiles) for all shipments in a given year in a given economy are calculated. The indicator is reported only for economies with more than ten observations/year is observed and with mean and median delivery times at destination exceeding half a day. More details on the methodology can be found here: https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099042226142027181 LPI Report 2025 The 2025 edition of the Logistics Performance Indicators (LPI 2.0) brings a fundamental redesign of the World Bank’s former survey-based Logistics Performance Index toward a system grounded in shipment-level, operational data. Drawing on large-scale tracking data from maritime, aviation, and postal operators, the LPI 2.0 provides standardized and comparable measures of supply chain connectivity, speed, and reliability across countries and over time. Data for 2023–24 reveal persistent connectivity gaps between high- and lower-income economies, substantial time penalties associated with transshipment and border procedures, and high unpredictability concentrated at ports, transshipment hubs, and inland checkpoints. By shifting the focus from perceptions to observed outcomes, the LPI 2.0 significantly enhances diagnostic precision and policy relevance, enabling governments to better prioritize reforms with the highest potential impact on supply chain connectivity, speed, reliability, and resilience. Supply chains are only as good as their weakest link. Investment Results Brief Sep 2, 2025 Transforming Logistics: The Power of Rail Investment The World Bank is transforming logistics through rail—cutting emissions, lowering costs, and boosting jobs for greener, more connected economies. Synopsis The World Bank's approach to supporting rail logistics focuses on enhancing the efficiency, sustainability, and resilience of rail transport systems globally, with a particular emphasis on shifting freight traffic from carbon-intensive transport modes, like road, to rail. Rail logistics is a key part of addressing the dual challenge of transport decarbonization and inclusive economic growth, helping countries reduce emissions while supporting competitiveness, job creation, and sustainable development. The World Bank applies an integrated approach built around three core pillars: infrastructure financing, policy and regulatory reform, and technical assistance and knowledge sharing. The World Bank is actively engaged in railway research, analysis, technical support, policy dialogue and lending projects in over 20 countries worldwide. World Bank-supported rail logistics projects are delivering tangible results: lowering transport costs, improving freight efficiency, enhancing railway and operating safety, and reducing emissions. Results Highlights In India, from 2011 to 2024, 1,200 kilometers (km) of new dedicated freight tracks were built, freight train capacity was boosted fourfold, train operational speeds were increased, logistics costs reduced by up to $58 million, about 9 million days of employment generated, and emissions (in 2024 alone) cut by 55,000 tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO₂e). By 2042, total cumulative emissions reductions are projected to reach 13.19 million tons, a reduction of 57 percent from pre-project levels in 2010. In Egypt, about 30 million people benefit from improved access to sustainable transport infrastructure and services. In Cameroon, road and rail infrastructure upgrades along the Douala–N’Djamena corridor lowered container shipping costs by over 7 percent between 2012 and 2022. In Uzbekistan, from 2015 to 2020, a new mixed-used rail link improved connectivity for over 740,000 people, cut passenger travel costs by 33 percent, reduced trip delays from 95 percent to 10 percent, and reduced freight costs for key goods by up to 80 percent. In Serbia, modernized rail infrastructure has reduced the fatality rate per train kilometer by about half, from 3.56 per train-kilometer in 2019 to 1.89 per train-kilometer in 2025. In China, institutional capacity for sustainable logistics was enhanced by developing national policies, technical standards, and tools to promote green and efficient freight systems. Separating freight traffic from passenger traffic is very important in a country like India. […] the double-stack container trains will be able to substantially reduce the unit cost of freight transport and hence save logistics costs. Next, the hubs located near EDFC & WDFC catchment areas will also grow due to an increase in EXIM traffic, furthering supply chain optimization. Harpreet Singh Malhotra Chairman & Managing Director, Tiger Logistics Challenge Rail logistics sits at the crossroads of economic growth, job creation, and climate action. As developing countries expand their economies and create job opportunities, demand for efficient, reliable and sustainable logistics systems keeps rising. Freight rail has a unique role to play in facilitating trade, lowering logistics costs, and linking production hubs to ports and markets. However, business-as-usual approaches to freight transport are no longer sustainable. In many low- and middle-income countries, rapid urbanization and economic growth are driving up freight demand. Relying primarily on road-based logistics will exacerbate congestion, accelerate infrastructure wear, inflate logistics costs, and worsen environmental and health outcomes due to higher emissions and air pollution. The rail logistics sector faces critical bottlenecks that limit its effectiveness. Outdated infrastructure, poor intermodal integration, and fragmented transport systems reduce the competitiveness of rail and make modal shifts from road to rail difficult. Even when the environmental and economic benefits are clear, the absence of enabling policy frameworks, limited institutional capacity, and financing constraints continue to stall progress. Approach The World Bank’s approach to rail logistics improvement is built on a comprehensive and integrated approach that combines infrastructure financing, policy and regulatory reform, and institutional capacity-building, to help countries develop efficient, competitive, and low-carbon logistics systems. The World Bank is actively engaged in railway research, analysis, technical support, and lending projects in over 20 countries worldwide. A core element of this approach is infrastructure development , with investments aimed at constructing and modernizing rail lines, logistics terminals, and multimodal hubs to strengthen connectivity and improve service quality. The World Bank’s support for policy and regulatory reforms enables countries to unlock the full potential of railways. In Serbia, for example, the engagement has gone beyond financing infrastructure to addressing institutional strengthening and environmental concerns, such as air quality. Complementing these efforts is a strong focus on technical assistance and knowledge sharing . The World Bank works closely with client governments to design and implement effective rail logistics strategies through continuous dialogue, analytical work, and the dissemination of best practices. Flagship reports such as Unlocking Green Logistics for Development provide actionable guidance on enhancing national logistics frameworks. Capacity-building initiatives, including training sessions and workshops (e.g., an Annual Railway Workshop on Cross-border Services ), further support institutions in managing and operating modern rail systems. Results World Bank-supported rail logistics projects are delivering tangible results, lowering transport costs, improving freight efficiency, enhancing railway and operating safety, and reducing emissions in several countries,thereby contributing to broader economic, environmental, and social impacts. In India , three Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor (EDFC) projects led to the construction of 1,200 km of newly built tracks, from 2011 to 2024. This investment is delivering major gains in efficiency, environment, economic competitiveness, and regional development. The EDFC projects have dramatically expanded rail capacity. On EDFC’s first section, daily freight train capacity increased fourfold, from 32 train pairs to over 130, boosting service reliability and customer satisfaction. Train operational speeds were increased significantly, with freight trains now operating at three times the speed of conventional services, reducing logistics costs by $58 million, and making rail more competitive for logistics providers. By shifting freight to dedicated tracks, the projects also freed up capacity on the conventional rail network. On the Khurja–Kanpur section alone, daily passenger train services increased from 69 to 128, improving frequency and punctuality for millions of rail users. Construction activities generated jobs and supported local livelihoods. Villagers near construction sites earned between $20 and $31 per day through skilled and unskilled labor, with additional monthly income opportunities for (mostly) women working in camp services. These opportunities contributed to tangible improvements in local economic development in project areas. In total, the EDFC projects generated about 9 million days of employment during project implementation. The projects are generating substantial climate benefits: in 2024 alone, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions were reduced by around 55,000 tCO₂. By 2042, total cumulative emissions reductions, caused by shifting freight transport from road to rail alongside the EDFC, are projected to reach 13.19 million tons, a reduction of 57 percent from pre-project levels in 2010. Each kilometer-long freight train on the EDFC replaces about 72 trucks, helping to reduce highway congestion, improve safety, and lower air pollution. This shift is expected to save India approximately Rs 4.9 billion ($58 million) in logistics costs and Rs 2.4 billion ($28 million) in pollution-related health and environmental costs, over the lifetime of the project. These changes mean faster, cleaner, and more affordable goods movement, improving both business efficiency and air quality. Building on earlier EDFC investments, the Rail Logistics Project , launched in 2022, aims to enhance the efficiency of freight and passenger transport while reducing greenhouse gas emissions (GHG). Feature Story Changing the Way We Move: A Win-Win for Climate and Development The World Bank and its new Global Facility to Decarbonize Transport (GFDT) are working toward innovative solutions that will help reduce the climate footprint of transport while boosting economic growth and development. News Decarbonizing road, rail, planes, and ships at COP26 The GFDT provides the World Bank with a vehicle to deliver catalytic funding to formulate, innovate, and scale up support to client countries to decarbonize transport and build resilience, while also meeting growing mobility needs. Blog Shaping the future of transport and climate action with four words Transport accounts for 20% of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions and, with urbanization and motorization on the rise in developing countries, this could grow to 60% by 2050. The Global Facility to Decarbonize Transport is designed to accelerate investments and innovation. publication Transport Decarbonization Investment series (TDI) This series of reports and events delivers practical recommendations for scaling up low-carbon transport, with a focus on overcoming investment barriers and developing innovative financial instruments. Annual Reports 2025 Annual Report The 2025 GFDT Annual Report covers January 1, 2025, to December 31, 2025. Throughout the year, GFDT-funded activities delivered advisory services to 58 government entities, provided technical assistance or capacity building in over 30 countries, and supported the preparation of 20 flagship studies, tools, and strategies. This upstream work catalyzed six World Bank-financed transport investments under implementation, with three additional operations under preparation—representing $3.6 billion in current and anticipated financing. These results underscore GFDT’s catalytic impact: for every $1 disbursed, $105 has been mobilized in World Bank financing for transport decarbonization, rising to $328 as projects advance and additional financing is unlocked. 2024 Annual Report The 2024 GFDT Annual Report covers the period from January 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024. Throughout 2024, GFDT-funded activities delivered advisory services to 55 government entities, provided technical support to 28 countries, and produced or are developing 48 flagship reports, technical studies, and transport decarbonization roadmaps. This work has mobilized two approved World Bank-financed green mobility investments, with eight more in preparation.   GFDT-funded activities are projected to avoid ~508,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent (tCO₂e) from the two approved investments, rising to ~3 million tCO₂e when including the additional eight in preparation.   These GFDT-supported green mobility projects demonstrate the multiplier effect of GFDT’s approach: for every $1 invested into GFDT, $63 has been mobilized in World Bank financing for transport decarbonization, and an $149 additional is on track to be mobilized, resulting in a total expected leveraging ratio of 1:212.   2023 Annual Report The 2023 Annual Report of the Global Facility to Decarbonize Transport (GFDT) covers the period from September 1, 2022 to December 31, 2023. This is GFDT’s first annual report.   During the reporting period, GFDT-funded activities engaged 13 countries and 94 government entities via advisory services, technical support or capacity building; published numerous action plans, strategy documents, and policy recommendations; and informed and enhanced 8 World Bank lending operations under preparation, and 12 operations under implementation.   In addition, GFDT allocated $3.2 million in grants to seven activities, which are expected to catalyze $480 million in World Bank financing for green mobility projects. About the Program The Global Facility to Decarbonize Transport (GFDT) is a multi-donor trust fund that accelerates innovation and investment in low-carbon mobility solutions. international transport currently account for about 20% of global GHG emissions. If no action is taken, transport emissions will continue to increase rapidly, with the latest estimates projecting a rise of as much as 60% by 2050. In that context, the decarbonization of the transport sector has become an urgent priority, and will be instrumental in winning the global race against climate change. However, by most measures, action is well off-track. While a growing number of green mobility innovations are emerging, market uptake has been slow. Transport stakeholders need targeted and more effective interventions to accelerate the transformation of the sector and scale up investment in climate-smart mobility. To support this transition, the World Bank, the government of the Netherlands, and the World Resources Institute have jointly developed a new series of publications and events that aim to deliver actionable recommendations, with a focus on overcoming investment barriers and developing innovative financial instruments to decarbonize transport. The Transport Decarbonization Investment series will include a total of six papers to be launched in the leadup to the COP26 Climate Conference. Financing Low Carbon Transport Solutions in Developing Countries (TDI paper 6) The rationale to decarbonize transport is clear and the investment gap has been identified, but can governments gather the much-needed resources? There is no simple answer, and the solution depends on each country context. The COP26 Transport Day event will be the culmination of the efforts, with the release of a sixth and final paper that will synthesize the main findings of the five papers produced in TDI series, identifying opportunities for investment, accompanied with concrete recommendations for transport to pursue a low carbon pathway. In addition, innovative financing approaches are put forward from a developing market perspective to overcome market barriers that are constraining climate friendly transport solutions. Building on the recommendations proposed in the TDI series, the event will bring together government leaders and development partners, who will map out priority actions and next steps for climate action across the transport sector. Download the full report Watch launch event Decarbonizing the Freight and Logistics Sector (TDI paper 5) Freight and logistics are a major contributor to climate change (10-11% of overall emissions). The sector is currently almost entirely dependent on fossil fuels, and is expected to see demand surge from 112 trillion ton–kilometers in 2015 to 329 trillion in 2050. As a result, emissions from freight transport are predicted to continue rising, with much of that growth coming from non-OECD countries. To avoid this scenario, the paper looks at possible decarbonization initiatives across three sub-sectors— maritime, inter-urban and urban freight—with a focus on their efficacy and applicability to the developing country context. The measures considered in the report fall into five broad categories: restraining or reversing the growth of freight movement; making greater use of lower-carbon transport modes; improving vehicle/vessel utilization; increasing energy efficiency; and switching to lower carbon energy sources. Download the full report Investing for Momentum in Active Mobility (TDI Paper 4) Beyond being the most environmentally friendly form of transport, active mobility also provides significant social, economic and health benefits. Yet, active mobility continues to be underfunded, resulting in users being the most vulnerable due to a lack of suitable infrastructure and protection from motorized vehicles. This discussion paper argues these issues are a consequence of misconceptions regarding the benefits from investment and failure to view active mobility as part of an integrated transport network. The paper looks to debunk these misconceptions, identify financing alternatives, and highlight investment opportunities at the local, national and international level to expand the role of active mobility as part of a decarbonized and integrated transport network. Download the full report Watch session recording Decarbonizing Cities by Improving Public Transport and Managing Land Use and Traffic (TDI Paper 3) Cities in developing countries have a unique opportunity to preserve and encourage sustainable urban passenger mobility by building on their existing modal shares in public transport, walking, and biking—low carbon modes. This will require significant improvements to urban infrastructure for public transit, walking, and biking—a reprioritization of investment and space allocation away from the cars driven by the minority to the modes used by the majority—and reforms to public transit service provision that reduce competition within the market, address underfunding, and put the needs of the user first. If cities accompany these investments with the right policies and enabling environment—e.g., making land use regulations more efficient and disincentivizing and managing further car ownership and use—they can raise additional funds to continue to invest in greener transport facilities. Download the full report Watch session recording Cleaner Vehicles and Charging Infrastructure: Greening Passenger Fleets for Sustainable Mobility (Paper 2) Transport sector emissions have grown faster than those of almost any other economic sector over the past 50 years, with additional increases predicted (by as much as 60% by 2050) if no action is taken. Governments worldwide need to take ambitious steps to limit global warming and achieve the Paris Agreement's Climate Agreement's goals. In this context, the transport sector's electrification has never been more prominent and relevant to the ongoing debate on the future of mobility. The newly released discussion paper “Cleaner Vehicles and Charging Infrastructure” identifies tangible actions and policies that policymakers can adopt to promote electric mobility adoption. It highlights that every country needs to develop its own long-term sustainable EV ecosystem— both in terms of (i) transitioning the vehicle fleet from ICE to EV and (ii) deployment of charging infrastructure—based on its own infrastructure condition. Download the full report Watch session recording Motorization Management and the Trade of Used Vehicles (Paper 1) While there are many ways we can help lessen the climate impact of transport, one key priority is to manage motorization more effectively. In developing countries, the number of vehicles on the road is expected to double in the next 15-20 years, and much of that growth will come from used vehicles imported from high-income countries. This creates significant challenges, as the oldest and most poorly maintained vehicles in a national fleet contribute disproportionately to the transport-related local air pollution, GHG emissions, road injuries and fatalities. To address this, the paper explores options and best practices that can help counties improve the environmental and safety standards of their vehicle fleet, improve regulations around the trade of used vehicles, and transition to more sustainable motorization. Active Projects Policy Dialogue Partners Sign-up for the Decarbonising Transport Newsletter Video of Reshaping transport for a cleaner environment and fairer society The Decarbonising Transport initiative promotes carbon-neutral mobility to help stop climate change. It provides decision makers with tools to select CO 2 mitigation measures that deliver on their climate commitment. Climate change affects lives around the globe. Rising temperatures cause droughts, rising sea levels threaten low-lying regions, ever more extreme weather leads to severe disruptions. Climate change cannot be stopped without decarbonising transport. Transport emits around 23% of the energy-related CO 2 that feeds global warming. Without imm ediate action, its share could reach 40% by 2030. Transport emissions have grown faster than those of any other sector over the past 50 years.  Demand for transport will continue to grow massively in the coming decades. As a result CO 2 emissions from transport activity will not fall, but could increase by 60% by 2050. And because transport relies on oil for 92% of its energy, it is particularly hard to decarbonise .  The Decarbonising Transport initiative helps  governments and industry to translate climate ambitions into actions. Specifically, it: Builds a catalogue of effective CO 2 mitigation measures: the Transport Climate Action Directory . Provides  targeted analytical assistance for countries and partners to identify climate actions that work. Gathers and shares evidence for best practices that will accelerate the transition to carbon-neutral mobility. Shapes the climate change debate by building a global policy dialogue and by bringing the transport perspective to the broader climate change discussions.  The Decarbonising Transport initiative is organised in five work streams: Tracking progress: The initiative evaluates how current mitigation measures contribute to reaching objectives for reducing transport CO 2 . In-depth sectoral studies: The initiative identifies effective policies for decarbonising urban passenger transport, road freight transport, maritime transport, aviation and inter-urban transport. Focus studies: The initiative analyses specific decarbonisation issues and feeds the results into other work streams. National pathways: The initiative assesses available policy levers for decarbonising transport from a country perspective. Projects may also examine regional or sub-national levels. Policy Dialogue: The initiative organises global dialogue on transport and climate change through high-level roundtables, policy briefings and technical workshops. It acts as a conduit for transport sector input to climate change negotiations. The Decarbonising Transport initiative does not advocate specific measures or policies. Building on an evidence-based assessment of mitigation impacts, it identifies options for decision-makers to achieve their targets -  for   instance   the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) submitted by countries under the Paris Agreement, as well as targets set by sectors, companies or cities.    The assessments of the Decarbonising Transport initiative are grounded in data analysis and advanced modelling . Uniquely, the ITF modelling framework derives projections of transport activity from analysing the drivers of demand. It then models how changes in mobility patterns affect CO 2 emissions. All work streams of the Decarbonising Transport initiative are open for involvement. The initiative currently unites more than 70 governments, organisations , institutions, foundations and companies. Partners contribute in different roles including as funders and knowledge partners. The Decarbonising Transport initiative was launched in 2016 with core funding from the ITF’s Corporate Partnership Board (CPB). Other funding partners currently include the governments of France, Korea, Ireland and the Netherlands, the World Bank, the European Commission, the Climate Works Foundation, the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the FIA Foundation, the International Road Transport Union (IRU) and the Swedish Shipowners' Association. In recognition of the work of its Decarbonising Transport initiative, the UN Climate Change Secretariat (UNFCCC) has named the International Transport Forum a focal point for transport under its Marrakech Partnership. In this role, the ITF acts as a conduit for the exchange of information between the transport sector and the UNFCCC, as well as providing inputs to the UNFCCC process. The DT initiative has evolved into a broader initiative focused on implementing sustainable transport policies. **Current phase:** Signal-to-pressure conversion is partial. Four corridors have reached realisation stage; the majority remain pre-commercial or stalled.

FACT: "For the first time since the report's inception in 2022, four green shipping corridors have now reached the 'realisation stage', an important milestone at which the construction and/or operation of vessels, infrastructure, and/or fuel plants takes place." *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

FACT: "Many of the 84 initiatives remain stalled by a 'feasibility wall' created by the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels." *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

**Named conversion triggers, sourced:**

1. **IMO Net-Zero Framework adoption** — the primary mechanism that could bridge the cost gap and convert stalled corridors into active commercial operations. FACT: The framework was "delayed until at least next October" from the perspective of the November 2025 report. *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/ FACT: As of May 2026, the news index notes "Negotiations signal progress but uncertainty remains on the Net-Zero Framework" (6 May 2026). *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

2. **IMO 5% zero-emission fuel target by 2030** — the near-term milestone corridors are designed to support. FACT: "Shipping off track to meet 5% zero-emission fuel target by 2030 as new report issues 'serious wakeup call'" [September 2024]. *Source: Green Corridors news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors FACT: "2030 shipping goal at risk despite historic progress made by IMO" [September 2025]. *Source: Green Corridors news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

3. **Cargo-owner demand aggregation** — identified by the coalition as the commercial unlock when regulatory mechanisms lag. FACT: The report recommends engaging "cargo owners who may be more willing to pay a premium for cleaner fuels." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

4. **First-mover reward mechanism.** FACT: Fahnestock stated: "Those who act now will be best positioned to benefit when regulation catches up." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

*Analytical inference:* The trajectory indicates two distinct timelines: (a) the realisation-stage corridors — four as of end-2025 — are likely to produce commercially observable fuel-cost and routing data within 2–4 years, driving a second wave of corporate procurement decisions; (b) the stalled majority converts only if the IMO framework provides financial bridging, which is now indexed to a Q4 2026 decision window at earliest.

*Analytical inference:* The pattern of emerging-economy engagement (China, India, Brazil) suggests that future corridor growth will increasingly be driven by fuel-supply-side economics — green hydrogen, green ammonia, e-methanol production at scale — rather than solely by demand-side shipping company commitments. This shifts corridor relevance from a carrier-procurement question to a supply-chain routing and sourcing question.

**Monitoring window set:** Re-check this brief at Q4 2026 against IMO Net-Zero Framework adoption outcome. Secondary re-check at publication of Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2026 (expected Q4 2026 based on annual publication pattern; *Analytical inference:* consistent with 2022–2025 annual cadence).

---

*Note: The C40 Cities source (https://www.c40.org/what-we-do/scaling-up-climate-action/ports-and-shipping/green-shipping-corridors/) and the S&P Global source (https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/2025/11/series-of-new-green-shipping-corridors-emerge-despite-imo-regulatory-setback) and the RMI source (https://rmi.org/green-shipping-corridors-can-help-scale-indias-green-hydrogen-ecosystem/) returned access-blocked or cookie-wall responses at retrieval time. Specific cost figures, corridor-level operational data, and India ammonia TCO analysis from those sources cannot be span-grounded and are therefore omitted. The cost and operational picture below is grounded only in the GMF primary sources.*

**Ocean freight — primary mode affected:**

*Operational implication:* For workspaces routing ocean freight on trade lanes that overlap with active corridor initiatives — including Asia–Europe, Australia–Asia, South America–Europe, and intra-Asia routes — the shift from conventional heavy fuel oil to zero-emission fuels (methanol, ammonia, e-fuels) on those corridors will alter carrier fuel cost structures and may translate into freight rate differentiation between corridor-compliant and non-compliant vessel calls.

*Operational implication:* The "feasibility wall" — the sourced gap between conventional and zero-emission fuel costs — is the primary near-term cost implication. Workspaces tendering ocean freight today are likely to encounter green-premium line items as carriers on realisation-stage corridors seek cost recovery. The magnitude of that premium is not available in the sourced content; this is an explicit research gap requiring carrier-specific data.

*Specific cost gap figure not available from primary sources as of June 2026.*

FACT: The report identifies that corridors "remain stalled by a 'feasibility wall' created by the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels." *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

**Air freight — secondary mode:**

*Operational implication:* Air freight operations are not directly within the scope of the green shipping corridors initiative, which is maritime-specific. However, workspaces that split shipments between ocean and air on the same trade lanes will face diverging sustainability cost trajectories: ocean lanes on active corridors will attract green premiums while SAF mandates drive parallel cost increases on air legs. The interaction effect on total-lane cost is a research gap.

**Fuel types under development in corridors:**

FACT: "Methanol and ammonia progressing rapidly as zero-emission shipping fuels, but extra push needed to scale" [August 2025]. *Source: Green Corridors news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

FACT: "First-of-a-kind ammonia-powered gas carriers could be commercially viable from 2026, new study finds" [August 2023]. *Source: Green Corridors news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

FACT: A June 2026 news item references "New consortium to advance e-fuel green corridor between Brazil and Belgium." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

*Analytical inference:* For workspaces moving cargo on Brazil–Europe trade lanes, the e-fuel corridor consortium announced in June 2026 is the most proximate near-term corridor development to track. If e-fuel supply is established on that lane, carriers deploying compliant vessels will have a differentiated cost and compliance profile relative to conventional-fuel competitors.

**Shore power and port infrastructure:**

*Operational implication:* Corridor realisation includes port-side infrastructure investment. Workspaces with cargo moving through ports participating in active corridors may see changes in port call scheduling, vessel turnaround, and berth allocation as zero-emission vessel calls are prioritised. Specific port-level data is not available in the grounded sources; this requires port-authority confirmation per relevant gateway.

FACT: "Port call optimisation provides critical opportunity for shipping efficiency and emissions reduction" [April 2025]. *Source: Green Corridors news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

**Book-and-claim implications:**

FACT: "Major maritime companies agree to develop book and claim approaches in order to accelerate shipping's decarbonisation transition" [June 2023]. *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

*Operational implication:* If book-and-claim mechanisms for zero-emission fuels mature within corridor frameworks, workspaces tendering freight on non-corridor routes could purchase zero-emission fuel certificates to satisfy client Scope 3 reporting requirements without routing cargo through corridor lanes. This has direct implications for sustainability-reporting obligations under frameworks such as ISO 14083 and CSRD Scope 3 disclosures, but the linkage to specific standards requires legal and compliance confirmation.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether zero-emission fuel certificates generated under corridor book-and-claim schemes would satisfy a workspace's Scope 3 reporting obligations under CSRD or customer contractual sustainability requirements depends on how those standards define "chain of custody" and "additionality" — legal and standards review required.

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- Green shipping corridors are now at 84 active initiatives globally, up from 59 a year prior, with four having reached the stage at which vessels, infrastructure, and fuel plants are being constructed or operated. This is a sourced fact from the coalition's own annual report and is defensible in a client meeting.
- The initiative is backed by a 200+ organisation coalition including major ocean carriers, energy companies, ports, and financial institutions — this is not a pilot fringe programme. It is the primary industry-level coordination mechanism for maritime decarbonisation.
- The cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels remains the primary obstacle to scale. The initiative does not yet eliminate that gap; it is building the commercial and technical knowledge base that makes scale possible when regulation or demand catches up.
- Four corridors have reached "realisation stage" — meaning physical construction or operation of relevant assets is underway. These corridors are the closest to producing observable market data on cost and performance.

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- Does your sustainability reporting framework differentiate between ocean freight on corridor-participating lanes versus conventional lanes? If so, the workspace can prioritise carrier selection accordingly.
- Are you a signatory to the Sea Cargo Charter or similar maritime sustainability commitment? If so, corridor-participating carriers may offer a better alignment story than non-participants.
- Are any of your supply chain routes covered by the named corridor geographies — Asia–Australia, South America–Europe, South Africa–Europe, Rotterdam–Singapore? These are the corridors closest to commercial deployment.

**Claims to avoid:**

- Do not claim that green corridor shipping is commercially available at scale today. The sourced record is clear that most initiatives are pre-commercial and stalled by a feasibility wall.
- Do not claim specific fuel-cost premiums without carrier-level data. The cost gap is documented as real but not quantified in the grounded sources.
- Do not present corridor participation as a compliance solution for any specific reporting obligation without legal review of what the relevant standard accepts. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether corridor-derived zero-emission fuel certificates satisfy specific contractual or regulatory Scope 3 requirements is a legal and standards question, not a factual one at this stage.
- Do not characterize the IMO Net-Zero Framework as adopted or in force. As of May 2026, it remains under negotiation with uncertainty. FACT: "Negotiations signal progress but uncertainty remains on the Net-Zero Framework" [6 May 2026]. *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

---

**The headline fact:** The green shipping corridors movement has reached 84 active initiatives globally as of November 2025, up from 59 the prior year — a 40% increase documented in the 2024 edition and continued through 25 new initiatives identified in 2025.

FACT: "The report identifies 25 new green corridor initiatives, expanding the global total to 84 active initiatives." *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum / Getting to Zero Coalition, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

FACT: "Green corridors, which are specific trade routes where the feasibility of zero-emission shipping is catalysed by public and private action, can accelerate shipping's transition to zero emissions by testing and deploying fuels, vessels, and infrastructure in a coordinated way, generating the knowledge required to unlock the rest of the sector's energy transition." *Source: Green Corridors, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

FACT: "Plans for the first green corridor were announced in 2021 and there are now well over 50 initiatives in various stages of development." *Source: Green Corridors, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

Three triggers drove the 2025 expansion:

1. **Emerging-economy entry.** FACT: "Initiatives have been launched in major developing economies like China, India, Brazil, Chile, Ghana, and Kenya, reflecting the significant economic opportunities that can be seized through the development of zero-emission marine fuels and bunkering capabilities in these regions." *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

2. **First corridors reaching realisation stage.** FACT: "For the first time since the report's inception in 2022, four green shipping corridors have now reached the 'realisation stage', an important milestone at which the construction and/or operation of vessels, infrastructure, and/or fuel plants takes place." *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

3. **IMO Net-Zero Framework delay — ambiguous pressure.** FACT: "The report cautions that many of the 84 initiatives remain stalled by a 'feasibility wall' created by the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels – a challenge that the Net-Zero Framework, delayed until at least next October, could help overcome." *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

FACT: "Negotiations at International Maritime Organization adjourn without a decision on shipping's Net-Zero Framework" [17 October 2025]. *Source: Green Corridors news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

*Analytical inference:* The regulatory delay functions as a dual signal for workspaces with ocean freight exposure: it extends the window for voluntary positioning inside corridor programmes before binding obligations force participation, but it also reduces the cost-bridging incentive that the IMO reward mechanism was intended to provide, prolonging the feasibility wall.

*Analytical inference:* The 2024 reporting noted green corridors grew "by 40% worldwide, but face a 'feasibility wall'", signalling that volume growth and structural readiness are moving on separate tracks. The 40% growth figure and the feasibility-wall characterisation are now corroborated by the 2025 edition's data.

FACT: "Green corridors grow by 40% worldwide, but face a 'feasibility wall', says Global Maritime Forum report" [19 November 2024]. *Source: Green Corridors news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

---

**The coalition architecture:** The Getting to Zero Coalition is the primary institutional engine, operating alongside the Global Maritime Forum.

FACT: "The Getting to Zero Coalition is a powerful alliance of more than 200 organisations (including over 180 private companies) within the maritime, energy, infrastructure, and finance sectors. The Coalition is committed to getting commercially viable zero-emission vessels powered by zero-emission fuels into operation by 2030." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

FACT: "The Getting to Zero Coalition was launched in 2019 with 70 signatories." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

FACT: Coalition working groups include "green corridor task forces, a book and claim task force, a policy action group, and a Latin America task force." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

Named member companies active in the coalition include, among others: A.P. Moller–Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd, MSC Mediterranean Shipping Company, ONE, NYK Line, K Line, Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, CMA CGM (not listed), Kuehne+Nagel, DHL Global Forwarding, CEVA Logistics, DSV, Rio Tinto, BHP, Anglo American, Tata Steel, Shell, TotalEnergies, BP, Yara, Siemens Energy, and Wärtsilä. FACT: This member list is drawn verbatim from the coalition members section. *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

FACT: "Some 30 governments facilitate green corridor development, helping to trigger a race to the top as they explore multiple policy pathways to increase the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of their support." *Source: Green Corridors, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/green-corridors

**What the parties want — sourced statements of intent:**

FACT: Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum, stated: "Countries that move early stand to gain competitive industrial and geopolitical advantages across energy, trade, and technology." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

FACT: The 2025 report "calls for action at the national level to drive progress, create first-mover advantage, and position for early access to future IMO incentives." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

FACT: The report recommends corridors "capitalise on the opportunity to shape IMO policy, like the reward mechanism, and be well-positioned to benefit from eventual regulation." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

FACT: The report recommends corridors "better engage those with ambitious decarbonisation goals that can help scale solutions, particularly cargo owners who may be more willing to pay a premium for cleaner fuels." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

*Analytical inference:* The explicit targeting of cargo owners willing to pay a premium signals that the coalition's commercial strategy depends on shipper-side demand aggregation. Forwarders with cargo-owner client relationships — particularly in sectors with public ESG commitments — sit at a leverage point for accelerating corridor economics.

*Analytical inference:* The coalition's advocacy impact is documented: FACT: "Advocacy through the Coalition has also played a key role in recent policy developments, including the International Maritime Organization's decision to introduce much more ambitious targets, the European Union's Fit for 55, and national frameworks for international shipping." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

**National policy vehicles being deployed:** FACT: The report points to "emerging policies and programmes from national governments, such as the EU's Global Gateway initiative, H2Global, and Australia's Hydrogen Headstart programme" as tools to "unlock progress ahead of a global framework." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

---

The following actions are positioning moves, not compliance actions. Severity: MONITORING.

**1. Map current carrier relationships against corridor participation.**
Action: For each ocean carrier in the workspace's current tender set, determine whether that carrier is a Getting to Zero Coalition member and whether they have disclosed participation in any of the 84 active corridor initiatives. Coalition membership list is publicly available at https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/ and is the starting screen. This is a desk exercise, not a procurement commitment.
*Why now:* Four corridors are at realisation stage. Carriers on those corridors are the first movers who will have real performance data and will be the ones targeted by ESG-driven cargo owners seeking premium-compliant routing. Early identification of those carriers positions the workspace ahead of a client request that is coming.

**2. Add sustainability-corridor language to carrier tender documents.**
Action: When issuing ocean freight RFQs, include a question asking carriers to declare whether the relevant trade lane is covered by a green corridor programme and whether zero-emission fuel options are available. Do not make this a disqualifying criterion; make it a data-gathering clause.
*Why now:* The 2025 report explicitly recommends engaging cargo owners who will pay a premium. Carriers are beginning to segment their commercial conversations accordingly. A forwarder who cannot answer "which of your carriers are corridor-active on this lane?" is behind in that conversation.

**3. Track the IMO Net-Zero Framework Q4 2026 decision.**
Action: Set a review trigger for Q4 2026 when the IMO is expected to revisit framework adoption. The outcome — adoption, further delay, or modified proposal — will determine whether the feasibility wall begins to close and whether corridor economics become self-sustaining without national subsidy.
FACT: The framework was "delayed until at least next October" as of November 2025. *Source: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025, Global Maritime Forum, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/report/annual-progress-report-on-green-shipping-corridors-2025/

**4. Evaluate Getting to Zero Coalition engagement.**
Action: Assess whether the workspace's ocean freight volumes and client ESG profile qualify for coalition membership consideration, noting the invitation-only structure. Alternatively, identify which carrier members are operationally relevant to the workspace's trade lanes and engage them directly on corridor-lane availability and green-fuel pricing.
FACT: "Membership in the Coalition's 'race to the top' for the future of our industry is by invitation only." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

**5. For South America–Europe lanes specifically: track the Brazil–Belgium e-fuel corridor.**
Action: The June 2026 announcement of a new consortium to advance an e-fuel green corridor between Brazil and Belgium is the most recent corridor development. For workspaces with cargo on Brazil–Europe lanes, monitor this consortium's progress through the GMF news feed. This is the lane most likely to produce a commercial green-fuel option on a timeframe relevant to the workspace's near-term, multi-year procurement decisions.
FACT: "New consortium to advance e-fuel green corridor between Brazil and Belgium" [4 June 2026]. *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

**6. Build corridor geography into lane-level sustainability reporting.**
Action: When preparing Scope 3 emissions data for clients or internal reporting, flag ocean legs that transit lanes covered by active corridor initiatives. This is a positioning and readiness action: it documents the workspace's awareness, enables a more detailed response to client sustainability audits, and positions the workspace to shift those legs to corridor-compliant carriers when fuel availability matures.

---

**Coalition membership as a differentiator:**

FACT: Named logistics and forwarding companies in the Getting to Zero Coalition membership include Kuehne+Nagel, DHL Global Forwarding, CEVA Logistics, and DSV. *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

*Analytical inference:* These four named competitors have direct access to the coalition's working groups — including green corridor task forces, the book-and-claim task force, and the policy action group — which gives them earlier visibility into corridor programme design, fuel procurement frameworks, and reward-mechanism structuring than non-members. Workspaces that are not coalition members and do not have relationships with corridor-participating carriers are operating with a structural information lag on this topic.

*Analytical inference:* The coalition's membership-by-invitation structure (FACT: "Membership in the Coalition's 'race to the top' for the future of our industry is by invitation only." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/) means access is not simply purchasable. Workspaces seeking membership should assess whether their cargo volumes and client base constitute a meaningful contribution to the coalition's demand-aggregation objectives.

**Cargo-owner premium willingness — competitive leverage:**

*Analytical inference:* The coalition's explicit recommendation to "better engage those with ambitious decarbonisation goals that can help scale solutions, particularly cargo owners who may be more willing to pay a premium for cleaner fuels" directly affects how forwarders should be positioning with ESG-driven clients. A forwarder that can credibly connect cargo owners to corridor-participating carriers creates a differentiated commercial proposition relative to forwarders offering only conventional routing.

**First-mover access to IMO reward mechanism:**

FACT: "Those who act now will be best positioned to benefit when regulation catches up." *Source: China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors, Global Maritime Forum Press Release, 27 November 2025. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/press/china-india-and-brazil-move-on-green-shipping-corridors/

*Analytical inference:* The reward mechanism referenced is the IMO Net-Zero Framework's incentive structure for early movers. Its specific design — who qualifies, at what threshold, on what timeline — is not yet finalized. FACT: As of May 2026, "negotiations signal progress but uncertainty remains on the Net-Zero Framework." *Source: Getting to Zero Coalition news index, Global Maritime Forum. https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition/

*Specific reward mechanism thresholds and eligibility criteria not available from primary sources as of June 2026.*

**Geographic competitive positioning:**

*Analytical inference:* The entry of China, India, and Brazil into corridor development has competitive implications for forwarders with significant trade volume on Asia–Europe, South America–Europe, and intra-Asia lanes. Carriers based in or serving those markets who participate in national corridor programmes may be subject to preferential port access, national financing, or green-fuel subsidies that alter their cost competitiveness relative to non-participating carriers on the same lanes. This requires tracking at the carrier-tender level.

March 2023 Critical window of opportunity for shipping at IMO Green corridors Background Decarbonising shipping is difficult, but some trade routes offer relative advantages either because they are near potentially attractive fuel supply hubs, have comparatively simple operational profiles, or are likely to have favourable economics. The idea behind green corridors is to identify and leverage these advantageous routes to kickstart shipping’s transition to new fuels. Plans for the first green corridor were announced in 2021 and there are now well over 50 initiatives in various stages of development. Members Shipping companies, ports, cargo owners, fuel producers, and the civic sector are among the nearly 200 stakeholders involved in green corridors. Some 30 governments facilitate green corridor development, helping to trigger a race to the top as they explore multiple policy pathways to increase the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of their support. The Global Maritime Forum supports several green corridor initiatives through the Getting to Zero Coalition . Impact Green corridors can help the shipping industry rapidly decarbonise in the 2030s by providing the conditions for ambitious companies to test zero-emission technologies and infrastructure at scale this decade. In the process, they will offer opportunities for forward-looking governments to future-proof their trade, become green technology and climate leaders, and support economic development. China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors as industry awaits climate regulations | Global Maritime Forum Global Maritime Forum logo Decarbonisation Underline Human Sustainability Underline Library Underline Annual Summit Underline Menu toggle graphic Library / China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors as industry awaits climate regulations 27 November 2025 China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors as industry awaits climate regulations Green corridors Download the Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025 Annual progress report on green shipping corridors finds 25 new zero-emission trade routes launched in 2025, bringing total to 84 worldwide.   China, India, and Brazil look to capture major opportunities in zero-emission shipping amidst regulatory uncertainty.  Report warns against ‘wait and see’ attitude following delay to the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework.  Report calls for action at the national level to drive progress, create first-mover advantage, and position for early access to future IMO incentives.  27 November 2025, Copenhagen – The movement to create green shipping corridors – trade routes designed to demonstrate and scale novel zero-emission fuels, vessels, and technologies – has expanded in numbers and geographic scope, according to a new progress report published today by the Getting to Zero Coalition and the Global Maritime Forum.   This year’s edition, At a Crossroads: Annual Progress Report on Green Shipping Corridors 2025 , identifies 25 new green corridor initiatives, expanding the global total to 84 active initiatives. Initiatives have been launched in major developing economies like China, India, Brazil, Chile, Ghana, and Kenya, reflecting the significant economic opportunities that can be seized through the development of zero-emission marine fuels and bunkering capabilities in these regions.   The news comes only a month after discussions to adopt the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) landmark Net-Zero Framework, designed to establish a path for shipping to reach net-zero emissions by 2050, were delayed for at least one year.   “The move of major countries like China, India, and Brazil into green corridors is hugely promising, as these are markets that will determine whether zero-emission shipping scales fast enough to meet global climate goals,” Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum, said. “But even more importantly, we’re seeing recognition from these countries that green corridors are more than just environmental projects – they are strategic economic infrastructure. Countries that move early stand to gain competitive industrial and geopolitical advantages across energy, trade, and technology.”    For the first time since the report’s inception in 2022, four green shipping corridors have now reached the ‘realisation stage’, an important milestone at which the construction and/or operation of vessels, infrastructure, and/or fuel plants takes place. However, the report cautions that many of the 84 initiatives remain stalled by a 'feasibility wall' created by the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels – a challenge that the Net-Zero Framework, delayed until at least next October, could help overcome.   Despite this delay, the report warns that industry and governments should not surrender the next year to a 'wait and see' approach. Instead, corridors should make use of emerging policies and programmes from national governments, such as the EU’s Global Gateway initiative, H2Global, and Australia’s Hydrogen Headstart programme – something that would unlock progress ahead of a global framework and put participants among the frontrunners to benefit from future IMO incentives.  “We have at least 12 months before the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework is adopted,” Fahnestock said. “That time can either be spent waiting, or used to build projects that create strategic economic advantages, generate learnings that can influence the IMO’s reward mechanism, and put participants first in line for future global rewards. Those who act now will be best positioned to benefit when regulation catches up.”    To best expand and progress green corridors, the report recommends the industry:    Pursue strategies to break inertia and maintain momentum , closing the cost gap and ensuring corridors are advanced enough to qualify for first mover rewards once they’re available. Capitalise on the opportunity to shape IMO policy , like the reward mechanism, and be well-positioned to benefit from eventual regulation.  Better engage those with ambitious decarbonisation goals that can help scale solutions, particularly cargo owners who may be more willing to pay a premium for cleaner fuels.  Utilise emerging national policy and adapt it for new geographies to accelerate change and encourage industry buy-in.   Stay true to original principles , remembering that green corridors’ greatest contribution to maritime decarbonisation comes from fostering collaboration and prioritising harder-to-deploy e-fuels over more readily available solutions. March 2023 Critical window of opportunity for shipping at IMO Background The Getting to Zero Coalition was launched in 2019 with 70 signatories. Today, more than 200 companies, key governments, and intergovernmental organisations support the Coalition’s mission to make zero-emission fuels and vessels a scalable and affordable reality by 2030 in order to achieve shipping’s 2050 zero-emission target. The Coalition is managed by the Global Maritime Forum, which initially founded it together with the World Economic Forum and Friends of Ocean Action. Activities The Coalition’s strategy focuses on two key objectives: fostering progress around first-mover projects and preparing a full, just, and equitable transition at scale. These objectives are achieved through working groups targeting policy action and industry action, and activities like workshops, webinars, and knowledge pieces. Working groups include green corridor task forces, a book and claim task force, a policy action group, and a Latin America task force. Impact The Coalition has explored pathways toward full shipping decarbonisation and built a solid knowledge base. Members have already taken concrete action, solidifying through initiatives like green corridors. Advocacy through the Coalition has also played a key role in recent policy developments, including the International Maritime Organization’s decision to introduce much more ambitious targets, the European Union’s Fit for 55, and national frameworks for international shipping. Members Getting to Zero Coalition Over 180 maritime, energy, infrastructure, and finance companies are members of the Getting to Zero Coalition. The Coalition is also supported by more than 20 NGOs and intergovernmental organisations and more than ten knowledge partners. It is also endorsed by the governments of 14 countries. All members and supporters are committed to the Getting to Zero Coalition’s Ambition Statement. Membership in the Coalition’s “race to the top” for the future of our industry is by invitation only.
