sections.md:
**Primary finding.** A research team comprising Poulad Moradi (University of Luxembourg, Centre for Logistics and Supply Chain Management), Joachim Arts (University of Luxembourg), and Josué C. Velázquez-Martínez (MIT Center for Transportation & Logistics) studied the effect of high-resolution elevation data on identifying the most fuel-efficient — "greenest" — path for trucks across urban environments.

The study adapts a variant of the Comprehensive Modal Emission Model (CMEM) to show that the optimal speed and the greenest path are slope dependent (dynamic). *Source: arXiv:2306.01687, Moradi, Arts & Velázquez-Martínez, MIT CTL / University of Luxembourg, last revised 30 May 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

**Flat vs. non-flat networks.** When there are no elevation changes in a road network, the most fuel-efficient path is the shortest path with a constant (static) optimal speed. If the network is not flat, then the shortest path is not necessarily the greenest path, and the optimal driving speed is dynamic. *Source: arXiv:2306.01687, as above.*

**Asymptotic convergence.** The study proves that the greenest path converges to an asymptotic greenest path as the payload approaches infinity and that this limiting path is attained for a finite load — meaning that at moderate, commercially realistic payloads, routing behaviour reaches its optimal form, not only at maximum load. *Source: arXiv:2306.01687, as above.*

**Key determinants.** Based on an analysis of variance, the main determinants of the CO₂ emissions reduction potential are the variation of the road gradients along the shortest path as well as the relative elevation of the source from the destination. *Source: arXiv:2306.01687, as above.*

**Speed optimization asymmetry.** Speed data estimates for rush hour in New York City were used to test CO₂ emissions reduction by comparing the greenest paths with optimized speeds against the fastest paths with traffic. While speed optimization on uphill arcs can significantly help CO₂ reduction, the potential to leverage gravity for acceleration on downhill arcs is limited due to traffic congestion. *Source: arXiv:2306.01687, as above.*

**Geographic scope.** Numerical experiments cover 25 major cities across 6 continents, benchmarking the CO₂ emissions reduction of dynamic speed and greenest path policies against policies that ignore elevation. *Source: arXiv:2306.01687, as above. Geographic scope corroborated at: https://sustainable.mit.edu/sustainable-transportation

**Methodology.** The team transitions from static to dynamic optimization by adapting a refined Comprehensive Modal Emission Model (CMEM), incorporating terrain elevations. *Source: https://sustainable.mit.edu/sustainable-transportation, MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab, 2023.*

**Publication status.** The paper was first submitted 2 June 2023 (v1) and last revised 30 May 2025 (v2), with a Related DOI linking to a journal publication at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00291-024-00793-9, indicating peer review and formal publication have advanced. *Source: arXiv:2306.01687, as above.*

**Scope and limitations.** The study focuses on urban routing with high-resolution geospatial data. Results are derived from numerical experiments, not live fleet deployments. Reduction potential is modelled, not measured from operational telematics. The study does not address highway-dominant long-haul corridors, multi-stop consolidation logic, intermodal handoffs, or driver compliance with algorithmically derived paths. For workspaces operating primarily on air with road as a secondary drayage mode, the findings apply specifically to the urban last-mile and port-drayage segments of the road operation, not to the primary air movement.

---

**Highway and long-haul corridors.** The study's scope is urban networks with geospatial data from major cities. *Analytical inference:* Long-haul highway corridors — relevant for overland movements between cities, airport-to-venue transfers over regional distances, or port-to-distribution-centre legs — are not addressed. Whether greenest-path deviation from shortest-path logic is material on relatively flat motorway networks is an open question the study does not answer.

**Multi-stop and consolidation routing.** The study addresses point-to-point greenest path, not vehicle routing problems with multiple stops. *Analytical inference:* For workspaces where road carriers make multi-stop deliveries of exhibition equipment, luxury retail replenishment, or event production kit, the interaction between stop sequencing and elevation-optimal routing is unresolved.

**Driver compliance and telematics validation.** The study is a modelled, algorithmic result. It does not address whether drivers follow algorithmically derived routes in practice, or how to measure and verify compliance. No measured fleet data from live deployments is cited in the source blocks.

**Intermodal handoffs.** The finding does not address how road-leg routing optimisation interacts with air or ocean schedule constraints at intermodal handoff points (airports, ports), which is the dominant operational context for workspaces where road is secondary.

**Commercial availability of CMEM-based tools.** The paper describes a research model; the source blocks do not identify a commercially available routing product built on this specific methodology. *Specific commercial product availability not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

**Related and converging research.** The Supply Chain Management Review article by Caplice & Velázquez-Martínez (2025), "Navigating the Road to Zero-Emission Trucking," is identified as a corroborating source at https://www.scmr.com/article/navigating-the-road-to-zero-emission-trucking and addresses zero-emission trucking strategy at the operational level. Its content was not available in the source blocks provided for this run and could not be span-grounded; it is surfaced under New Sources Identified as a high-priority retrieval target for a follow-on brief. *Specific [findings and operational implications from Caplice & Velázquez-Martínez 2025] not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

**Re-check window.** The v2 revision of arXiv:2306.01687 was posted 30 May 2025, suggesting active development. *Analytical inference:* A journal-publication follow-on with expanded results or a companion practitioner brief is plausible within 6–12 months of the v2 revision. Monitor over the next 6-12 months for a published journal version (Related DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00291-024-00793-9) and for any MIT CTL practitioner translation of the findings.

---

**Routing software procurement decisions.** *Operational implication:* Workspaces evaluating routing software for their contracted drayage or urban delivery carriers should now include elevation-aware path optimization as a selection criterion, not merely ETAs and distance. This is a specific, sourceable change to vendor evaluation criteria.

**Carrier dialogue.** *Analytical inference:* The finding provides a sourced basis for the workspace to ask contracted road carriers whether their dispatching software incorporates elevation-aware routing, and to flag the CO₂ reduction evidence as a reason this question is material. This is a low-friction, no-cost positioning move.

**CO₂ intensity per tonne-kilometre on road legs.** *Analytical inference:* If a contracted carrier adopts elevation-aware routing on urban legs, the CO₂ intensity figure reported under ISO 14083 or similar frameworks for those legs should decrease, improving the workspace's Scope 3 transport emissions disclosure. The magnitude is city- and gradient-specific and cannot be generalised from the study without carrier-specific modelling.

**Partial-load cargo verticals benefit most.** *Analytical inference:* Because the asymptotic optimum is reached at moderate payloads, workspaces handling fine art, luxury goods, or live event equipment — cargo that is typically high-value but partial-load — are in the payload range where the finding's reduction potential is maximal. This changes how the workspace should prioritise applying the finding: partial-load urban drayage is the highest-leverage scenario.

**What the finding does NOT change.** The finding does not support renegotiating carrier rates based on a claimed fuel saving, because reduction potential is modelled, not measured, and is city- and gradient-specific. It does not support marketing claims about the workspace's own carbon footprint unless the workspace can document that its contracted carrier is actually using elevation-aware routing. It does not affect air-mode decisions, ocean-mode decisions, or SAF procurement strategy.

---

**Road-mode CO₂ exposure.** *Analytical inference:* For workspaces where road is a secondary transport mode used for airport drayage, port-to-warehouse transfers, and urban delivery of high-value or time-sensitive cargo, road-segment emissions form part of the Scope 3 downstream transport emissions that clients and regulators increasingly request in granular form. The finding is directly relevant to that segment.

**The routing-vs.-speed insight is operationally actionable without new capital.** *Operational implication:* Unlike fleet electrification or SAF procurement, greenest-path routing and dynamic speed profiles operate through software and data — dispatch algorithm changes, not hardware investments. This positions the finding as a near-term, low-capital-intensity lever for road-mode CO₂ reduction. *Analytical inference:* For workspaces already using routing software for drayage and urban delivery legs, the incremental cost of adopting elevation-aware routing may be substantially lower than other decarbonization pathways.

**Payload at moderate commercial loads triggers asymptotic optimum.** *Operational implication:* The finding that the asymptotic greenest path is attained for a finite load — meaning moderate, not maximum, payloads — implies that road legs operating at typical commercial fill rates (not just near-maximum capacity) can realize near-optimal CO₂ reductions if elevation-aware routing is applied. This is relevant for workspaces handling cargo verticals (live events equipment, fine art, high-value automotive) where loads are often partial.

**Traffic congestion limits downhill gravity gains.** *Operational implication:* Urban operations in congested environments — characteristic of live event setups, luxury goods delivery to urban venues, or high-value automotive movements to city showrooms — face a structural constraint: the ability to use downhill gravity for free deceleration is reduced by stop-start traffic. Speed optimization benefit is therefore asymmetric and concentrated in uphill segments.

**Regulatory linkage — EU road transport decarbonization.** *Analytical inference:* The EU's CO₂ standards for heavy-duty vehicles (HDV Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 as amended) set fleet-average CO₂ targets for vehicle manufacturers and are a no-connection item at the fleet-operator level in their current form. However, emerging Scope 3 reporting frameworks (notably CSRD/ESRS and ISO 14083 for transport emissions) create a reporting obligation for shippers and logistics operators on the emissions of transport they procure. Greenest-path routing, if applied by the road carrier, reduces the Scope 3 figure the workspace must report. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether and how the workspace's specific reporting entity scope under CSRD triggers ISO 14083-aligned transport emissions quantification for drayage legs requires counsel and reporting-framework review.

**Regulatory linkage — US context.** *Analytical inference:* The US EPA's Clean Trucks Plan and California's Advanced Clean Trucks regulation impose fleet composition targets on vehicle manufacturers and, in California's case, fleets above threshold size. These do not directly regulate routing algorithms, but they create the broader regulatory context in which road-carrier CO₂ reduction — including routing efficiency — is commercially valued and increasingly procured. *Legal Confirmation Required:* California Advanced Clean Trucks applicability to any specific carrier contracted by the workspace requires carrier-level legal review.

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**
- "MIT CTL research published across 25 cities on 6 continents finds that elevation-aware routing — choosing the greenest path, not the shortest — can significantly reduce CO₂ on urban truck legs, with the benefit concentrated in cities with gradient variation and reaching near-optimal performance even at moderate payloads, not just maximum load."
- "We are reviewing whether our contracted road carriers use elevation-aware dispatch software, because this is one of the lower-capital CO₂ reduction levers available on drayage and urban delivery legs."
- "The research models CO₂ reduction potential — it doesn't replace measured telematics data. Any claim we make about actual CO₂ savings on road legs would need to come from carrier-reported actuals, not from the study alone."

**Questions to pose to clients:**
- "Do your sustainability KPIs currently capture road-leg emissions separately from air-mode emissions? If so, we can discuss what routing-level improvements your contracted carriers could report against."
- "For your urban delivery or exhibition setup legs, how granular does your Scope 3 reporting need to be — tonne-kilometre averages, or city-specific actuals?"

**Pitfalls to avoid:**
- Do not cite a specific percentage CO₂ reduction figure as applicable to the workspace's road operations — the study benchmarks across 25 cities and the reduction is gradient-specific. No general figure is defensible without city-level modelling.
- Do not represent the workspace as having implemented greenest-path routing unless a contracted carrier has confirmed this.
- Do not conflate this routing research with fleet electrification or SAF — they are separate levers; mixing them in a client brief invites credibility risk.

---

Velázquez Martínez from MIT Center for Transportation & Logistics. The reduction of fuel consumption has become increasingly more important as its price and volatility continue to rise. This objective aligns with the sustainable efforts to reduce CO2 pollution. Recent research has found that high-resolution elevation data reshapes the paths of diverse trucks for maximum fuel efficiency. Then, the greenest path swiftly departs from the shortest route, reaching its optimal state even with moderate payloads. Leveraging a refined Comprehensive Modal Emission Model (CMEM), we’ve transitioned from static to dynamic optimization, adapting to terrain elevations. In flat road networks, fuel efficiency aligns with the shortest route and constant speed. Introduce elevation changes, and the greenest path deviates, adapting its optimal speed dynamically. Also, the analysis identifies road gradient fluctuations and relative elevation as key factors shaping a sustainable future. This groundbreaking discovery reveals the greenest path converges to an asymptotic state with increasing payload, achieved remarkably with a finite load. Numerical experiments across 25 major cities on 6 continents showcase the CO2 reduction prowess of our dynamic speed and greenest path policies. Moradi, Poulad, Joachim Arts, and Josué Velázquez-Martínez. “Load Asymptotics and Dynamic Speed Optimization for the Greenest Path Problem: A Comprehensive Analysis.”  arXiv preprint arXiv:2306.01687  (2023). sections.md:
**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "The Carbon Trust is a UK-incorporated, financially independent (no-shareholder) climate consultancy established in 2001, with SBTi-validated Net Zero targets and over 2,796 organisations supported globally." (Grounded in sourced facts above.)
- "Their Supply Chain Standard is independently described as the world's first certification for supply-chain GHG emissions management — directly applicable to logistics providers." (Grounded in the Wikipedia source.)
- "Their Route to Net Zero Standard offers three tiers of independently verified certification, allowing a phased approach from initial action to full 1.5C alignment." (Grounded in the Carbon Trust Route to Net Zero Standard page.)
- "Their maritime work includes a study of alternative shipping fuel commercial readiness across the European context, Blue Visby co-founding, and Getting to Zero Coalition membership." (Grounded in the maritime decarbonisation source.)

**Questions to pose to clients:**
- Does your organisation's Scope 3 reporting framework specify which third-party verification standards it accepts for logistics provider emissions data?
- Is your organisation engaged with the Carbon Trust or an equivalent body for supply chain standard certification, and does that programme extend to freight providers?
- For ocean-mode shipments on European routes, are you tracking how your carriers' fuel mix will change under FuelEU Maritime, and do you need verified data to feed into your own CSRD disclosure?

**Pitfalls to avoid:**
- Do not claim that Carbon Trust certification automatically satisfies EU Green Claims Directive requirements — this is *Legal Confirmation Required* pending finalisation of the Directive's substantiation rules.
- Do not present the Carbon Trust's 17x efficiency figure for shipping vs air as an argument that ocean mode is "low carbon" in absolute terms — the same source flags that shipping represents ~3% of global CO2 and could reach 17% by 2050 if unchecked.
- Do not cite the 400-business Net Zero barriers survey with specific statistics unless you have read the full published report — the source blocks do not contain the granular findings.

---

| # | Title | Issuing Body | Type | URL |
|---|-------|-------------|------|-----|
| 1 | THE CARBON TRUST company overview | Companies House, GOV.UK | Tier 1 – Government register | https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/04190230 |
| 2 | Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024 | The Carbon Trust | Tier 4 – Organisation self-publication | https://publications.carbontrust.com/ |
| 3 | Carbon Trust – Wikipedia | Wikipedia | Tier 6 – Secondary encyclopaedic | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Trust |
| 4 | Route to Net Zero Standard | The Carbon Trust | Tier 4 – Organisation self-publication | https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/net-zero-transition-planning-and-delivery/route-to-net-zero-standard |
| 5 | Maritime Decarbonisation | The Carbon Trust | Tier 4 – Organisation self-publication | https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation |

---

This brief does not resolve:
- Whether the Carbon Trust's certifications — Route to Net Zero Standard, Supply Chain Standard, or product carbon footprint label — are accepted by any specific client's procurement or sustainability framework. Acceptance is client- and tender-specific.
- The fee structure, audit frequency, or contractual terms of Carbon Trust certification services. *Specific rate and contract information not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*
- How the Carbon Trust's PAS 2050-based product carbon footprint methodology compares to ISO 14067 or the GHG Protocol Product Standard for the purposes of CSRD-aligned Scope 3 reporting. This is an open methodological question with regulatory implications.
- The current status and findings of the Commercial Readiness of Alternative Shipping Fuels Study — the source block confirms its existence and scope but does not reproduce its findings.
- The specific philanthropic partners and programme designs under the Carbon Trust's philanthropic partnerships programme. *Specific partner names not available from the provided source block content at the time of this authoring pass.*

---

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating as freight forwarders across air, road, and ocean modes, the Carbon Trust's certification and advisory ecosystem sits at the intersection of three active regulatory and commercial pressures: Scope 3 emissions disclosure under frameworks such as CSRD and the GHG Protocol; product-level carbon footprint claims that clients in fast-moving consumer goods, food, and manufacturing verticals are beginning to attach to tender requirements; and maritime fuel transition obligations emerging from the IMO's revised GHG Strategy and FuelEU Maritime.

*Operational implication:* The Carbon Trust Supply Chain Standard is specifically designed for organisations measuring and reducing supply chain emissions, which is the precise scope a freight forwarder occupies on behalf of shipper clients. A workspace that can demonstrate alignment with or certification under this standard signals verified supply-chain emissions management to clients whose own sustainability reports depend on the quality of Scope 3 data flowing from logistics providers.

*Operational implication:* The Route to Net Zero Standard's three-tier structure (Taking Action → Advancing → Leading) is architecturally compatible with a phased adoption approach. A workspace at the Taking Action tier achieves an independently verified entry point without needing to have resolved science-based targets, while the Advancing and Leading tiers create a visible progression narrative for commercial relationships with sustainability-conscious clients.

*Operational implication:* The Carbon Trust's maritime work — including the Alternative Shipping Fuels Study, Blue Visby founding partnership, and Getting to Zero Coalition membership — positions it as a technically credible counterpart for ocean-mode decarbonisation conversations. For workspaces with ocean-tertiary exposure, this is a potential source of pre-competitive intelligence on alternative fuel readiness by route and vessel type.

*Analytical inference:* The Carbon Trust's stated finding that "nearly 60% of the technologies crucial for reaching Net Zero by 2050 haven't achieved commercial scale" (from the Impact Report) implies that client-facing claims about Net Zero transport solutions carry material greenwashing risk if not grounded in verified, certified pathways — reinforcing the operational case for third-party certification rather than self-declaration.

---

**Organisational status and structure.** The Carbon Trust is a UK-incorporated private company limited by guarantee (Company Number 04190230), registered active at Level 5, Arbor, 255 Blackfriars Road, London, England, SE1 9AX. *Source: THE CARBON TRUST overview, Companies House, GOV.UK, https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/04190230.

The Carbon Trust describes itself as having "no shareholders" and investing "profit back into enhancing the breadth and reach of our work." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024, The Carbon Trust, https://publications.carbontrust.com/.

The organisation reports 282+ experts, offices in 8 countries (UK, Netherlands, Germany, South Africa, Singapore, Mexico, and others), and work across 75 countries. It states it has supported 2,796+ organisations to date. *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024, The Carbon Trust, https://publications.carbontrust.com/.

**Certification products directly relevant to freight and supply chain.** The Carbon Trust operates several certification standards with operational relevance to the workspace:

- The **Carbon Trust Carbon Standard** certifies companies that measure and reduce their carbon emissions year on year. It was introduced in June 2008. *Source: Carbon Trust – Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Trust.
- The **Carbon Trust Supply Chain Standard**, launched in 2015, is described as "the world's first independent certification for organisations that are measuring, managing and reducing greenhouse gas (CO2e) emissions in their supply chains." *Source: Carbon Trust – Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Trust.
- The **Route to Net Zero Standard** is described as "the only certification that guides and supports your organisation on your journey towards Net Zero and climate leadership." It offers three certification tiers: Taking Action, Advancing, and Leading, with progressively more demanding requirements including science-aligned targets and 1.5C-aligned reductions. *Source: Route to Net Zero Standard, The Carbon Trust, https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/net-zero-transition-planning-and-delivery/route-to-net-zero-standard.
- The **Carbon Reduction Label** (product carbon footprint label), introduced in March 2007, covers embodied emissions of products and commits the label holder to reduce that footprint every two years. It is grounded in the PAS 2050 methodology, developed by the Carbon Trust in conjunction with BSI and Defra. *Source: Carbon Trust – Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Trust.

**Maritime decarbonisation programme.** The Carbon Trust's maritime work is directly relevant to ocean-mode operations. Key grounded facts:

- The Carbon Trust states that "shipping goods can be 17 times more efficient than air, and 10 times more efficient than road," while the sector "represents almost 3% of global CO2 emissions," citing the IMO's Fourth Greenhouse Gas Study 2020. *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust, https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation.
- There have been "projections that maritime shipping could account for 17% of total annual CO2 emissions by 2050, if left unchecked." *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust, https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation.
- The Carbon Trust produced a **Commercial Readiness of Alternative Shipping Fuels Study** that "assessed the merits and drawbacks of five alternative shipping fuels across each supply chain stage, with a focus on the European context." *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust, https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation.
- The Carbon Trust is a founding partner of **Blue Visby**, described as existing "to make shipping more sustainable by eradicating certain maritime practices to reduce a ship's carbon footprint," combining "technology with long-established maritime traditions of cost-sharing and collaboration." *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust, https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation.
- The Carbon Trust is a signatory to the **Getting to Zero Coalition** (Global Maritime Forum), which "brings together decision-makers and stakeholders from across the shipping and energy sectors." *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust, https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation.
- The Carbon Trust is an active member of the **Just Transition Maritime Task Force** under the United Nations Global Compact. *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust, https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation.

**Net Zero Intelligence Unit.** The Carbon Trust operates a dedicated Net Zero Intelligence Unit described as "a dedicated team focused on raising ambition, awareness and action on Net Zero by drawing on the Carbon Trust's 20 years of experience working with businesses, governments and financial institutions globally." Research output includes a survey of 400 businesses on Net Zero barriers, with findings covering internal business case and Scope 3 emissions. *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024, The Carbon Trust, https://publications.carbontrust.com/.

*Specific figures / conclusions from the 400-business survey not available in full from the provided source blocks at the time of this authoring pass.*

**SBTi-validated targets.** The Carbon Trust's own Net Zero targets have been validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). The organisation's published targets include: reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 50% by 2030 from a 2018 base year; reduce business travel emissions by 65% per FTE by 2030; ensure that by 2026 at least 56% of suppliers by emissions are covered by a science-based target; reach Net Zero and reduce absolute emissions by 90% by 2050 from a 2018 base year. *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024, The Carbon Trust, https://publications.carbontrust.com/.

**Philanthropic partnerships.** A Carbon Trust page titled "Philanthropic Partnerships" exists at https://www.carbontrust.com/our-work-and-impact/philanthropic-partnerships. The impact report names philanthropic organisations as a partner category. *Specific partner names and programme details not available from the provided source block content at the time of this authoring pass.*

**Product footprint certification.** A Standards Map entry for "Carbon Trust Product Footprint Certification" is noted at https://standardsmap.org/en/factsheet/7/overview. This aligns with the Carbon Reduction Label and PAS 2050-based product carbon footprint methodology described in the Wikipedia source. *Specific certification scope, fees, and scheme rules not available from the provided corroborating source block content at the time of this authoring pass.*

---

*Operational implication:* For workspaces currently managing Scope 3 emissions reporting manually or using carrier-provided data without independent verification, engagement with the Carbon Trust's footprinting and Supply Chain Standard services changes the evidentiary quality of emissions data available to clients — which in turn changes the workspace's position in sustainability-linked tender evaluations.

*Operational implication:* The Route to Net Zero Standard's independent verification component changes the claims the workspace can credibly make in client-facing materials. A self-declared Net Zero pathway and a Carbon Trust-certified pathway are not equivalent from a procurement or legal claims perspective; the distinction matters in jurisdictions with active greenwashing enforcement (notably the EU, under the Green Claims Directive currently in legislative process).

*Analytical inference:* The Carbon Trust's 2026 supplier engagement target (56% of suppliers by emissions covered by an SBTi target) is the organisation's own internal procurement benchmark; for a freight forwarding workspace, this signals that sophisticated climate-active clients will increasingly apply analogous supplier engagement thresholds to their logistics providers, with non-certified providers progressively filtered from approved lists.

*Analytical inference:* The Blue Visby founding partnership and Getting to Zero Coalition membership position the Carbon Trust as embedded in the pre-commercial maritime fuel transition ecosystem. For workspaces with ocean-mode exposure on European trade lanes specifically, the Carbon Trust's Alternative Shipping Fuels Study is a structured analytical input to procurement decisions about carrier selection as FuelEU Maritime blending requirements phase in from 2025.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether a Carbon Trust certification — Route to Net Zero Standard, Supply Chain Standard, or product carbon footprint label — satisfies the substantiation requirements of the EU Green Claims Directive (once finalised) for logistics-related sustainability claims made by a freight forwarder to clients requires legal review; the Carbon Trust's certification methodology and the Directive's substantiation standard are not confirmed as co-extensive in the source material available.

---

Arrange a free consultation What is the Route to Net Zero Standard? The Carbon Trust’s  Route to Net Zero Standard  helps organisations measure and manage their emissions, inform carbon reduction strategies, and align targets for the future – all with tailored advice from our trusted experts. Whether you’re just getting started or leading the way to Net Zero, we will independently verify your carbon reductions, and guide you in taking the next steps towards decarbonisation. We will provide all the support you need to clearly and confidently communicate your commitment to a global audience. Download brochure Image The Route to Net Zero will be challenging, but wherever you are on your journey, we have the expertise to help you succeed. Laura Timlin Delivery Director, the Carbon Trust   The Net Zero challenge We recognise that businesses are at different stages on their Net Zero journey; and will have different needs to turn their climate ambition into reality. Wherever you are on your journey, our expertise can guide you in answering key questions such as: How will we set the right targets?  Do we have the right financial and operational setup to achieve these targets? How will we know when we are making progress, and if we are on track? How can we communicate progress inside and outside of our organisation? How will we inspire people to trust that we will deliver on our climate ambition? That is why we’ve created the  Route to Net Zero Standard , helping organisations measure and manage their emissions, inform carbon reduction strategies, and align targets for the future.     Planning your route We have developed 3 certification tiers to guide you on your journey to Net Zero.  As you progress through the levels, the qualifying requirements become more challenging and cover more aspects of carbon management.  Our experts will guide you through the whole process, so you and your stakeholders can be confident that you are successfully meeting the targets needed to reach your Net Zero destination. and governments globally to decarbonise the transport sector. While shipping goods can be 17 times more efficient than air, and 10 times more efficient than road, figures suggest that the sector represents almost 3% of global CO2 emissions. 1 There have also been projections that maritime shipping could account for 17% of total annual CO2 emissions by 2050, if left unchecked.  That’s why we are working with the maritime transport industry to find practical solutions to carbon emissions, and share our knowledge and expertise. How we can help Strategic thinking We are delivering a Maritime Decarbonisation and Economy Strategy for South Hams District Council in Devon. This will help drive decarbonisation in the council’s marine sector and assess the economic opportunities that brings. Insight and analysis Our report – Roadmap for the Decarbonisation of the European Recreational Marine Craft Sector – provided a clear plan for policymakers and industry leaders to steer the sector towards decarbonisation. Meanwhile, our in-depth Commercial Readiness of Alternative Shipping Fuels Study assessed the merits and drawbacks of five alternative shipping fuels across each supply chain stage, with a focus on the European context. Partnership and collaboration We work with other organisations to bring about change to the shipping sector:  Just Transition Maritime Task Force We are a signatory to the United Nations Global Compact, which bills itself as ‘the world’s largest corporate sustainability initiative’. As part of this, we are an active member of the Just Transition Maritime Task Force, which aims to lead and coordinate efforts to work with governments, industry, workers and their representatives to ensure a safe and human-centred approach to achieving green shipping. Getting to Zero Coalition We are a signatory to the Global Maritime Forum’s coalition, which brings together decision-makers and stakeholders from across the shipping and energy sectors. Blue Visby Solution  We are a founding partner of Blue Visby, which exists to make shipping more sustainable by eradicating certain maritime practices to reduce a ship's carbon footprint. The Blue Visby Solution combines technology with long-established maritime traditions of cost-sharing and collaboration.    1.    Fourth Greenhouse Gas Study 2020 (imo.org) Find out more and speak to one of our experts Contact us to find out more about how we can help organisations and governments to decarbonise the transport sector. Find sources:   "Carbon Trust"  –  news   · newspapers   · books   · scholar   · JSTOR ( June 2013 ) ( Learn how and when to remove this message ) The Carbon Trust Company type Not for Dividend Private Company Limited by Guarantee Industry Carbon management and reduction Founded March 2001 ; 25 years ago  ( 2001-03 ) in London , United Kingdom Headquarters London , United Kingdom Number of locations 7 Key people Michael Rea (CEO) Baroness Brown of Cambridge (Chair) Number of employees 400+ Website carbontrust .com The Carbon Trust is a consultancy established in March 2001, with offices across the world. Its aim is to accelerate the pace of private and public sectors decarbonisation and increase energy efficiency in organisations worldwide. The Carbon Trust was originally funded by around £50m of UK tax revenue generated from the Climate Change Levy (CCL), a tax on business energy use. The Carbon Trust's initial goal was to help businesses reduce energy costs and therefore offset the additional cost of paying the CCL. The establishment of the Carbon Trust was announced in the 2000 UK White Paper "Climate Change - the UK Programme" (Cmd 4913). [ 1 ] The Carbon Trust was conceived as a business-led, publicly funded organisation operating at arm's length from the UK government. [ 2 ] The early concept, design, and governance were carried out in close consultation with business. Senior officials from the Devolved Administrations and the UK department (the Department of the Environment, Transport and the Regions) would sit on the Trust's Board, where non-business non-executive Directors were in the majority. However, the chair, CEO and most of the executive team were appointed from the private sector, most notably the oil and gas and management consultancy sectors. Founding CEO Tom Delay previously worked at Shell for 16 years before beginning his 22-year tenure as CEO of the trust. In July 2023, Delay announced his retirement from his role as CEO of the Carbon Trust. [ 3 ] In January 2024, the Carbon Trust appointed Chris Stark , former head of the UK Climate Change Committee , as CEO, with Stark's term beginning in Spring 2024. [ 4 ] Stark resigned after three months to take up a role in government and was replaced by COO Michael Rea. Remit and initial programmes [ edit ] Source: [ 5 ] [ 6 ] The Trust began its work with three core activities: [ 7 ] To ensure that UK business and the public sector contribute fully to meeting ongoing targets for greenhouse gas emissions. To improve the competitiveness of UK business through resource efficiency; and To support the development of a UK industry sector that capitalises on the innovation and commercial value of low carbon technologies nationally and internationally. The need to recycle CCL revenues back to business by reducing energy costs through energy efficiency was a key early driver of the Carbon Trust's work. Its first act was to take over the UK government's £17m pa Energy Efficiency Best Practice Programme (EEBPP) in 2002, [ 8 ] a UK-wide information-based measure providing independent advice and support on existing energy efficient technologies and energy management practices. The Trust reconfigured the EEBPP to improve its focus and services to business under a new branding called "Action Energy". The Carbon Trust also initiated work on new and emerging low carbon technologies using a range of programmes and measures including traditional research, development, and demonstration support to supporting early stage companies developing new technologies and practices. These activities came under the banner of the "Low Carbon Innovation Programme". Current work [ edit ] The Carbon Trust is a global organisation, with offices in Mexico, the Netherlands, Germany, Singapore, South Africa and the UK. Services [ edit ] The Carbon Trust provides sustainability education to businesses to help them save energy, [ 9 ] as well as voluntary carbon certification services and carbon labelling schemes that verify carbon footprint data and companies' adherence to standards. It also works with governments and corporations on low carbon technologies, [ 10 ] including offshore wind and marine energy. [ 11 ] Carbon footprinting, verification and Carbon Trust standard [ edit ] Carbon Trust standards [ edit ] The Carbon Trust runs a series of environmental standards that certify measurement and reduction. Currently, these cover carbon, water and waste and have been awarded to hundreds of leading companies and organisations across the world. In June 2008 the Carbon Trust introduced the Carbon Trust Carbon Standard to address what it describes as business greenwash . [ 12 ] The Carbon Trust Carbon Standard is only awarded to companies and organisations who measure and reduce their carbon emissions year on year. [ 13 ] Examples of organisations who have held the Carbon Standard include Sky , Aldi , Eurotunnel , Bupa , PricewaterhouseCoopers , Samsung Electronics , Angus Council , Capital & Regional , O2 , npower , Credit Suisse and the Scottish Government . In February 2013 the Carbon Trust introduced the Carbon Trust Water Standard to recognise those companies reducing their water use year on year. The first four companies to receive the Water Standard were Sainsbury's , Coca-Cola , Sunlight Services Group and Branston. [ 14 ] In July 2013 the Carbon Trust introduced the Carbon Trust Waste Standard. [ 15 ] In November 2013 the waste standard was awarded to the first wave of organisations, which included The Football Association , Renishaw , Whitbread , PricewaterhouseCoopers and AkzoNobel Decorative Paints. These last three became the first in the world to gain the triple crown of reaching the carbon, water and waste standard. In 2015, the Carbon Trust launched the Carbon Trust Supply Chain Standard to look at carbon footprints across the supply chain. [ 16 ] It is the world's first independent certification for organisations that are measuring, managing and reducing greenhouse gas (CO2e) emissions in their supply chains. Carbon footprint label [ edit ] The Carbon Trust helps companies to measure the carbon emissions associated with their products ( embodied emissions ) and also provides a label for these products carbon footprint . Measuring the embodied emissions of products enables reductions to be identified and achieved across the supply chain. The label demonstrates a commitment by the product owner to reduce that footprint every two years. The Carbon Reduction Label was introduced in March 2007. [ 17 ] Examples of products that have featured the carbon footprint label are Amazon Devices, Evian water, Tetra Pak packaging, Kingsmill bread, Quorn foods, Silver Spoon sugar, Walkers crisps, a range of own brand products in Tesco supermarkets, Halifax ( HBOS ) bank accounts, Dyson airblades, Marshalls building products, Quaker oats , Lafarge cement, and Pompeian Olive Oil. The standards behind carbon labelling are now formally recognised through the PAS 2050 developed by the Carbon Trust in conjunction with BSI and Defra . This methodology is now gaining international acceptance following its launch in October 2008. [ 18 ] However, currently [ when? ] this standard has been revised to the PAS 2050: 2011 version, but the Carbon Trust has not received UKAS accreditation. sections.md:
### India as a Structural High-Cost Logistics Environment

*Analytical inference:* India's 13% logistics cost-to-GDP ratio (vs. global norms) means that workspaces routing cargo through India — whether for origin/destination or transshipment — face a structurally higher road freight cost base than equivalent lanes through more logistics-efficient markets. This is not a temporary spike; it reflects infrastructure, fragmentation, and fuel-dependency conditions that policy is now actively targeting but has not yet resolved.

### The Port Capacity Trajectory and Its Relevance to Ocean-Routed Cargo

India's Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 targets expansion of port capacity from the current 2,500 MMTPA to more than 10,000 MMTPA, supported by hydrogen and ammonia hubs, carbon-neutral operations, and shore power at all major ports.

*Source: ICCT, "Three policies," op. cit. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

*Analytical inference:* For workspaces routing ocean freight through Indian gateway ports, this capacity trajectory is a 20-year infrastructure signal, not a near-term operational change. The more immediately relevant signal is the Harit Sagar 2030 renewable energy target for ports, which may begin affecting port-side operational costs and green-lane eligibility for sustainability-reporting purposes within the workspace's planning horizon.

### Trucks and Freight as a Decarbonization Priority

Medium and heavy-duty trucks are responsible for 44% of India's transport GHG emissions despite comprising just 3% of vehicles on the road.

*Source: ICCT, "Three policies," op. cit. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

*Analytical inference:* This concentration of emissions in a small vehicle population is exactly the policy logic that has driven PM e-DRIVE's extension to trucks (July 2025) and will likely drive increasingly mandatory fuel-efficiency and ZET targets. Workspaces with Scope 3 emissions reporting obligations (CSRD, or client-facing carbon disclosure) should monitor Indian road freight's GHG intensity as a material contributor to reported transport emissions on India-originating lanes.

---

### Logistics Cost as a Share of GDP

India's logistics costs stand at approximately 13% of GDP, far exceeding the global average.

*Source: "India's transport transformation: Three policies to shape the road ahead," ICCT / Hindustan Times, September 15, 2025. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

At the corporate level, logistics spending runs at 10–15% of company expenses for transporting goods to and from factories.

*Source: "Accelerating India's Freight Decarbonization," WRI India, 2026. https://wri-india.org/initiatives/accelerating-indias-freight-decarbonization

*Operational implication:* For workspaces moving high-value or time-sensitive cargo by road within India, this structural cost burden is a margin-compression risk that is built into every lane, not episodic. The gap between India's logistics cost share and the global average is not narrowing through market forces alone; it is a policy target, with fuel dependency identified as a primary driver.

### Fuel Consumption Baseline

India's trucking sector — 6.3 million trucks handling 70% of domestic freight — consumes 838 billion liters of diesel annually.

*Source: WRI India, op. cit. https://wri-india.org/initiatives/accelerating-indias-freight-decarbonization

*Specific current diesel retail price (INR/litre, national average, mid-2026) not available from primary sources as of this generation date.* Industrial and retail diesel pricing is subject to Government of India administered pricing mechanisms; current rate requires carrier-specific or fuel-data-specific sourcing.

### Electric Vehicle Baseline

India currently has only 869 electric medium- and heavy-duty freight vehicles in service as of the WRI India reporting date.

*Source: WRI India, op. cit. https://wri-india.org/initiatives/accelerating-indias-freight-decarbonization

*Operational implication:* For workspaces evaluating or tendering green freight contracts on India's road network, this baseline figure confirms that electric trucking capacity is negligible at present. Any client-facing green road freight commitment in India as of mid-2026 is aspirational, not operationally deliverable at scale.

### Industrial Electricity Rate, SAF Price, Port Handling, and Drayage

*Specific industrial electricity rate (INR/kWh), SAF price, port handling tariff, and drayage cost not available from primary sources provided as of this generation date.* These figures require sourcing from CERC (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission), DGCA, or major port authority tariff schedules. They are research gaps for this brief; see Section 8 (Pending Changes) for port-sector trajectory data that is sourced.

---

MONITORING — Re-check window: Q1 2027

### PM e-DRIVE Scheme for Electric Trucks

**Status:** Guidelines released July 2025 by the Ministry of Heavy Industries. Scheme is active for electric buses, two-wheelers, and three-wheelers; truck guidelines are the new extension.

**Design intent:** Reduce upfront cost of electric truck acquisition, strengthen domestic manufacturing of heavy-duty batteries and charging systems, improve air quality on highway corridors.

**Participants/parties:** Ministry of Heavy Industries (issuing authority), Indian OEMs, fleet operators, NITI Aayog (policy coordination).

**Current phase:** Guidelines issued; scheme implementation and disbursement mechanics are in active rollout as of July 2025.

**What it is investigating:** Whether incentive support can catalyze commercial ZET adoption at scale in the absence of mandatory ZET targets.

*Source: ICCT, "Three policies," op. cit. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

*Analytical inference:* The scheme's effectiveness will depend on uptake rates and the gap between incentive levels and actual TCO premiums, which are not yet publicly available. Re-check recommended at Q1 2027 when first disbursement data and fleet operator responses should be reportable.

### BEE Fuel Efficiency Standards for Commercial Vehicles

**Status:** The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) has released draft fuel-efficiency regulations for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty vehicles; finalization is in progress as of September 2025.

**Design intent:** Require automakers to achieve fleet-wide average fuel consumption targets for commercial vehicles; create regulatory backbone for efficiency alongside ZET transition.

*Source: ICCT, "Three policies," op. cit. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

*Specific finalization date for BEE HDV fuel-efficiency regulations not available from primary sources as of this generation date.*

*Analytical inference:* These standards, once finalized, will define the minimum efficiency floor for new commercial vehicles sold in India. For workspaces specifying fleet standards in carrier contracts or green logistics tenders, finalization of these norms creates a contractual reference point. Estimated finalization window: 2026–2027 based on typical BEE rulemaking timelines, but this is an analytical inference, not a sourced date. MONITORING.

### Bharat ZET Policy Advisory — 30 Targeted Interventions

**Status:** Published. WRI India worked with the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India and CoEZET, IIT Madras to develop India's first national-level ZET policy roadmap, covering 30 targeted interventions across incentives, regulation, infrastructure, financing, and stakeholder engagement.

**Participants/parties:** Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser (Government of India), CoEZET IIT Madras, WRI India (technical partner), ministries, state governments, industry players.

**Current phase:** Advisory published; recommendations are informing national policy conversation and driving coordinated action across ministries.

*Source: WRI India, op. cit. https://wri-india.org/initiatives/accelerating-indias-freight-decarbonization

*Analytical inference:* The Bharat ZET Advisory's 30 interventions represent the policy architecture that will shape India's mandatory ZET regulatory trajectory. Workspaces should monitor which of the 30 interventions are adopted into binding regulation vs. remaining advisory, as the mandatory vs. voluntary line directly affects carrier contract requirements and Scope 3 reporting obligations.

### Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 and Harit Sagar Green Port Guidelines

**Status:** Published policy framework. Targets: 60% renewable energy at ports by 2030, 90% by 2047; half of port equipment electrified by 2030, 90% by 2047; shore power at all major ports by 2047; CO₂ intensity per ton of cargo reduced by more than 70% by 2047; port capacity expansion from 2,500 MMTPA to 10,000+ MMTPA.

*Source: ICCT, "Three policies," op. cit. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

*Specific implementing authority, enforcement mechanism, and penalty structure for Harit Sagar non-compliance not available from primary sources as of this generation date.* Legal Confirmation Required on binding status.

---

### What the Workspace Can Credibly Say

- India's road freight sector accounts for 44% of transport GHG emissions and 70% of domestic freight movement, making it the highest-priority decarbonization lever in the country's net-zero 2070 pathway. The workspace can cite this structure accurately when positioning India-specific sustainability programs.
- India currently has fewer than 900 electric medium- and heavy-duty trucks in service nationally. Any client expecting green road freight in India at scale in the near term should be advised that the operational baseline does not yet support it.
- India's port sector has published a credible long-range sustainability roadmap (Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047, Harit Sagar Guidelines), with 2030 milestones for renewable energy and equipment electrification. This is legitimate policy direction the workspace can reference, with the caveat that it is a target framework, not current operational reality.

### What the Workspace Should Not Claim

- Do not claim that India ZET capacity is commercially available for client freight contracts. The 869-vehicle baseline and infrastructure gap mean this is aspirational, not contractually deliverable at scale.
- Do not cite the Harit Sagar Guidelines as binding regulation on port operators without Legal Confirmation. Their enforcement status requires counsel review.
- Do not present logistics-cost improvement forecasts as near-term — the 13% of GDP figure reflects structural conditions that policy is targeting but has not resolved.

### Questions to Pose to Clients

- Does your sustainability reporting require Scope 3 data for India-origin road freight? If so, the workspace should discuss the current absence of standardized carrier-level GHG reporting and the gap between BS VI compliance (a floor) and full carbon accounting.
- Is your India freight volume concentrated in Gujarat, Rajasthan, or Maharashtra? If so, the workspace can discuss early ZET pilot proximity.

---

### Road Freight — Diesel Fleet

FACT: Diesel-powered HDVs operating in India are subject to Bharat Stage VI (BS VI) emission standards, which the ICCT describes as a "leapfrog from Euro IV to Euro VI" for heavy-duty vehicles. BS VI aligns PM, NOx, and particle number (PN) limits with European Euro VI standards and includes OBD and real-driving emissions (PEMS) provisions.

*Source: "India Bharat Stage VI Emission Standards (Policy Update)," ICCT, June 2021. https://theicct.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/India-BS-VI-Policy-Update-vF.pdf [New source — see New Sources Identified table]

*Operational implication:* Carrier fleets tendering road freight capacity to the workspace on Indian lanes should be operating BS VI vehicles. Workspaces tendering green freight contracts or responding to Scope 3 client data requests should confirm BS VI compliance status with road carriers as a baseline data point.

### Electric Truck Pilots

Early electric truck pilots have been facilitated in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra through the e-FAST India platform.

*Source: WRI India, op. cit. https://wri-india.org/initiatives/accelerating-indias-freight-decarbonization

*Analytical inference:* These three states represent India's early ZET pilot geography. Workspaces with logistics nodes in these states are in the highest-probability corridors for early commercial ZET availability from fleet operators, but the timeline to commercial scale remains uncertain given the 869-vehicle national baseline.

### On-Site Solar and Port Shore Power

India's Harit Sagar Green Port Guidelines target over 60% renewable energy use at ports by 2030 and 90% by 2047, and electrification of half of port equipment by 2030 and 90% by 2047.

*Source: ICCT, "Three policies," op. cit. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

*Analytical inference:* Shore power at Indian ports is in the policy-roadmap phase, not yet operationally available at scale. The Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 states the ambition of shore power at all major ports by 2047; the 2030 renewable energy targets for ports are directional milestones, not yet confirmed operational capabilities.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether the Harit Sagar Green Port Guidelines constitute binding regulatory obligations on port operators or remain advisory framework targets requires counsel review of the issuing authority's implementing instruments.

---

MONITORING

### ZET Early-Mover Positioning

Industry commitments secured under e-FAST India total 7,750 e-trucks, raised at the Clean Energy Ministerial.

*Source: WRI India, op. cit. https://wri-india.org/initiatives/accelerating-indias-freight-decarbonization

*Analytical inference:* These commitments represent the committed-demand side of the ZET market, concentrated among the 90 industry partners and 22 knowledge partners of e-FAST India. Workspaces not currently in the e-FAST network are outside the primary demand-aggregation and early-pilot access channel in India. Competitors who have joined e-FAST or committed volumes gain preferential positioning with OEMs and fleet operators piloting ZETs.

*Specific named competitors and their ZET or e-FAST positioning not available from primary sources as of this generation date.* Competitive positioning at the named-company level is a research gap requiring trade-press sourcing.

### PM e-DRIVE Scheme — Access Window

In July 2025, the Ministry of Heavy Industries released guidelines for electric trucks under the PM e-DRIVE scheme.

*Source: ICCT, "Three policies," op. cit. https://theicct.org/indias-transport-transformation-three-policies-to-shape-the-road-ahead-sep25/

*Analytical inference:* The PM e-DRIVE scheme's extension to trucks represents a subsidy-access window. Fleet operators and logistics companies who engage early with scheme eligibility criteria gain preferential access to incentive-supported ZET acquisition. Workspaces tendering India road freight contracts with multi-year terms should consider whether carrier ZET adoption plans are anchored to PM e-DRIVE eligibility, as this affects the credibility of green fleet transition timelines offered in commercial proposals.

---

### Diesel vs. Electric Trucking — India

The high upfront cost of electric trucks, coupled with limited charging infrastructure, remains a significant roadblock to ZET adoption in India.

*Source: WRI India, op. cit. https://wri-india.org/initiatives/accelerating-indias-freight-decarbonization

*Specific TCO breakeven or payback period figures for electric vs. diesel trucks in India not available from primary sources as of this generation date.* WRI India's Financial Impact Assessment for Zero-Emission Trucks (Fi-ZET) is cited in WRI India's own materials as a relevant resource; its specific figures are not reproduced in the source block provided and cannot be stated as FACT here. Fi-ZET is listed under New Sources Identified for retrieval.

*Analytical inference:* With fuel making up a large portion of trucking costs and logistics costs running at 13% of GDP, the economic case for electric trucks on high-utilization corridors (fuel savings offsetting capital premium) mirrors the pattern China has already demonstrated, but India's charging infrastructure gap and fragmented ownership model (owner-operators, not large fleet operators) create structural barriers that slow the breakeven calculation relative to Chinese or European comparators.

### Manual vs. Automated Freight Operations

*No sourced cost-comparison data for manual vs. automated freight handling in Indian warehousing or distribution was available in the source blocks provided as of this generation date.* This is a research gap.

---

Blog India’s transport transformation: Three policies to shape the road ahead September 15, 2025 This piece was originally published in the Hindustan Times . Transportation emissions account for nearly 25% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. In India, the sector contributes almost 14% of the country’s CO₂ emissions, with about 90% coming from road transport. Given India’s commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2070, decarbonizing road transportation is both urgent and essential. India today stands at a remarkable turning point in its mobility journey. For decades, transport meant traffic congestion, high logistics costs, and patchy connectivity. But a quiet revolution is underway. Transport is no longer seen as a background sector—it is becoming a central pillar in India’s ambition to become a developed economy, a Viksit Bharat, by 2047 , while meeting its net-zero target by 2070. Globally, countries that have transformed their transport systems have unlocked not just economic efficiency but also growth, sustainability, and competitiveness. India has the same opportunity—if it makes the right choices now. Three recent policy moves have the potential to transform India’s transport landscape, offering a blueprint for a cleaner, more efficient, and future-ready system. 1. Electrifying trucks Transport accounts for 14% of India’s GHG emissions, with medium and heavy-duty trucks responsible for 44% of that share—despite comprising just 3% of vehicles on the road. India’s logistics costs, at about 13% of GDP, far exceed the global average. With 70% of freight moving by road and fuel making up a large portion of costs, electrifying trucks is both an environmental and economic imperative. In July 2025, the Ministry of Heavy Industries released guidelines for electric trucks under the PM e-DRIVE scheme —a vital first step in transitioning India’s trucking sector toward a cleaner and more atma-nirbhar (self-reliant) future. Until now, the spotlight has been on electric buses, two-wheelers, and three-wheelers. By supporting electric trucks, e-DRIVE addresses three challenges at once: Reducing logistics costs through lower fuel dependency. Strengthening domestic manufacturing of advanced EV technologies such as heavy-duty batteries and charging systems. Improving air quality along highways and in cities, with health benefits for millions. China has already demonstrated how electrifying freight can transform supply chains. India now has the chance to leapfrog the diesel-dependent model and build a greener logistics backbone. 2. Improving fuel efficiency The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) has proposed Phase 3 and 4 of the Corporate Average Fuel Efficiency (CAFE) norms for passenger cars, and they are currently under finalization. Additionally, BEE has released draft fuel-efficiency regulations for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty vehicles—regulations with immense potential to reshape the road transport sector. Fuel economy standards form the regulatory backbone of efficiency. They require automakers to achieve fleet-wide average fuel consumption targets, while providing flexibility in how to meet them—whether through advanced engine technologies or accelerated EV adoption. Without strong fuel economy standards, India risks drifting toward fuel-guzzling vehicles, weakening fleet efficiency, raising emissions, and deepening dependence on imported oil. This creates a vicious cycle of higher costs and energy insecurity. Finalizing CAFE for cars and fuel-efficiency standards for commercial vehicles will provide manufacturers long-term clarity and direction, paving the way for cleaner vehicles across the Indian market. 3. Expanding beyond road transport India’s Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 sets an ambitious agenda for transforming the shipping and port sector into a globally competitive, sustainable system. It envisions expanding port capacity from 2,500 million metric tonnes per annum (MMTPA) today to more than 10,000 MMTPA, supported by world-class infrastructure, digital innovation, hydrogen and ammonia hubs, carbon-neutral operations, and shore power at all major ports by 2047. The vision also positions India among the top five global shipbuilding nations. Complementing this initiative, the Harit Sagar Green Port Guidelines provide a framework to shrink the environmental footprint of ports—targeting over 60% renewable energy use by 2030 and 90% by 2047, electrifying half of port equipment by 2030 and 90% by 2047, and reducing CO₂ intensity per ton of cargo handled by more than 70% by 2047. Together, these measures show India’s commitment to making maritime transport efficient, sustainable, and globally competitive. The road ahead India’s transport story is being rewritten. Today’s policy announcements will shape not only how we move tomorrow, but also how competitive India’s economy will be in a decarbonizing world. If implemented with urgency and foresight, the PM e-DRIVE scheme, fuel-efficiency regulations, and Maritime Vision 2047 can deliver far more than emissions reductions. They can lower logistics costs, create green jobs, strengthen energy security, and boost India’s global standing. This transformation of transportation is not just about reducing emissions or improving public health—it is about seizing a generational economic opportunity . A recent NITI Aayog report estimated that electric vehicles alone represent a $200 billion opportunity for India as the country moves toward achieving a 30% EV sales share by 2030. Add to this the multiplier effects of cleaner logistics, efficient ports, and world-class vehicle standards, and it is clear that transport modernization can unlock vast new avenues for investment, innovation, and industrial leadership. India can transform transportation from a long-standing challenge into one of its greatest strengths. The nation stands at the cusp of transformation—and the road to a Viksit Bharat, a developed India by 2047 , is being built right now. Accelerating India's Freight Decarbonization is a part of the Sustainable Cities program.  Contact Ankita Rajeshwari for media inquiries. India’s trucking industry—comprising 6.3 million trucks and handling 70% of domestic freight—is the backbone of the nation’s economy. However, it is also a major contributor to pollution, consuming 838 billion liters of diesel annually and emitting 120 million tCO₂e—nearly 60% of India’s ground transport emissions. Logistics costs remain high, with companies spending 10–15% of their expenses on transporting goods to and from factories.   Despite the urgent need for decarbonization, India has only 869 electric medium- and heavy-duty freight vehicles . The high upfront cost of electric trucks, coupled with limited charging infrastructure, remains a significant roadblock. While corporate sustainability goals are driving early adoption, large-scale electrification requires deeper structural changes. Additional barriers, including a fragmented industry, the absence of standardized contracts, and a lack of strong regulatory mandates, further slow progress.   Through several projects, WRI India works at the intersection of clean energy, logistics, and freight decarbonization — advancing zero-emission trucking through targeted policy design, real-world pilots, and cross-sector collaboration with government, fleet operators, OEMs, and financiers.   e-FAST In dia: Paving the Way for Zero-Emission F reight   Launched in 2022 by NITI Aayog, with WRI India as the lead partner, the Electric Freight Accelerator for Sustainable Transport (e-FAST India) platform is the first-of-its-kind platform to advance freight electrification.        Impact in Action 90 industry partners & 22 knowledge partners. Raising industry awareness and securing commitments for 7,750 e-trucks at the Clean Energy Ministerial. Expanding international collaboration through the launch of a freight decarbonization platform in Brazil. Facilitating early e-truck pilots in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra, placing freight electrification at the forefront of the industry’s agenda. By fast-tracking ZET adoption, e-FAST India not only supports India’s Net-Zero vision but also positions the country as a leader in zero-emission freight, inspiring global action in sustainable transport innovation.   Electrifying Mobility in Cities: Accelerating India’s E-Mobility Transition   The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), with NITI Aayog and WRI India, is leading a four-year GEF-funded project to drive India’s shift to electric mobility. Key components include scaling zero-emission trucks (ZETs) through financing models, developing a sustainable battery ecosystem, piloting e-mobility solutions, and ensuring a just transition for workers and MSMEs. The project strengthens policy, finance, and infrastructure to enable a low-carbon, inclusive transport system. By addressing adoption barriers, it supports India’s climate goals and positions the country as a leader in sustainable mobility innovation.   Bharat ZET Policy Advisory: Shaping India’s Zero-Emission Trucking Future   WRI India worked closely with the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India and CoEZET, IIT Madras to shape the Bharat Zero Emission Trucking (ZET) Policy Advisory — India’s first national-level roadmap of interventions required decarbonize the trucking sector. As a technical partner, WRI India supported the development of the advisory’s 30 targeted interventions across incentives, regulation, infrastructure, financing, and stakeholder engagement. These recommendations inform the national conversation on freight electrification and are helping drive coordinated action across ministries, state governments, and industry players.   Read the Bharat ZET Policy Advisory   Additional Resources:    Decarbonizing India’s Road Freight   Assessing the Viability of Using Autorickshaws for Urban Freight Delivery in India   Accelerating Freight Electrification in India   More Related Sustainable Cities Fi-ZET: Powering India’s Transition to Electric Freight Perspectives March 16, 2026 Sustainable Cities Financing Electric Medium- and Heavy-Duty Vehicles in India Research February 17, 2026 Sustainable Cities Financial Impact Assessment for Zero-Emission Trucks (Fi-ZET) Research August 14, 2025 Energy The Future Electricity Grid Research May 1, 2016 Media Contacts Ankita Rajeshwari Senior Communications Manager - Sustainable Cities & Transport Featured Experts Sharvari Patki Program Head - Electric Mobility Garima Agrawal Senior Program Manager - Electric Mobility Chandana K Senior Program Associate - Sustainable Cities & Transport Stay Informed Email Footer menu - main Programs Research Perspectives What’s New Footer menu - secondary Our Work Programs Food, Land and Water Climate Energy Sustainable Cities Footer menu - Additional Contact About 15 Years of WRI India Our Approach Resources Events Privacy Policy Whistleblower Policy Cookie Preferences Terms of Use WRI India 1st Floor, Godrej & Boyce Premises, Gasworks Lane, Lalbaug, Parel Mumbai 400012, India PHONE: +91 22 24713591 2nd Floor, No. 93/2, G Towers, South End Road, Basavanagudi, Bengaluru 560004, India PHONE: +91 80 4890 8806 LGF, AADI, 2 Balbir Saxena Marg, Hauz Khas, New Delhi 110016, India PHONE: +91 11 20904223 Social menu Linkedin Instagram Youtube X Spotify © 2026 WRI India
