sections.md:
**Primary driver — MPA (Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore)**

MPA developed the Blueprint "in consultation with industry partners" and committed to spending "at least $300 million to support initiatives outlined in the Blueprint." *Source: COS 2022 Media Factsheet, MPA, 09 March 2022. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/cos-2022---media-factsheet---maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint-working-towards-2050

MPA's stated strategic interest is to "strengthen our value proposition as a leading global hub port and international maritime centre." *Source: MPA Blueprint overview page, MPA, accessed 2026. https://mpa.gov.sg/maritime-singapore/sustainability/maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint

*Analytical inference:* MPA is acting as a competitive national infrastructure authority, not simply a regulator. The $300 million commitment is an infrastructure bet that Singapore retains bunkering and transshipment dominance as the fuel mix shifts from HSFO/VLSFO to methanol, ammonia, and future net-zero fuels. This is a sovereign interest play with commercial implications for every carrier, shipper, and forwarder that uses Singapore as a hub.

**Execution vehicle — GCMD (Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation)**

The GCMD was "launched on 1 August 2021" as "a non-profit organisation that supports the decarbonisation of the maritime sector through pilots and trials," with founding "support of industry partners, alongside funding from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) for qualifying research and development programmes." The GCMD has "expanded its ecosystem to include more than 130 centre- and project-level partners." *Source: About GCMD, GCMD, accessed 2026. https://www.gcformd.org/about-us/

*Analytical inference:* GCMD functions as MPA's operational arm for pre-commercial testing: it co-funds pilots "that lack immediate commercial viability," provides "a neutral platform for collaboration" across nominal competitors, and works "closely with governments and regulators to develop sandboxes for such trials." For workspaces evaluating green-shipping credentials, GCMD participation or GCMD-piloted solutions are the proximate access point to Singapore's decarbonisation infrastructure.

**Industry signal — methanol bunkering EOI**

MPA received 50 submissions in response to its expression of interest for methanol marine fuel supply, with "over 60 regional and international companies comprising energy companies, fuel suppliers, traders, bunker operators, and storage companies" participating. Approximately 40% proposed "end-to-end solutions covering all three areas highlighted in the EOI." On aggregate, the proposals "have the potential to supply over one MTPA of low-carbon methanol by 2030." *Source: Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping, MPA, 17 April 2024. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/singapore-gears-up-to-meet-net-zero-needs-of-shipping

*Analytical inference:* Sixty-plus companies submitting commercial methanol supply proposals — with several projects already past Final Investment Decision — is a credible leading indicator that Singapore's multi-fuel bunkering transition is commercially, not just aspirationally, in motion. The workspace should treat the methanol supply pathway as a real option for carrier partners, not a speculative future state.

**Bilateral corridor partner — Australia**

The Singapore–Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor (GDSC) "was formalised in March 2024 through a memorandum of understanding." MPA and Australia's DITRDCSA are jointly leading the GDSC, with four Australian port authorities currently involved: Fremantle Ports Authority, Pilbara Ports Authority, Ports Victoria, and Gladstone Ports Corporation. *Source: Singapore and Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor – Factsheet 2025, DFAT/MPA, 2025. https://www.dfat.gov.au/trade-and-investment/singapore-and-australia-green-and-digital-shipping-corridor-factsheet-2025

**International alignment — IMO and IEA**

At MEPC 80, Singapore "worked actively with the IMO and other Member States to forge consensus in the adoption of the 2023 Strategy for the Reduction of GHG emissions from ships." MPA and the International Energy Agency (IEA) signed an MoU on the Energy Transition of the Maritime and Port Industries at the conference, supporting "the development of the IEA Regional Cooperation Centre to be hosted by Singapore." *Source: Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping, MPA, 17 April 2024. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/singapore-gears-up-to-meet-net-zero-needs-of-shipping

---

**Singapore's position versus competing hubs:**

*Analytical inference:* Singapore is acting as a first-mover among major bunkering hubs in constructing a multi-fuel infrastructure framework with sovereign backing. The $300 million Blueprint commitment, the GCMD's 130+ partner ecosystem, and the methanol EOI's 60+ company responses together represent a concentration of investment that competing hubs (Rotterdam, Fujairah, Port Klang) have not matched in a single sovereign-coordinated document as of the sourced content. Workspaces routing cargo through Singapore gain access to this emerging multi-fuel bunkering capability ahead of hubs that have not made equivalent commitments.

**Named competitor activity:**

No specific competitor freight forwarder positioning at Singapore was available in the sourced content. *Specific competitor freight forwarder activity at Singapore's green bunkering infrastructure not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

*Industry interpretation:* Major ocean carriers that have publicly ordered methanol-capable or ammonia-ready vessels — and whose vessel deployment intersects Singapore call patterns — will be the first to benefit from and market green bunkering capability at Singapore. Freight forwarders that have preferred-carrier relationships with these operators can credibly include Singapore multi-fuel access in client-facing sustainability claims before the infrastructure is universally available. Those without such relationships cannot.

**SRS green ship incentive:**

The Blueprint targets "50% of the SRS fleet to be green ships by 2050." *Source: COS 2022 Media Factsheet, MPA, 09 March 2022. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/cos-2022---media-factsheet---maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint-working-towards-2050 *Analytical inference:* Shippers and forwarders whose cargo moves on Singapore-registered vessels have a direct interest in the SRS green ship incentive structure: as MPA develops recognition and incentive programmes for green SRS vessels, selection of SRS-flagged, green-certified carriers may carry preferential port cost treatment that downstream forwarders can pass on.

---

**Action 1 — Map Singapore-transiting ocean legs against Blueprint focus areas.**
For every trade lane that calls Singapore as a primary or transshipment port, identify which carrier operates the vessel, whether that carrier has methanol-capable or dual-fuel vessels in rotation, and what their CII trajectory looks like. This is a data-collection exercise that positions the workspace for client RFPs that include green-shipping criteria. The 2030 harbour craft transition target means Singapore port costs may shift before the next contract renewal cycle.

**Action 2 — Brief commercial teams on the methanol EOI result.**
The 50-submission EOI result and the 1 MTPA demand projection are credible, sourced commercial signals — not aspirational policy. Commercial teams can use these facts in client conversations about Asia-Pacific ocean sustainability options without overclaiming. Set a watch for MPA's publication of the methanol bunkering regulatory framework, which the EOI process was designed to inform.

**Action 3 — Track the IMO mid-term measures adoption window (Q4 2025).**
The GHG pricing mechanism and fuel standard are the single most consequential regulatory trigger for Singapore-transiting freight costs. Set a calendar re-check for Q4 2025. If the mechanism is adopted, it converts from a MONITORING item to a COST ALERT requiring carrier surcharge clause review in existing freight contracts.

**Action 4 — Evaluate GDSC as a corridor intelligence asset for Australia-lane clients.**
For workspaces handling cargo on Singapore–Australia trade lanes, the GDSC's operationalisation — particularly the Pilbara and Gladstone bunkering standards workstreams — is the most concrete near-term green corridor development in the region. Establishing a data feed from DFAT and MPA's GDSC updates costs nothing and gives the workspace forward visibility to offer clients. Visit https://www.dfat.gov.au/trade-and-investment/singapore-and-australia-green-and-digital-shipping-corridor-factsheet-2025 for current factsheet and contact details.

**Action 5 — Monitor GCMD for pilot programme participation opportunities.**
GCMD has 130+ partners across founding/strategic, impact, coalition, knowledge, enabling, and project tiers. The centre runs real-world pilots "that mimic commercial conditions," and participation generates emissions data usable in Scope 3 reporting. *Analytical inference:* For a freight forwarding operation whose clients request Scope 3 ocean emissions data, a GCMD project-level partnership would provide access to verified per-voyage emissions figures that generic carrier averages do not. Evaluate the partnership tiers at https://www.gcformd.org/about-us/.

---

The Blueprint sets the following sourced targets by focus area:

**Port terminals:**
- "At least 60% reduction in absolute emissions from 2005 levels by 2030"
- "Net zero emissions by 2050"

**Domestic harbour craft:**
- "All harbour craft will operate on low-carbon energy solutions by 2030 and full electric propulsion and net zero fuels by 2050"
- "15% reduction in absolute emissions from 2021 levels by 2030"
- "50% reduction in absolute emissions from 2030 levels by 2050"

**Singapore Registry of Ships:**
- Working towards "50% of the SRS fleet to be green ships by 2050"

*Source: COS 2022 Media Factsheet, MPA, 09 March 2022. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/cos-2022---media-factsheet---maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint-working-towards-2050

**IMO mid-term measures — conversion trigger:**

The IMO Secretary-General stated that mid-term measures including a goal-based marine fuel standard and a GHG pricing mechanism are "on track to adopt... by late 2025." *Source: Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping, MPA, 17 April 2024. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/singapore-gears-up-to-meet-net-zero-needs-of-shipping

*Analytical inference:* Adoption of the IMO fuel standard and pricing mechanism in late 2025 is the principal conversion trigger: it would move Singapore's multi-fuel bunkering investments from competitive positioning into regulatory necessity, and would impose GHG-cost signals on every vessel calling Singapore. This is the single event that shifts this signal from MONITORING to ACTION REQUIRED for carrier-facing freight operations.

**Methanol demand trajectory:**

MPA assessed that "the demand for methanol as a marine fuel in Singapore can potentially exceed one million tons per annum (MTPA) before 2030, subject to the pace of developments of supply chains, infrastructure, and regulations globally." *Source: Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping, MPA, 17 April 2024. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/singapore-gears-up-to-meet-net-zero-needs-of-shipping

*Analytical inference:* The "before 2030" horizon for methanol demand exceeding 1 MTPA means carrier partners operating methanol-capable vessels calling Singapore are likely to have commercial fuel options within the workspace's current medium-term planning cycle. Freight operations that book capacity on methanol-capable vessels may be able to credibly claim lower-carbon ocean legs on Asia-Pacific routes within this window.

**Green corridor — GDSC trajectory:**

The GDSC is currently in an operationalisation phase, with MPA and DITRDCSA facilitating "discovery platforms for potential suppliers and off-takers" and exchanging "views on regulatory requirements" and "procedures for bunkering." Eight projects were selected for funding under the Australia-Singapore Low Emissions Technologies (ASLET) Initiative. *Source: Singapore and Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor – Factsheet 2025, DFAT/MPA, 2025. https://www.dfat.gov.au/trade-and-investment/singapore-and-australia-green-and-digital-shipping-corridor-factsheet-2025

*Analytical inference:* The GDSC is pre-commercial: it is building regulatory alignment and supply-chain discovery infrastructure, not yet delivering operational green-fuel bunkering at scale between the two ports. For workspaces moving cargo on Singapore–Australia lanes, this means the corridor is the right signal to track, but it is not yet an operational procurement reality.

---

*Note: Current cost figures for alternative marine fuels at Singapore are not drawn from the source blocks provided. The MPA sources do not publish bunker fuel price differentials. No cost figures are asserted. Directional guidance follows from sourced structural facts.*

**Bunkering cost direction:**

*Analytical inference:* Multi-fuel bunkering transitions historically carry a green premium during the scale-up phase. Methanol demand potentially exceeding 1 MTPA before 2030 is a positive supply signal, but the scale of the premium over conventional VLSFO at Singapore will depend on commercial decisions and global supply chain development — both of which MPA's own assessment flagged as conditions. Workspaces that have contractual pass-through mechanisms for bunker surcharges will be better positioned than those with fixed-rate ocean contracts over the coming years.

**Harbour craft and port call costs:**

The Blueprint targets all harbour craft operating "on low-carbon energy solutions by 2030." *Source: COS 2022 Media Factsheet, MPA, 09 March 2022. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/cos-2022---media-factsheet---maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint-working-towards-2050

*Operational implication:* Port handling costs at Singapore — drayage, towage, pilotage — will be affected by harbour craft fuel transitions ahead of 2030. For freight operations that are high-frequency Singapore-port callers (FCL ocean imports/exports, transshipment on Asia–Europe or Asia–Americas lanes), harbour craft cost escalation is a near-term operational cost signal to monitor in carrier contracts.

**GHG pricing mechanism — IMO:**

If the IMO GHG pricing mechanism is adopted late 2025 as indicated, *Analytical inference:* ocean carriers will face a direct cost on GHG emissions that will be passed through as surcharges on freight contracts. The mechanism's scope applies to "the entire shipping sector," per the IMO Secretary-General's statement. *Source: Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping, MPA, 17 April 2024. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/singapore-gears-up-to-meet-net-zero-needs-of-shipping The surcharge quantum is not yet determinable from available sourced content. *Specific per-TEU or per-tonne surcharge figure not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

**Carbon accounting and reporting:**

The Blueprint identifies "carbon awareness, carbon accounting and green financing" as a seventh focus area, with a stated ambition to be a "green maritime finance hub by promoting green financing landscape and strengthening carbon accounting and reporting." *Source: COS 2022 Media Factsheet, MPA, 09 March 2022. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/cos-2022---media-factsheet---maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint-working-towards-2050

*Operational implication:* For workspaces whose clients request Scope 3 emissions data on ocean freight, Singapore-transiting supply chains will benefit from improved data infrastructure as Singapore's carbon accounting focus area matures. However, this is a medium-term development — no specific reporting infrastructure deployment timeline is available from the sourced content.

---

MONITORING

The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore published the *Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint: Working Towards 2050* in 2022. The Blueprint is described as charting "ambitious and concrete long-term strategies to build a sustainable Maritime Singapore," developed "in consultation with industry partners." *Source: MPA Blueprint overview page, MPA, accessed 2026. https://mpa.gov.sg/maritime-singapore/sustainability/maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint

The Blueprint was positioned explicitly against three external frameworks: Singapore's commitments under "the United Nations' 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda, Paris Agreement and the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships." *Source: MPA Blueprint overview page, MPA, accessed 2026. https://mpa.gov.sg/maritime-singapore/sustainability/maritime-singapore-decarbonisation-blueprint

The trigger for accelerated action extends beyond the Blueprint itself. At MEPC 80 in July 2023, the IMO adopted the 2023 Strategy for the Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships. IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez, speaking at MPA's Accelerating Digitalisation and Decarbonisation Conference, stated that the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy sets "indicative checkpoints to reach by 2030 (cut GHG emissions by at least 20%, striving for 30%), and 2040 (cut GHG emissions by at least 70%, striving for 80%)," with the overall goal of "achieving net-zero GHG emissions by or around 2050." He also confirmed that "mid-term measures, which are currently being discussed by Member States, include a goal-based marine fuel standard, and a pricing mechanism for maritime GHG emissions," with adoption targeted for "late 2025." *Source: Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping, MPA, 17 April 2024. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/singapore-gears-up-to-meet-net-zero-needs-of-shipping

**MONITORING — re-check Q4 2025:** IMO mid-term measure adoption (fuel standard + GHG pricing mechanism) is the conversion trigger from signal to binding commercial pressure on Singapore-calling vessels. The brief is current as of the generation date; the outcome of the late-2025 adoption window is pending.

*Analytical inference:* The combination of Singapore's sovereign Blueprint, the 2023 IMO Strategy, and the imminent mid-term measures creates a layered pressure structure: Singapore is not waiting for IMO to compel action — it is building bunkering infrastructure, incentive regimes, and corridor agreements in anticipation of the IMO pricing mechanism, positioning itself to retain hub status as the fuel transition accelerates. For freight operations with ocean legs transiting Singapore, this means the infrastructure change is ahead of the regulatory mandate, not trailing it.

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- Singapore has published a national decarbonisation Blueprint with a $300 million government funding commitment, seven focus areas, and quantified 2030 and 2050 targets across port terminals, harbour craft, and fleet. This is a verifiable, sourced public document, not a corporate pledge.
- Singapore completed the world's first ship-to-containership methanol bunkering in 2023, and MPA received 50 commercial proposals — from over 60 companies — for methanol marine fuel supply, with "several projects already in operation or have crossed Final Investment Decision." *Source: Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping, MPA, 17 April 2024. https://www.mpa.gov.sg/media-centre/details/singapore-gears-up-to-meet-net-zero-needs-of-shipping This is commercial progress on a specific fuel pathway, not a roadmap aspiration.
- The Singapore–Australia GDSC was formalised in March 2024 and is in active operationalisation, with four Australian port authorities and eight ASLET-funded technology projects. For clients with Australia-facing supply chains, this corridor is the most concrete bilateral green-shipping infrastructure in the Asia-Pacific as of the sourced content.

**Questions to pose to carrier partners:**

- Which vessels in your Singapore-call rotation are methanol-capable or dual-fuel? What is your timeline for methanol bunkering at Singapore?
- Are you participating in any GCMD pilot programmes? If so, what emissions data do those pilots generate per voyage?
- What is your current CII rating for vessels on Singapore-transiting lanes, and how does that trajectory interact with your 2030 commitments?

**Claims to avoid:**

- Do not claim that Singapore's Blueprint targets are binding obligations on carriers or forwarders. They are sovereign policy ambitions, not IMO-level enforceable regulations. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any specific Blueprint target has been codified into enforceable Singapore law requires counsel review.
- Do not claim the IMO GHG pricing mechanism is adopted. As of the generation date, it is in discussion at Member State level with a late-2025 adoption target stated — not yet adopted.
- Do not quote a specific green fuel price premium at Singapore. No sourced figure is available.
- Do not present the Singapore–Australia GDSC as an operational green bunkering route. It is in a discovery and regulatory alignment phase, not a commercial fuel-delivery phase.

Close notification Home > Maritime Singapore > Sustainability > Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint > Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint Maritime Singapore Green Initiative Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint Share: Share to LinkedIn Share to Facebook Share to Twitter Print this page Share to Email Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint: Working Towards 2050. The Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint: Working Towards 2050 charts ambitious and concrete long-term strategies to build a sustainable Maritime Singapore. Developed by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) in consultation with industry partners, the Blueprint will contribute to Singapore’s commitments under the United Nations’ 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda, Paris Agreement and the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, and strengthen our value proposition as a leading global hub port and international maritime centre.    This Blueprint takes on board the recommendations made by the International Advisory Panel on Maritime Decarbonisation, and inputs from a two-month long public consultation and sector-specific consultations.   The Blueprint, published in 2022, outlines seven focus areas, which MPA will focus on to support the decarbonisation of the maritime industry: Port terminals; Domestic harbour craft; Future marine fuels, bunkering standards and infrastructure; Singapore Registry of Ships; Efforts at IMO and other international platforms; Research & development and talent; and Carbon awareness, carbon accounting and green financing. Given the dynamic developments in the global maritime decarbonisation landscape, MPA constantly refines and reviews our strategies and initiatives to ensure alignment with our local and global net-zero targets. Periodic updates will continue to be provided to the industry at relevant fora. Download the Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint  here . Developed by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) in consultation with industry partners, the Blueprint will contribute to Singapore’s commitments under the UN’s 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda, Paris Agreement and the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, and strengthen our value proposition as a leading global hub port and International Maritime Centre.   2.      The Blueprint takes on board the recommendations made by the International Advisory Panel on Maritime Decarbonisation, and inputs from a two-month long public consultation and sector-specific consultations.   3.      The Blueprint outlines seven key areas which MPA will focus on to support the decarbonisation of the maritime industry:   s/n Focus Area Target/Ambition 1 Port terminals Transit towards a low-carbon future through the adoption of cleaner energy, automation, and digitalisation, to achieve: At least 60% reduction in absolute emissions from 2005 levels by 2030 Net zero emissions by 2050 2 Domestic harbour craft All harbour craft will operate on low-carbon energy solutions by 2030 and full electric propulsion and net zero fuels by 2050, to achieve: 15% reduction in absolute emissions from 2021 levels by 2030 50% reduction in absolute emissions from 2030 levels by 2050 3 Future marine fuels, bunkering standards and infrastructure Be ready for a multi-fuel bunkering transition to support the future of international shipping, by supplying low and zero-carbon marine fuels including biofuels, methanol, ammonia, and potentially hydrogen, while enabling green technologies such as carbon capture, storage and utilisation. 4 Singapore Registry of Ships Recognise and incentivise owners to operate green ships, working towards 50% of the SRS fleet to be green ships by 2050. 5 Efforts at IMO and other international platforms Standard-setter and bridge builder, advocating for strong, credible, and inclusive climate action at the IMO and international fora. 6 Research & development and talent Global hub for maritime decarbonisation R&D, enabled by a vibrant ecosystem with talent and expertise to develop and deploy innovations. 7 Carbon awareness, carbon accounting and green financing Green maritime finance hub by promoting green financing landscape and strengthening carbon accounting and reporting.    4.      To move more decisively on maritime decarbonisation, MPA will commit additional funds of at least $300 million to support initiatives outlined in the Blueprint.  Media Releases To Top Maritime and Port Authority Close notification Singapore gears up to meet net-zero needs of shipping Published 17 Apr 2024 Share: Share to LinkedIn Share to Facebook Share to Twitter Print this page Share to Email      More than 500 participants from the industry, academia and international organisations gathered at the Accelerating Digitalisation and Decarbonisation Conference to discuss how value-chain stakeholders can work together to produce, transport, and bunker net-zero fuels safely, explore promising digital and data technology and solutions to decarbonise the maritime industry, and seed opportunities for collaboration on pilots and trials. The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) updated participants on Singapore’s methanol and ammonia bunkering capability developments, and net-zero pathways for the domestic harbour craft sector. The 3rd MaritimeSG LowCarbon50 Awards ceremony was also held during the event. 2.   Speaking at the conference, Mr Teo Eng Dih, Chief Executive, MPA said, “As an international maritime centre and global hub port, Singapore will work with our tripartite partners and international shipping community to digitalise, enhance energy efficiency, and deploy low and zero-carbon emission marine fuels. MPA is working with stakeholders to develop pathways for these marine fuels, especially in areas of provision of necessary infrastructure, crew training, regulations, and safety standards for bunkering of such fuels. A key priority is to establish the end-to-end value chains for these new fuels.” 3.   In his opening address, International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez highlighted the concrete steps taken by IMO Member States following the landmark adoption of the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships. Mr Dominguez said, “The IMO 2023 GHG Strategy demonstrates the shared commitment of Member States and the global shipping industry. We are on track to adopt mid-term measures by late 2025 to cut GHG emissions, to reach net zero targets. These mid-term measures, which are currently being discussed by Member States, include a goal-based marine fuel standard, and a pricing mechanism for maritime GHG emissions. These will help us progress towards achieving net-zero GHG emissions by or around 2050, with indicative checkpoints to reach by 2030 (cut GHG emissions by at least 20%, striving for 30%), and 2040 (cut GHG emissions by at least 70%, striving for 80%). The targets are for the entire shipping sector.” 4.   At the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 80) in July 2023, Singapore had worked actively with the IMO and other Member States to forge consensus in the adoption of the 2023 Strategy for the Reduction of GHG emissions from ships. Mr Dominguez thanked Singapore for its support to ensuring that the green and digital transition in maritime reaches all parts of the world, bringing on board LeastDeveloped Countries and Small Island Developing States. Specific projects include the joint IMO- MPA NextGEN initiative 1  (where “GEN” stands for “Green and Efficient Navigation”) and the IMO-Singapore Single Window for Facilitation of Trade (SWiFT) project 2 . 5.   MPA and the International Energy Agency (IEA) signed an MoU on the Energy Transition of the Maritime and Port Industries and announced the partnership at the event. The MoU will enable the sharing of best practices across maritime and energy industries, support the adoption and transition of zero and near-zero emission fuels by these industries through capacity building training programmes, and contribute to relevant fuel-related projects and initiatives such as the IMO-Singapore NextGEN and NextGEN Connect Initiatives. This will support the development of the IEA Regional Cooperation Centre to be hosted by Singapore. IEA Chief Economist, Mr Tim Gould, shared that the IEA warmly welcomes this MoU as a major step forward in their cooperation with the MPA, a critical player in the region and the world, to improve access to low-emission fuels. 50 proposals for the supply of methanol as a bunker fuel in Singapore. 6.   Following the completion of the world’s first ship-to-containership methanol bunkering in Singapore last year, MPA launched an expression of interest (EOI 3 ) for the supply of methanol as a marine fuel in Singapore. The EOI sought proposals covering three areas; methanol supply, methanol bunkering operating model at commercial scale, and alternatives to the physical transfer of methanol molecules to Singapore, to enable a resilient fuel supply to meet the needs of methanol-capable vessels in Singapore in the coming years. Based on consultations with the industry, the demand for methanol as a marine fuel in Singapore can potentially exceed one million tons per annum (MTPA) before 2030, subject to the pace of developments of supply chains, infrastructure, and regulations globally. 7.   There was strong interest in the EOI. MPA received a total of 50 submissions, out of which 40% of them proposed end-to-end solutions covering all three areas highlighted in the EOI. Over 60 regional and international companies comprising energy companies, fuel suppliers, traders, bunker operators, and storage companies, participated in the EOI, signalling clear business confidence in Singapore as a key offtake location for methanol by international shipping. 8.   The proposals received for the low carbon methanol supply and delivery are promising, with several projects already in operation or have crossed Final Investment Decision. On aggregate, these projects have the potential to supply over one MTPA of low-carbon methanol by 2030, subject to commercial decisions and global developments. Many of the companies plan to use ready storage infrastructure in Singapore and will partner craft operators to build or procure bunker tankers capable of carrying and delivering methanol, taking into consideration MPA’s safety and quality assurance standards, crew training requirements, and methanol bunker tanker specifications. The proposals received provide strong indications that the industry is preparing for methanol bunker demand to scale up in the coming years, most notably seen in the scheduled delivery of Type II bunker tankers capable of supplying methanol this year. 9.   Insights from the EOI submissions will inform the development of the methanol bunkering regulatory framework to ensure the safe and efficient supply of methanol as a marine fuel in Singapore at a commercial scale. MPA and Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG), through Singapore Standards Council (SSC), are developing national standards on methanol and also ammonia bunkering. The standards aim to ensure the safe operations and handling of these fuels and will support the maritime industry’s transition to sustainable alternative fuels. They span areas including custody transfer requirements, operational and safety requirements for the delivery of methanol and ammonia from a bunker tanker to receiving vessels, as well as crew training and competencies. The standards for methanol are expected to be published by EnterpriseSG in 2025. MPA’s regulatory framework for methanol bunkering licence is expected to be finalised in the coming months. MPA will call for applications for a licence to supply methanol as a marine fuel in Singapore by the end of the year. 10.  MPA will work closely with the consortiums on the selected chain-of-custody proposals on pilots that assess the feasibility of these approaches and methods, with the aim for further development on a global scale. Next steps for the development of ammonia bunkering capabilities 11.  In March 2024, the world’s first ocean-going ammonia-powered vessel, Fortescue Green Pioneer, successfully conducted its first fuel trial in Singapore4 over a period of six weeks. The Fortescue Green Pioneer received flag approval from the Singapore Registry of Ships (SRS) and the ‘Gas Fuelled Ammonia’ notation by classification society DNV to use ammonia, in combination with diesel, as a marine fuel. A second tranche of three tonnes of liquid ammonia will be loaded for the Fortescue Green Pioneer to conduct further tests and trials over the next few weeks. As part of the line-up of events at Singapore Maritime Week 2024, Fortescue Green Pioneer will be berthed at Keppel Bay. Newsroom Partner with us Who we are Launched on 1 August 2021, the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation is a non-profit organisation that supports the decarbonisation of the maritime sector through pilots and trials. GCMD is strategically located in Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering hub and busiest transshipment port. Explore our partners Explore our people Our mIssion Driving towards our mission Our goal is to help international shipping decarbonise along a trajectory that meets or exceeds key targets, including reaching net zero around 2050. We aim to support decarbonisation across the industry through four pillars. 1 Shaping standards We share learnings from our projects at relevant national and international technical committee meetings to assist and accelerate the drafting of guidelines and standards. 2 Financing projects We co-fund projects, especially ones that lack immediate commercial viability or ones that may not lead to commercial returns, so learnings may lower the barriers for adoption. 3 Deploying solutions We rally partners and execute projects to demonstrate the viability of decarbonisation solutions. 4 Fostering collaboration We provide neutral ground for stakeholders across the value chain to convene, ensuring a diversity of inputs to scope and operationalise pilots. Our Approach Adding value through pilots and trials We prioritise real-world testing, translating 2D recommendations to 3D solutions. Our pilots and trials aim to mimic commercial conditions, ensuring that the learnings can be translated directly into knowledge to lower adoption barriers. How we run our pilots and trials Transparent, deliberate, and practical – we combine academic rigour with industry realism to curate and demonstrate viable decarbonisation solutions. Domain + technical expertise Domain + technical expertise We exercise our technical and domain expertise to curate and demonstrate viable decarbonisation solutions. Collaboration across sectors Collaboration across sectors Decarbonisation will require us all to work together. GCMD provides a neutral platform for collaboration. Our unique position allows us to bring together stakeholders in adjacent sectors, as well as nominal competitors in the same space, to address common pain points. Agile funding + co-funding Agile funding + co-funding The need for deep investments is one of the hurdles that can delay the commissioning of pilots and trials. GCMD is uniquely positioned to overcome these roadblocks by co-funding projects, especially ones that lack immediate commercial viability or ones that may not lead to commercial returns, such as helping to establish safety standards and operating procedures to handle new fuels. Early involvement of regulators + policy makers Early involvement of regulators + policy makers Regulatory frameworks can also stall the commissioning of pilots and trials. That’s why GCMD works closely with governments and regulators to develop sandboxes for such trials. Our partners GCMD was founded with the support of industry partners, alongside funding from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) for qualifying research and development programmes. Since its founding, GCMD has expanded its ecosystem to include more than 130 centre- and project-level partners contributing funds, expertise, and in-kind support to pilot, accelerate the deployment, and scale the adoption of decarbonisation solutions. Partnerships Given the complexities of the maritime ecosystem and urgency of the decarbonisation agenda, collaboration across the value chain is key. Become a partner Founding / Strategic Partners Shape our strategic direction, participate in project ideation, and contribute to our financial resource pool Impact Partners Take part in early project conversations, fund cash and in-kind contributions, and provide domain expertise for pilots Coalition Partners Shed light on industry challenges, collaborate to shape standards, and share findings from projects Knowledge Partners Enrich our understanding of subject matter to build on the work of our peers and optimise resource utilisation Enabling Partner Support us in advancing our mission by providing resources or assistance to our back-end operations Project Partners Help us deploy solutions and execute pilots And more than 100 project partners. The Singapore-Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor (GDSC) was formalised in March 2024 through a memorandum of understanding. The initiative aims to accelerate the decarbonisation and digitalisation of the maritime sector and focuses on three key action areas: Enabling the supply of zero or near-zero greenhouse gas emission maritime fuels between Singapore and Australia Enhancing efficiency of maritime operations through digitalisation Supporting research and development of related technologies and solutions. The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and the Australian Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts (DITRDCSA) are jointly leading the GDSC, working closely with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, relevant Australian State and Territory Governments, Designated Agencies, and Industry Partners to operationalise the action areas. The GDSC aligns with the Green Shipping Cooperation initiative outlined in the Singapore-Australia Green Economy Agreement signed in October 2022. Supply of zero or near-zero emission maritime fuels To establish a supply chain of zero or near-zero greenhouse gas emission maritime fuels, MPA and DITRDCSA are facilitating discovery platforms for potential suppliers and off-takers (buyers) to meet and discuss business opportunities. Both sides are also working to create an enabling environment for the adoption of zero or near-zero emission fuels by: exchanging views on regulatory requirements sharing procedures for bunkering developing emergency response and training programmes for maritime workers. These efforts aim to provide greater certainty to stakeholders, build confidence and capacity in the handling of these new fuels and address safety concerns. Efficiency through digitalisation MPA and DITRDCSA are exploring digital solutions to optimise maritime operations and reduce vessel fuel consumption. This includes exploring collaboration on data exchange for efficient port clearance and sharing learnings on cybersecurity. DITRDCSA is also drawing on MPA's experience developing Digitalport@SG, a one-stop digital shipping platform. Research and development MPA, DITRDCSA and relevant government agencies are working with research communities, startups and industry to support research, development and innovation for maritime decarbonisation. Eight projects were selected for funding as part of the Australia-Singapore Low Emissions Technologies (ASLET) Initiative to accelerate emissions reduction in the maritime sector. For more detail, visit the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) website and the MPA website . Singapore and Australia are also exploring ways our relevant startup incubators and accelerators can collaborate (e.g. PIER71, an initiative to drive digital transformation and innovation within the maritime industry). Both countries are also sharing information on innovation initiatives with each other's startups to encourage mutual participation. Participating Port Authorities Australian port authorities currently involved under the GDSC include Fremantle Ports Authority, Pilbara Ports Authority, Ports Victoria and Gladstone Ports Corporation. Each is working with MPA on their own identified priority areas: Fremantle Ports Authority–digital solutions for port optimisation Pilbara Ports Authority–bunkering standards and procedures for zero or near-zero emission maritime fuels Ports Victoria–digital solutions for port optimisation and bunkering standards for zero or near-zero emission maritime fuels Gladstone Ports Corporation–information exchange on bunkering and supply chains for alternative fuels. sections.md:
**Air-priority operations.** *Operational implication:* Battery-grade materials and EV power units are predominantly air-sensitive due to dangerous-goods classification requirements (lithium batteries and cells under IATA DGR). Supply bottlenecks at battery-grade graphite and cobalt — the two minerals the Woodley et al. study identifies as particularly profound constraints — would increase the pressure to airfreight intermediate materials to maintain assembly schedules, raising per-unit cost per kilogram for affected cargo verticals while simultaneously tightening dangerous-goods documentation cycles.

*Specific cost-per-kilogram rate for airfreight of battery-grade materials not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

**Road-secondary operations.** *Operational implication:* Drayage and cross-border road movements of critical minerals are affected by tariff escalation at each processing stage. FACT: Tariffs applied by WTO members to battery packs and EVs are considerably higher than those on raw minerals and battery minerals, with a clear pattern of tariff escalation moving up the value chain. *Source: WTO/UNCTAD Data Blog, 1 August 2024. https://www.wto.org/english/blogs_e/data_blog_e/blog_dta_01aug24_e.htm For workspaces moving goods across US-Mexico or US-Canada borders, origin-certification documentation for IRA mineral-sourcing thresholds introduces a new documentation layer that is not currently standardised.

**Trade-lane implications — Americas.** *Operational implication:* The IRA's domestic-and-FTA-partner sourcing requirement means that mineral shipments from non-FTA origins lose commercial viability for IRA-qualifying EV production. This creates a lane bifurcation: FTA-origin minerals (Australia, Chile, Japan via agreements) versus non-FTA origins. Workspaces routing minerals from non-covered origins should anticipate shipper requests to re-examine routing through qualifying processing jurisdictions, generating new transhipment movements.

**Trade-lane implications — Europe and Asia.** FACT: The IEA Outlook 2025 explores key techno-economic issues such as policy mechanisms to support diversification; mineral supply chains for emerging battery technologies; recent innovations in mining, refining and recycling. *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025, 21 May 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2025 *Analytical inference:* European clients facing EU battery regulation due-diligence and carbon-footprint requirements for battery cells will generate demand for provenance-documented mineral shipments, requiring chain-of-custody documentation from mine to cell manufacturer — a new information obligation across the freight forwarding function that does not currently exist in standard airwaybill or bill-of-lading documentation.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether a freight forwarder, acting as intermediary rather than importer of record for battery materials, bears direct compliance obligations under the EU Battery Regulation's due-diligence and carbon-footprint provisions requires counsel review; the forwarding role's specific position in the obligation chain is not settled by the sources available.

**Recycling reverse-logistics stream.** *Operational implication:* FACT: Battery recycling can reduce 58% of environmental impacts of making mixed salt solutions compared to conventional mining. *Source: Nature Communications, Machala et al., 24 January 2025. https://www.nature.com/collections/eaebjccaab The commercial case for battery recycling strengthens as primary mineral costs rise; workspaces positioned to move end-of-life battery packs (classified under IATA DGR Special Provision A183/A199 and ADR for road) will encounter growing volume from EV fleet operators and OEMs pursuing secondary-material recovery. The dangerous-goods documentation, segregation, and carrier approval requirements for spent lithium batteries remain more operationally intensive than for new cells.

---

**Regulatory bodies — US.** FACT: The most ambitious US effort — introduced by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 2023 — envisions a 14.41% reduction in US transportation-related emissions (the equivalent of 7.2 billion metric tons of CO₂e through 2055) by regulating tailpipe emissions for new light duty vehicles. The standards necessitate — for vehicles sold after 2026 — realization of an industry-wide average target for the light-duty fleet of 82 grams/mile of CO₂ by 2032. *Source: Nature Communications, Woodley et al., 9 August 2024. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51152-9

*Specific implementation status of EPA standards post-2024 (whether finalized as proposed or revised) not available from primary sources provided at the time of this authoring pass.*

**Trade policy bodies — WTO/UNCTAD.** FACT: More than three-quarters of the economies surveyed exhibit rising tariffs from the first to the fifth processing stages, with the highest tariffs applied in stage 5 (EV production). Developed economies tend to have lower tariffs across all stages of the EV value chain, but their tariffs rise across the supply chain, with the highest tariffs applied to processed and finished goods, potentially hindering the ability of developing economies to move up the value chain. *Source: WTO/UNCTAD Data Blog, 1 August 2024. https://www.wto.org/english/blogs_e/data_blog_e/blog_dta_01aug24_e.htm

**IEA — multilateral policy guidance.** FACT: The IEA Sustainable and Responsible Critical Mineral Supply Chains report explores how the environmental, social and governance impacts of mining and processing operations can limit the critical mineral supplies needed for clean energy transitions and outlines five key recommendations for policy makers. Published 13 December 2023. *Source: IEA, Sustainable and Responsible Critical Mineral Supply Chains, IEA, Paris, 13 December 2023. https://www.iea.org/reports/sustainable-and-responsible-critical-mineral-supply-chains

*Specific text of the five policy recommendations not available verbatim from the source block provided at the time of this authoring pass.*

**Academic research community — Nature cross-journal collection.** FACT: The Nature cross-journal collection on critical materials supply chain sustainability has a submission deadline of 26 October 2026, inviting manuscripts that offer novel insights into resilient supply chains, digital transformation, circularity in materials, and governance for a secure energy transition, covering Communications Sustainability, Communications Earth & Environment, Nature Communications, and Scientific Reports. *Source: Nature, "Critical materials supply chain sustainability" collection, Nature Portfolio. https://www.nature.com/collections/eaebjccaab

*Analytical inference:* The open submission window through October 2026 signals that the research community regards this as an active, unsettled domain — not a concluded one — meaning that freight operations whose clients require ESG-grounded supply-chain traceability claims should expect the evidentiary baseline to shift as new peer-reviewed findings enter the record before year-end 2026.

**Recycling as an emerging counter-driver.** FACT: Battery recycling LCA shows that recycling can reduce 58% of environmental impacts of making mixed salt solutions compared to conventional mining; electricity and hydrometallurgical processes dominate impacts and show improvement opportunities. *Source: Nature Communications, "Life cycle comparison of industrial-scale lithium-ion battery recycling and mining supply chains," Machala et al., 24 January 2025. https://www.nature.com/collections/eaebjccaab

*Analytical inference:* The 58% environmental-impact reduction claim from recycling is the strongest current quantitative case for a circular materials flow, but it applies specifically to mixed salt solutions; the freight implication is that battery-end-of-life logistics (reverse logistics, classification of spent batteries as hazardous goods, cross-border movement) is moving from a niche to a volume-significant cargo stream.

---

**MONITORING — re-check window: Q4 2026**

*Analytical inference:* The signal converts from monitoring to active commercial pressure when one or more of the following events occurs:

1. **IRA mineral thresholds tighten (2027 deadline).** FACT: Assessing the feasibility of the IRA's EV critical mineral targets notes that the US Inflation Reduction Act sets that in 2027, for an electric vehicle to be tax-credit eligible, 80% of the market value of critical minerals in its battery must be sourced domestically, from US free-trade partners or from North American recycling. *Source: Nature Sustainability, Trost & Dunn, "Assessing the feasibility of the Inflation Reduction Act's EV critical mineral targets," 6 March 2023. https://www.nature.com/collections/eaebjccaab The viability of this target has been evaluated for different battery chemistries; the authors find it uncertain. When compliance with this threshold becomes verifiable (post-2027 model year), it directly determines which mineral shipment origins and processing routes are commercially viable — altering freight flow volumes and origin selections.

2. **Graphite and cobalt production shortfall materialises.** FACT: Limited production of battery-grade graphite and cobalt may represent particularly profound constraints. *Source: Nature Communications, Woodley et al., 9 August 2024. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51152-9 The conversion trigger is a visible supply gap event — producer output reporting, a mine suspension, or a processing-facility incident — that moves the constraint from projected to realised.

3. **Tariff escalation reaches battery-cell stage (Stage 4) in developing economies.** FACT: The EV value chain for cobalt, graphite and lithium consists of five stages: extraction of raw minerals, processing of minerals, production of electrodes for batteries, manufacturing of batteries, and production of EVs. *Source: WTO/UNCTAD Data Blog, 1 August 2024. https://www.wto.org/english/blogs_e/data_blog_e/blog_dta_01aug24_e.htm A new round of tariff increases at Stage 4 in major producing economies would redirect cell manufacturing to alternative jurisdictions, generating new freight lanes requiring infrastructure preparation.

4. **Nature research collection publication wave (before 26 October 2026).** *Analytical inference:* As peer-reviewed findings on LCA, recycling economics, and supply-chain resilience are published, they will be cited in client ESG requirements, procurement criteria, and potentially in revised regulatory guidance. Workspaces whose clients use sustainability data in freight-provider selection should track this collection actively.

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "Critical mineral supply constraints for EV battery production are quantified and peer-reviewed: the US-and-allies production base supports approximately 5.09 million EV deployments in the 2027–2032 window against a regulatory target requiring significantly more, creating freight demand for alternative-origin material." (FACT basis: Woodley et al. 2024, Nature Communications)
- "Battery recycling logistics is becoming a volume cargo stream, not a specialist niche; recycled material can reduce environmental impacts by up to 58% versus primary mining for certain intermediate products." (FACT basis: Machala et al. 2025, Nature Communications)
- "Tariff escalation affects every stage of the cobalt-graphite-lithium value chain from extraction through finished vehicle; origin documentation and HS code accuracy at each of the five stages is a compliance obligation, not a courtesy." (FACT basis: WTO/UNCTAD 2024)

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- "Which processing stage in the value chain are your mineral shipments at — extraction, battery-grade refining, electrode, cell, or finished vehicle? The tariff and documentation obligations differ materially at each stage."
- "Are your battery-material origins on the IRA qualifying list? If not, are you planning to re-route processing through a qualifying jurisdiction before 2027?"
- "Do you have ESG due-diligence documentation requirements from your downstream clients for water, GHG, and human rights impacts at origin? This will affect what we need from you at booking."

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not cite specific IRA threshold percentages (80% by 2027) as a confirmed compliance requirement without noting that the viability of this target is contested in peer-reviewed literature and that *Legal Confirmation Required* applies to your clients' specific battery chemistry and origin mix.
- Do not claim the workspace can provide "ESG-certified" mineral supply chains; the IEA's five policy recommendations for sustainable mineral supply chains are directed at governments and mine operators, not at forwarders.
- Do not represent that recycled-battery routing is a standard service until dangerous-goods certification and carrier approvals for the specific battery state (damaged, discharged, end-of-life) are confirmed.

---

*No named competitor positions or operator-level contract activity are available from the provided source blocks. Competitor-specific claims are omitted under the integrity rule. The following reflects structural competitive implications derivable from sourced findings.*

*Analytical inference:* Freight forwarders with existing IATA DGR-certified dangerous-goods handling capability and documented chain-of-custody processes for battery materials are structurally better positioned to capture growing EV critical-minerals freight as it scales, because clients will face increasing ESG-documentation requirements that casual forwarders cannot satisfy.

*Analytical inference:* FACT: The shift towards clean energy technologies and electric vehicles is gaining momentum as the world seeks to combat climate change; this transition requires increased use of critical minerals, such as cobalt, graphite and lithium, which are essential components of EV batteries. *Source: WTO/UNCTAD Data Blog, 1 August 2024. https://www.wto.org/english/blogs_e/data_blog_e/blog_dta_01aug24_e.htm Forwarders who have pre-qualified for FTA-origin routing corridors (Australia, Chile, Canada, Japan) before 2027 will be preferred partners when IRA threshold compliance becomes auditable.

*Analytical inference:* Workspaces without existing dangerous-goods handling certification for lithium cells and battery packs face a structural capability gap relative to those already certified; the gap widens as battery-end-of-life volumes grow. Building this capability now, before volume demands force it, is a defensible competitive positioning investment.

*Analytical inference:* The tariff escalation analysis — FACT: more than three-quarters of the economies surveyed exhibit rising tariffs from the first to the fifth processing stages — *Source: WTO/UNCTAD Data Blog, 1 August 2024* — means that forwarders with multi-stage value chain routing experience (extractive-to-processed-to-electrode-to-cell) have a service breadth advantage over those operating only at Stage 5 (finished EV) or only at Stage 1 (raw ore).

---

The global EV supply chain is experiencing converging pressure across three distinct vectors: mineral demand growth, geopolitical concentration of supply, and tariff escalation that structurally disadvantages developing-economy participation in higher-value processing stages.

**Demand trajectory.** FACT: The production of EVs and their batteries requires aluminium, copper, cobalt, graphite, nickel, lithium, manganese and rare earth elements. *Source: WTO/UNCTAD Data Blog, "Tariffs on critical minerals and their role in the electric vehicle value chain," WTO Secretariat, 1 August 2024. https://www.wto.org/english/blogs_e/data_blog_e/blog_dta_01aug24_e.htm

FACT: Projections suggest a fivefold increase in demand for cobalt, graphite and lithium by 2050 due to their intensive use in new energy technologies. *Source: WTO/UNCTAD Data Blog, 1 August 2024. https://www.wto.org/english/blogs_e/data_blog_e/blog_dta_01aug24_e.htm

**Supply-chain bottleneck severity.** FACT: Compared to ICEVs, five minerals — cobalt, graphite, lithium, nickel, and rare earths — are used to a significantly higher degree in the manufacturing of EVs; an EV also requires twice the weight of copper and manganese relative to ICEVs. *Source: Nature Communications, "Climate impacts of critical mineral supply chain bottlenecks for electric vehicle deployment," Woodley et al., 9 August 2024. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51152-9

FACT: Mineral production capacities in the United States and amongst allies support the deployment of 5.09 million vehicles between 2027 and 2032, well short of compliance target; this shortfall produces at least 59.54 million tons of CO₂e in lost lifecycle emissions benefits. *Source: Nature Communications, Woodley et al., 9 August 2024. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51152-9

FACT: Limited production of battery-grade graphite and cobalt may represent particularly profound constraints. *Source: Nature Communications, Woodley et al., 9 August 2024. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51152-9

**Policy trigger — US regulatory framing.** FACT: Following the Inflation Reduction Act's passage, US policies require the total value added from mining and processing of critical minerals for an EV's battery by the US and partner countries to exceed certain thresholds for the EV to fully qualify for tax credit incentives. *Source: Nature Communications, Woodley et al., 9 August 2024. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51152-9

*Specific penalty or threshold value for the IRA critical minerals percentage requirement as of 2027 and beyond not available from the source blocks provided at the time of this authoring pass; the Nature Communications paper notes this is "a difficult criterion for researchers to model without access to considerable trade and proprietary information."*

**IEA 2025 monitoring context.** FACT: The Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 includes a detailed assessment of the latest market and investment trends, along with their implications for critical minerals security, providing medium- and long-term projections for the supply and demand of key energy minerals, taking into account the latest policy and technology developments. Published 21 May 2025. *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025, IEA, Paris, 21 May 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2025

*Analytical inference:* The convergence of US regulatory demand pull (IRA, EPA tailpipe standards), EU transition mandates, and an unresolved supply concentration in battery-grade graphite and cobalt has created a structural market signal — not a cyclical one — that is now producing measurable compliance risk for freight forwarding operations whose clients manufacture or assemble EVs, or whose cargo verticals move the intermediate materials at any stage in the five-stage cobalt-graphite-lithium value chain.

---

**MONITORING — severity assigned; re-check window Q4 2026**

The following are positioning actions, not compliance actions. They are sequenced by lead time required.

**Immediate (0–60 days):**

1. **Map existing client base against the five EV value-chain stages.** Identify which clients or prospective clients move goods at Stage 1 (raw ore), Stage 2 (battery-grade refining), Stage 3 (electrodes), Stage 4 (cells/packs), or Stage 5 (finished vehicles). The tariff, dangerous-goods, and documentation obligation set is materially different at each stage. *Basis: WTO/UNCTAD five-stage HS code framework, 2024.*

2. **Audit IATA DGR dangerous-goods certification coverage for lithium batteries and cells.** Determine whether current staff and station certifications cover both new (PI 965/966/967) and used/damaged (PI 968/969/970) battery packs. End-of-life battery logistics requires the higher-classification handling — and is the growing volume stream.

3. **Add IRA origin-qualifying status as a data field to shipper onboarding.** Before 2027, shippers of battery materials will need to demonstrate FTA-partner origin to qualify for IRA tax credits. Workspaces that collect and retain origin-processing documentation now build the audit trail their clients will need.

**Near-term (60–180 days):**

4. **Identify FTA-qualified routing corridors for key minerals.** Australia (lithium, nickel), Chile (lithium, copper), Canada (cobalt, nickel), and Japan (processing) are among the IRA-qualifying partner jurisdictions. Pre-qualify carriers, customs brokers, and drayage partners on these lanes before 2027 deadline pressure forces reactive sourcing.

5. **Track the Nature cross-journal collection through its October 2026 submission deadline.** *Basis: Nature collection submission deadline 26 October 2026.* New peer-reviewed findings on battery LCA, recycling economics, and supply-chain resilience will be cited in client ESG criteria. Monitoring publication output from this collection provides advance sight of what clients' procurement teams will require within 12–18 months.

6. **Establish a contract-clause template for chain-of-custody documentation obligations.** The IEA framework for sustainable and responsible supply chains identifies water, GHG emissions, biodiversity, and human rights as priority ESG dimensions. *Basis: IEA, Sustainable and Responsible Critical Mineral Supply Chains, 2023.* Forwarders who can contractually commit to documentation collection at each handoff — not just transport — will be differentiated from those who cannot.

**Strategic (180 days+):**

7. **Build reverse-logistics capability for end-of-life battery packs before volume demand forces it.** The 58% environmental-impact reduction from recycling versus primary mining creates a commercial case for closed-loop battery logistics programs. *Basis: Machala et al. 2025.* Workspaces that develop this capability proactively can offer it as a differentiator to EV OEM and fleet-operator clients before it becomes a procurement requirement.

8. **Set a re-check for this brief in Q4 2026** to incorporate: (a) IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 edition, (b) publication output from the Nature collection (submission deadline October 2026), (c) any US EPA or IRA regulatory revision on mineral thresholds. The current brief is grounded in the most recent available sources (IEA 2025, Nature Communications August 2024, WTO August 2024); the evidentiary landscape will shift materially before year-end 2026.

---

Join for free Join for free cross Reports Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 Download PDF This report is part of Critical Minerals Overview Previous editions 2 About this report Critical minerals, which are essential for a range of energy technologies and for the broader economy, have become a major focus in global policy and trade discussions. Price volatility, supply chain bottlenecks and geopolitical concerns make the regular monitoring of their supply and demand extremely vital. The  Global Critical Minerals Outlook  2025 includes a detailed assessment of the latest market and investment trends, along with their implications for critical minerals security. As in  last year’s  Outlook ,   it provides a snapshot of recent industry developments from 2024 and early 2025 and offers medium- and long-term projections for the supply and demand of key energy minerals, taking into account the latest policy and technology developments. The 2025  Outlook  also explores key techno-economic issues such as policy mechanisms to support diversification; mineral supply chains for emerging battery technologies; recent innovations in mining, refining and recycling; and a broader view on strategic minerals for applications beyond the energy sector. As a new chapter, the report also includes a comprehensive review of mineral markets and policy developments in different regions. The report will be accompanied by an updated version of our  Critical Minerals Data Explorer , an interactive online tool that allows users to explore the latest IEA projections. Demand projections encompass both clean energy applications and other uses, focusing on the three IEA Scenarios – the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), the Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) and the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) Scenario. Supply projections are based on a detailed review of all announced projects. They show how today's geographical concentration evolves over time, for both mining and refining and how expected supply compares with primary supply requirements. Join for free Join for free cross Reports Sustainable and Responsible Critical Mineral Supply Chains Sustainable and Responsible Critical Mineral Supply Chains Guidance for policy makers Download PDF Overview About this report As demand grows for critical minerals to support clean energy technology deployment, potential new mines and processing facilities will put growing pressure on people, the environment, communities and Indigenous Peoples. This report explores how the environmental, social and governance impacts of mining and processing operations can limit the critical mineral supplies needed for clean energy transitions and outlines five key recommendations for policy makers to ensure that critical mineral supply chains are sustainable and responsible. It also includes deep dives on six priority areas that have important implications for supply security: water, greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity, human rights, communities and corruption. This report is released alongside an update to the Critical Minerals Policy Tracker . The 2023 update includes over 200 new policies, laws and regulations and includes a special focus on policies aimed at environmental, social and governance issues.  Published 13 December 2023 Licence CC BY 4.0 Share Cite Online table of contents 1.0 Executive summary read Read online Critical Minerals Policy Tracker Since its launch in November 2022 covering 25 countries and 200 policies, the Tracker has expanded to include over 35 countries and 450 polices, with the expansion focusing on the third policy area on reducing environmental, social and governance impacts. Though not exhaustive, it aims to offer a valuable overview of evolving mineral supply chain governance. Updated yearly. Once optimized for efficiency, these systems must now adapt to ensure resilience and sustainability. Extreme weather events, rising carbon emissions, and disruptions in energy and raw material flows highlight the urgent need for transformation. Palmer   ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0001-4592-7550 4 , Laurena Huh   ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-4737-2747 5 , Seaver Wang 3 & … Ashley Nunes   ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6821-7837 2 , 3 , 6   Show authors Nature Communications volume  15 , Article number:  6813 ( 2024 ) Cite this article 17k Accesses 34 Citations 46 Altmetric Metrics details Abstract New tailpipe emissions standards aim to increase electric vehicle (EV) sales in the United States. Here, we analyze the associated critical mineral supply chain constraints and enumerate the climate consequences of these constraints. Our work yields five findings. First, the proposed standard necessitates replacing at least 10.21 million new internal combustion engine vehicles with EVs between 2027 and 2032. Second, based on economically viable and geologically available mineral reserves, manufacturing sufficient EVs is plausible and reduces up to 457.3 million tons of CO 2 e. Third, mineral production capacities in the United States and amongst allies support the deployment of 5.09 million vehicles between 2027 and 2032, well short of compliance target. Fourth, this shortfall produces at least 59.54 million tons of CO 2 e in lost lifecycle emissions benefits. Fifth, limited production of battery-grade graphite and cobalt may represent particularly profound constraints. Pathways that afford comparable emission reductions are subsequently explored.
