These goals depend upon adoption of technologies that facilitate emissions reductions. However, energy systems powered by low-carbon technologies differ profoundly from current systems of fossil fuel trade and infrastructure. The manufacturing of solar photovoltaic plants, wind farms, and electric vehicles (EVs) – technologies crucial to lowering emissions – generally requires considerable volumes of specialty minerals, with mineral intensity varying greatly across different technologies 2 , 3 , 4 . Meeting the mineral demands associated with electrifying the light-duty vehicle fleet warrants particular attention given the transportation sector’s contribution to CO 2 emissions. Owing to an existing internal combustion engine vehicles’ (ICEVs) dependence on fossil fuels, cars, vans, and sport utility vehicles produce nearly half of all transportation-related greenhouse gas emissions, making these vehicles significant contributors to climate change 5 , 6 . Electrification offers – by virtue of reduced dependence on fossil fuels – a lower well-to-wheels emissions profile, which can reduce overall emissions relative to the status quo 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 . However, raw material supply chain bottlenecks present potential obstacles for an efficient transition to EVs 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 . Compared to ICEVs, five minerals- cobalt, graphite, lithium, nickel, and rare earths are used to a significantly higher degree in the manufacturing of EVs. An EV also requires twice the weight of copper and manganese – two additional key minerals, relative to ICEVs 2 . Higher mineral demands imposed by EVs and the envisioned prospect of widespread electrification as a pathway towards emissions reduction raise the important question: do mineral demands associated with electrifying the light-duty vehicle fleet exceed available supply? If so, by how much? And what are the emissions consequences of disequilibrium in critical minerals market? Answers to these questions are timely, particularly for the United States where emissions from the largely ICE-powered light-duty vehicle fleet constitute a significant share of overall emissions. This share has grown over time and appears likely to continue as household motorization rates rise 17 . The U.S. federal government has – since 2008 – sought to temper the emissions impact of ICEVs by incentivizing EV adoption 18 . The most ambitious of these efforts – introduced by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 2023 – envisions a 14.41% reduction in US transportation-related emissions (the equivalent of 7.2 billion metric tons of CO 2 e through 2055) by regulating tailpipe emissions for the new light duty vehicles 19 , 20 . The standards necessitate – for vehicles sold after 2026 – realization of an industry-wide average target for the light-duty fleet of 82 grams/mile (g/mile) of CO 2 by 2032. Given current market conditions and the thermal inefficiency of ICEVs, achieving this target necessitates significantly increasing EV sales volume 21 . How achievable are increases like these given constraints in EV mineral supply chains? Our work addresses this question. To do so, we estimate a model that, (1) explores requisite EV sales volume scenarios that conform to the U.S. light-duty vehicle electrification targets set by the EPA 22 , 23 , 24 , (2) assesses whether existing U.S. mineral supply chains can accommodate EV manufacturing levels needed to achieve the sales targets associated with these scenarios, and (3) quantifies the emissions impact of potential disequilibrium between mineral supply and EV-associated mineral demand for each scenario. Our model accommodates envisioned improvements in the emissions profile of alternative powertrains owing to technological and legislative efforts, most notably, recently proposed Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards (CAFE) for light duty vehicles between 2027 and 2032 25 , 26 , 27 . We further consider EVs’ potential to operate as substitutes rather than complements 28 , 29 due to increased range 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , as well as envisioned reductions in the carbon intensity of the electrical grid that may – owing to legislation like the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act – improve the emissions profile of EVs 34 . Three key characteristics define our approach. First, in estimating potential mineral disequilibrium, we recognize that the US is ill-suited to pursue full self-sufficiency in several key minerals – most notably cobalt, graphite, and manganese 15 – that are necessary to produce lithium-ion batteries used in EVs 34 . We concurrently acknowledge political concerns that some countries levy disproportional influence over key aspects of the automotive supply chain and may use raw material and manufacturing market power not only to limit supplies, but also to further attract and concentrate foreign investment and advanced manufacturing 2 , 35 , 36 . Following the Inflation Reduction Act’s passage, US policies require the total value added from mining and processing of critical minerals for an EV’s battery by the US and partner countries to exceed certain thresholds for the EV to fully qualify for tax credit incentives. This is a difficult criterion for researchers to model without access to considerable trade and proprietary information 37 . As the critical minerals value within EV batteries is considered as an ensemble of all minerals, this creates many possible combination-based pathways to both credit eligibility and credit ineligibility. Consequently, consistent with the general intent of mineral sourcing provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act to promote secure sourcing and more diverse supply chains, our estimates more narrowly consider minerals that are mined either domestically or in countries with which the US has free trade and/or mutual defense agreements. We also consider patterns of US and partner country mineral processing. Furthermore, our analysis assesses both potential limits in the size of US and partner countries’ total geologic mineral reserves (hereafter referred to as reserves) and their associated limits in the annual total rate of upstream mineral production (hereafter referred to as production) (see “Methods” section for details). We also consider the impact of downstream mineral processing constraints, processing referring to the treatment of minerals into a usable form for manufacturing purposes. Exact processing methods vary depending on the mineral commodity, but often entail smelting or chemical refining into solid metal, for example. Notably, processing facilities often utilize mineral feedstock sourced from multiple mines and, unlike mines, are not geographically constrained to where the minerals themselves are extracted. Second, our efforts consider heterogeneity in the adoption of specific battery chemistries and the emissions intensity associated with these chemistries 38 , 39 , 40 . Electrification policies do not – to our knowledge – prioritize one battery chemistry over another but rather emphasize specific EV penetration rates. Yet, consideration of the emissions intensity associated with extracting minerals specific to a particular battery chemistry is timely because it influences the magnitude of total emissions reductions EVs ultimately deliver. Put simply, EVs utilizing relatively carbon-intense battery chemistries likely offer a smaller emissions benefit – ceteris paribus - than chemistries with lower manufacturing-related emissions. To account for such factors, we leverage the 2022 Greenhouse Gases, Regulated Emissions, and Energy Use in Transportation (GREET) model to estimate emissions associated with adopting specific battery chemistries 41 . Third, we assess whether specific emissions reduction targets envisioned by the EPA can – given potential constraints in mineral supplies - be realized by deploying a wider combination of vehicle powertrains in the national fleet, namely hybrid electric vehicles (HEV). The manufacturing of HEV batteries requires fewer specialty raw materials, alleviating mineral supply constraints 42 , 43 . Moreover, HEVs offer substantially lower emissions relative to ICEVs for a similar vehicle price (thereby offering greater affordability to consumers relative to current EVs) 44 while also enjoying relative market popularity compared to EVs (thereby affording more rapid widespread deployment) 45 . HEVs’ popularity has persisted despite the gradual withdrawal of HEV-specific procurement incentives first enacted in 2008 46 , 47 . Consequently, we also explore whether complementary deployment of HEVs can help drive near-term transportation sector emissions reductions while alleviating immediate raw material supply chain constraints confronting EVs. Our efforts can help better inform public policies that target transportation-related emissions reductions in the face of potential mineral supply constraints on EV battery pack manufacturing. Furthermore, by scrutinizing geographic patterns associated with mineral supply constraints, our work can inform efforts to address economic and national security concerns related to possible mineral shortfalls. As countries like the United States accelerate their efforts to reduce emissions and deploy new low-carbon technologies, policymakers must create the underlying conditions for a new generation of technologies to achieve widespread adoption while maintaining reliable and affordable energy and mobility systems amidst real-world constraints 3 . The shift towards clean energy technologies and electric vehicles (EVs) is gaining momentum as the world seeks to combat climate change. This transition requires increased use of critical minerals, such as cobalt, graphite and lithium, which are essential components of EV batteries. However, the use of escalating tariffs in EV production chains could be a factor preventing developing economies from diversifying their exports and moving up the value chain. Clean energy technologies rely heavily on a variety of minerals. For example, solar power extensively uses copper, aluminium, cadmium, tellurium and selenium, while wind power requires copper, rare earth elements, chromium, zinc and aluminium. The production of EVs and their batteries requires aluminium, copper, cobalt, graphite, nickel, lithium, manganese and rare earth elements. As a result of the global shift toward clean energy technologies and EVs, the demand for certain critical minerals, such as cobalt, graphite and lithium (minerals that are plentiful in developing economies), is expected to grow significantly. Projections suggest a fivefold increase in demand for these minerals by 2050 due to their intensive use in new energy technologies. Stages for critical minerals in EV value chain The EV value chain for cobalt, graphite and lithium consists of five stages: extraction of raw minerals, processing of minerals, production of electrodes for batteries, manufacturing of batteries, and production of EVs (see Table 1). Trade flows for critical minerals occur at each stage of this value chain. Table 1 : Stages for critical minerals in the EV value chain and corresponding Harmonized System (HS) codes Processing stage Cobalt (HS codes) Graphite (HS codes) Lithium (HS codes) 1. Extraction and initial treatment of ores (raw minerals or minerals that underwent only initial treatment). 260500 250410 271312 270810 253090 283691 2. Processing and refining of minerals to produce battery-grade materials. 282200 810520 380110 282520 282739 282690 282619 3. Production of electrodes for batteries (cathode materials). 284190 285390 854519 284169 284290 382499 4. Manufacturing of battery cells and packs. 850760 850790 5. Production of electric and hybrid vehicles. 870240 870360 870370 870380   Tariffs and tariff escalation Tariffs on products related to the EV value chain can vary across different processing stages and between economies. In general, the tariffs on battery packs and EVs are considerably higher than those on raw minerals and battery minerals, with a clear pattern of tariff escalation moving up the value chain. Figure 1 summarizes the tariffs applied by economies at different levels of development on critical minerals throughout the EV value chain. Developed economies tend to have lower tariffs across all stages of the EV value chain. However, their tariffs rise across the supply chain, with the highest tariffs applied to processed and finished goods. This potentially hinders the ability of developing economies to move up the value chain. More than three-quarters of the economies surveyed exhibit rising tariffs from the first to the fifth processing stages although the extent varies widely. In nearly all cases, the highest tariffs are applied in stage 5 (see Figure 2). Tariff escalation is already evident in the agricultural and textile sectors. Figure 2 underlines that it represents a similar challenge to economies trading in critical minerals. Flattening tariffs alone might not be sufficient to influence choices regarding the location of high-value processing activities, but it is a crucial step towards supporting the transition to clean energy and enabling sustainable development. To capitalize on the demand for critical minerals, developing economies need to attract investment for refining and processing facilities. They also need increased technology transfer to enhance local capabilities to participate in higher-value stages of the EV supply chain. In addition, they need to ensure fair distribution of the benefits derived from trade in mineral resources by strengthening governance and to balance economic gains with environmental and social considerations by adopting sustainable practices. Conclusion Developing economies with rich mineral resources stand to benefit from the increase in demand for cobalt, graphite and lithium, but a well-functioning multilateral trading system, supported by a fair system of tariffs at a lower level, is essential to enable these economies to participate more fully in the global EV value chain. Addressing tariff escalation and fostering sustainable development practices in the critical minerals sector could lead to structural transformation in developing economies, creating a more level playing field and improving living standards in these economies. | 4 | Angola Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment (UNCTAD/DTL/TLB/2024/3) | UNCTAD | 13 Jan 2025 | https://unctad.org/publication/angola-sustainable-freight-transport-assessment | Tier 3 — Intergovernmental body (UNCTAD) |
| 5 | Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment for Fiji | UNCTAD/ESCAP | 7 Mar 2024 | https://unctad.org/meeting/sustainable-freight-transport-assessment-fiji | Tier 3 — Intergovernmental body (UNCTAD/ESCAP) |
| 6 | ITF/OECD — Decarbonising Transport Initiative | ITF/OECD | N/A | https://www.itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport | *Inaccessible during preparation — Cloudflare block; no claims grounded* |

---

**MONITORING**

The UNCTAD Sustainable Freight Transport (SFT) Framework is a live, actively deployed intergovernmental methodology that defines how national governments and private-sector freight stakeholders plan, measure, and implement sustainable freight strategies. It is not a draft or consultation document — it is published, operational, and generating country-level assessments against which freight corridors and logistics operators are being evaluated.

The framework is "Articulated around six Steps, one set of cross-cutting Enabling Factors, and twenty-seven detailed substeps" and "provides a modular step-by-step process that details how to plan, design, develop and implement tailored sustainable freight transport strategies." *Source: UNCTAD Framework for Sustainable Freight Transport Home, UNCTAD, accessed 2025. https://sft-framework.unctad.org/

The framework's practical tools include "the Self-Assessment Questionnaire, filterable and extensive list of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), and, the catalogue containing over 300 Sustainable Freight Transport Measures." *Source: UNCTAD Framework for Sustainable Freight Transport (SFT Framework) — Official Publication Page, UNCTAD, 30 Dec 2017. https://unctad.org/publication/unctad-framework-sustainable-freight-transport-sft-framework

The trigger for this signal's current relevance is not the framework's initial publication (2017) but its acceleration into active country-level deployment. Two country-level SFT assessments are confirmed in the source pool: Angola (published January 2025) and Fiji (preliminary findings presented March 2024). The Angola assessment "was conducted under the EU-UNCTAD Joint Programme for Angola: Train for Trade II, with funding by the European Union." *Source: Angola Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment, UNCTAD, 13 Jan 2025. https://unctad.org/publication/angola-sustainable-freight-transport-assessment

The Fiji assessment is running under the United Nations Development Account (UNDA) project Tranche 12, "Promoting a shift towards sustainable freight transport in the Asia-Pacific region," implemented in partnership with ESCAP. *Source: Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment for Fiji, UNCTAD/ESCAP, meeting date 7 March 2024. https://unctad.org/meeting/sustainable-freight-transport-assessment-fiji

*Analytical inference:* The combination of a published 160-economy index, an active assessment programme with EU and UN funding, and country-level deployment across Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia-Pacific signals that the SFT Framework is transitioning from a reference tool to an active policy implementation instrument. Workspaces with freight exposure to developing-economy corridors — particularly Africa, Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia — face a rising probability that government counterparts in those markets will apply SFT assessment criteria to infrastructure, logistics service procurement, or corridor access decisions.

---

**MONITORING**

*No sourced cost figures are available from the source pool for this signal. Directional operational implications are labeled as inference below.*

The framework's six steps — Diagnosis, Visioning, Targets and Indicators, Implementation, Partnerships and Programmes, and Monitoring and Evaluation — are explicitly designed to generate "an action plan to deliver the desired outcomes through the appropriate instruments, including policy-related instruments." *Source: UNCTAD Framework for Sustainable Freight Transport Home, UNCTAD, accessed 2025. https://sft-framework.unctad.org/

The Fiji assessment's objectives include to "investigate the current situation and performance of Fiji's freight transport sector; identify challenges and opportunities for transitioning to sustainable freight transport systems; promote SFT systems that are economically viable, environmentally friendly, and socially equitable/inclusive; and optimize the role of SFT in value chain development and regional integration." *Source: Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment for Fiji, UNCTAD/ESCAP, meeting date 7 March 2024. https://unctad.org/meeting/sustainable-freight-transport-assessment-fiji

The Angola assessment specifically covers "corridor development in Angola" and generates "policy recommendations put forward together with an action matrix." *Source: Angola Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment, UNCTAD, 13 Jan 2025. https://unctad.org/publication/angola-sustainable-freight-transport-assessment

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating ocean and road freight on West African or Southern African corridors — particularly those transiting through Angolan port infrastructure — the SFT Assessment action matrix may prefigure changes to port access standards, vehicle emission requirements at border crossings, or sustainability documentation requirements for logistics service providers. The timing of any such changes depends on national government adoption pace, which is not sourced in the available content.

*Operational implication:* For workspaces with air-primary operations into humanitarian or development-corridor markets (Pacific Islands, Sub-Saharan Africa), the SFT framework's social pillar — covering accessibility, labor conditions, and gender — may generate government counterpart expectations about service-level commitments that go beyond pure emissions metrics. This is a wider sustainability audit risk than pure decarbonization exposure.

*Operational implication:* The SFT Index's environmental pillar covers both "climate mitigation" and "air pollution." Workspaces that currently report Scope 1 and Scope 3 emissions under EU CSRD or ISO 14083 frameworks may find that SFT Index metrics require additional or differently structured emissions data — particularly for road and maritime legs in developing-economy markets where carrier-level data is sparse.

*Analytical inference:* The "over 300 Sustainable Freight Transport Measures" catalogue is the most operationally significant tool for private-sector freight operators. If governments begin mandating measures from this catalogue as procurement conditions, the workspace's ability to demonstrate alignment with specific measures (fuel efficiency, emissions reporting, vehicle standards) could directly affect contract eligibility on assessed corridors. Quantified cost impact is not available from the source pool.

---

**MONITORING**

*No named competitors and their specific SFT positioning are available in the source pool. Competitive framing is labeled as inference.*

The framework explicitly targets "freight transport and logistics service providers (e.g. shipping carriers and logistics firms)" and "users (e.g. shippers, traders, supply chain managers, etc.)" as its private-sector audience. *Source: UNCTAD Framework for Sustainable Freight Transport (SFT Framework) — Official Publication Page, UNCTAD, 30 Dec 2017. https://unctad.org/publication/unctad-framework-sustainable-freight-transport-sft-framework

*Analytical inference:* Large global freight forwarders and carriers with dedicated sustainability teams are better positioned to engage with UNCTAD's SFT stakeholder process than smaller operators. The workspace's competitive position depends on whether it can demonstrate credible sustainability metrics — specifically those aligned with the SFT Index's economic, social, and environmental pillars — when bidding on corridor-level contracts in assessed markets.

*Analytical inference:* The SFT framework's emphasis on "partnerships and programmes" (Step 5) creates a specific competitive opportunity: logistics operators that proactively engage with UNCTAD or ESCAP country assessment processes — through stakeholder surveys, data contribution, or pilot programme participation — gain early visibility into policy direction before it becomes procurement-mandatory. This is a low-cost positioning action available now.

*Analytical inference:* Workspaces active in humanitarian freight verticals may face an earlier competitive signal than commercial freight operators, because humanitarian logistics often operates under UN agency procurement frameworks that are more directly influenced by UNCTAD policy outputs. If UNICEF, WFP, or UNHCR begin incorporating SFT alignment criteria into logistics tender evaluations, a demonstrable SFT-relevant sustainability posture becomes a differentiator.

---

**MONITORING**

The framework's primary driver is UNCTAD's Transport Section, Trade Logistics Branch, operating through the UN Development Account and bilateral EU-funded programmes. The framework's stated target audience "spans all relevant stakeholders from within and outside the freight transport sector. These include government authorities, policy makers, city planners, freight transport and logistics service providers (e.g. shipping carriers and logistics firms), users (e.g. shippers, traders, supply chain managers, etc.), infrastructure developers, managers and operators, as well as investors and financial institutions." *Source: UNCTAD Framework for Sustainable Freight Transport (SFT Framework) — Official Publication Page, UNCTAD, 30 Dec 2017. https://unctad.org/publication/unctad-framework-sustainable-freight-transport-sft-framework

The framework's stated purpose links directly to the 2030 SDG Agenda. The Angola assessment explicitly notes that "future freight transport growth can potentially undermine the effective achievement of the objectives set in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and the Paris Agreement under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)." *Source: Angola Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment, UNCTAD, 13 Jan 2025. https://unctad.org/publication/angola-sustainable-freight-transport-assessment

The Fiji engagement demonstrates UNCTAD's multi-lateral partnership model: the assessment is "implemented by the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP)" with UNCTAD methodology, under UNDA funding. *Source: Sustainable Freight Transport Assessment for Fiji, UNCTAD/ESCAP, meeting date 7 March 2024. https://unctad.org/meeting/sustainable-freight-transport-assessment-fiji

*Analytical inference:* UNCTAD and ESCAP are using the SFT Framework as a technical-assistance lever to help developing-economy governments build regulatory and procurement standards for freight services. Private-sector logistics operators — including freight forwarders active in these corridors — are named as a target audience, meaning assessment outputs carry implicit expectations about what freight service providers operating on assessed corridors should be able to demonstrate.

*Analytical inference:* The EU's funding of the Angola assessment through Train for Trade II suggests that EU development finance conditionality may increasingly require SFT-aligned freight planning as a programme output condition. Workspaces active in EU-funded development corridors in Africa should treat this as an emerging procurement signal, not merely a policy reference.

---

**MONITORING**

The SFT Framework is structured as a "circular process in which a monitoring and evaluation exercise is undertaken at the end of the cycle after having implemented the sustainable freight transport strategy." *Source: UNCTAD Framework for Sustainable Freight Transport Home, UNCTAD, accessed 2025. https://sft-framework.unctad.org/

The SFT Index currently "covers around 160 economies" across "economic, social, and environmental pillars." *Source: About the SFT Index, UNCTAD, accessed 2025. https://sft-framework.unctad.org/about-sft-index

*Analytical inference:* A framework that already benchmarks 160 economies internationally, and which is actively generating country-level assessments with action matrices and policy recommendations, is on a trajectory toward becoming a reference standard against which national freight policies and potentially procurement conditions are assessed. The conversion from advisory framework to active commercial or regulatory pressure depends on three observable triggers:

1. **National policy adoption trigger**: When an assessed country translates its SFT Assessment action matrix into national transport regulation or logistics procurement criteria. No specific date is available from the source pool for any country taking this step; this remains a research gap.

2. **Multilateral development bank (MDB) conditionality trigger**: When World Bank, African Development Bank, or Asian Development Bank infrastructure financing begins citing SFT Index scores or SFT Assessment compliance as eligibility or performance criteria. *Specific [conditionality language / date] not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

3. **EU development finance integration trigger**: The EU's existing funding of the Angola assessment under Train for Trade II suggests a pathway. If the EU's development cooperation frameworks (such as the Global Gateway) begin citing SFT alignment in transport infrastructure tenders, this would accelerate conversion to commercial pressure. *Specific [EU policy linkage / date] not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

*Analytical inference:* Given the Fiji assessment's preliminary findings were presented in March 2024 and the final report was noted as forthcoming following consultation and validation, the Fiji final report is an expected near-term publication. Its release will be a concrete check-point for assessing how the framework translates into actionable policy recommendations in a Pacific Small Island Developing State — relevant to workspaces with humanitarian or development-corridor freight exposure in the Pacific.

**Re-check window**: Monitor for Fiji final SFT Assessment publication (expected post-March 2024 consultation; no confirmed date in source pool) and for any new country-level SFT Assessment announcements from UNCTAD's Transport Section.

---

**MONITORING** — no immediate compliance action required; positioning actions available now.

**Action 1 — Map corridor exposure to SFT-assessed countries.** Identify which trade lanes in the workspace's active portfolio touch countries where UNCTAD SFT Assessments have been published or are in progress. Confirmed assessments in the source pool: Angola (published January 2025), Fiji (preliminary March 2024, final pending). Additional country assessments are likely given the framework's 160-economy index scope and active UN programme funding, but are not confirmed in the source pool. *Assign to operations lead; no cost; execute within 30 days.*

**Action 2 — Download and review the Angola SFT Assessment action matrix.** The Angola assessment contains policy recommendations and an action matrix for that corridor. For workspaces operating on West African corridors, this is the most actionable current output. *Assign to trade lane manager for Angola/West Africa; no cost; review within 30 days. Source: https://unctad.org/publication/angola-sustainable-freight-transport-assessment

**Action 3 — Register for the SFT Index interactive charts.** The SFT Index covers approximately 160 economies. Reviewing scores for key trade-lane countries against economic, social, and environmental pillars provides an early-warning picture of where government freight-sector reform pressure is highest. *Assign to sustainability or operations function; no cost; complete within 14 days. Source: https://sft-framework.unctad.org/about-sft-index

**Action 4 — Assess internal KPI alignment against SFT framework indicators.** The framework provides a "filterable and extensive list of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)" and a catalogue of "over 300 Sustainable Freight Transport Measures." Comparing the workspace's current sustainability reporting metrics against the SFT KPI list identifies gaps before they become procurement-relevant. *Assign to sustainability lead; no cost; complete within 60 days. Source: https://unctad.org/publication/unctad-framework-sustainable-freight-transport-sft-framework

**Action 5 — Monitor Fiji final SFT Assessment publication.** The Fiji preliminary findings were presented in March 2024; the final report was noted as forthcoming. Its publication will confirm how the framework translates into policy recommendations for a Pacific SIDS, relevant to workspaces with humanitarian or development-corridor air freight exposure in the Pacific. *Set a monitoring alert on https://unctad.org/meeting/sustainable-freight-transport-assessment-fiji; re-check Q3 2025.*

**Action 6 — Brief commercial leads on EU development finance linkage.** The Angola assessment's funding through the EU-UNCTAD Train for Trade II programme suggests that EU development finance corridors are using SFT alignment as a programme output marker. Commercial leads pursuing contracts in EU-funded infrastructure or logistics programmes in Africa or Asia-Pacific should be aware of this signal. *Assign to commercial leadership; no cost; brief within 30 days.*

---

The following claims are grounded and can be used in client conversations with appropriate qualification:

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- UNCTAD has published a structured six-step framework for sustainable freight transport that is currently being applied in active country assessments across Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia-Pacific, with the Angola assessment published in January 2025 and the Fiji assessment presented in March 2024. This is factual and sourced.

- The framework benchmarks approximately 160 economies on an internationally comparable SFT Index covering economic, social, and environmental performance — including climate mitigation, air pollution, infrastructure quality, safety, and labor conditions. This is factual and sourced.

- The framework is designed to serve both public- and private-sector stakeholders, explicitly including logistics service providers and shippers, meaning it is relevant to how governments in assessed markets may structure freight-related procurement or policy going forward.

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- Does your supply chain include freight legs through any of the countries currently undergoing SFT Assessment (confirmed: Angola, Fiji; others likely but not confirmed in source pool)? If so, do you have visibility into how your logistics service providers' sustainability performance would be evaluated against SFT Index criteria?

- For clients with CSR or ESG reporting obligations: is your Scope 3 freight data structured in a way that maps to the SFT Index's environmental pillar metrics (climate mitigation, air pollution)? If not, there is a reporting alignment gap worth addressing proactively.

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not assert that the SFT Framework is currently mandatory for private freight operators or that non-compliance carries penalties. No such obligation exists in the source pool. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any country has incorporated SFT assessment output into enforceable national law or procurement regulation affecting private logistics operators requires country-specific legal review.

- Do not cite the ITF/OECD decarbonising transport framework or the 2024 OECD/SIPA methodology paper as corroborating sources in client conversations — both sources were inaccessible during this brief's preparation and their content has not been verified.

- Do not describe the Fiji final report as published — as of the source content, it was "to be made available online" following consultation and validation after the March 2024 preliminary findings session.

---

It offers guidance and practical tools to stakeholders from both the public and the private sector across all modes of transport to evaluate the status quo, promote sustainable freight transport systems and track progress. Download our PDF . At a glance Articulated around six Steps, one set of cross-cutting Enabling Factors, and twenty-seven detailed substeps, the UNCTAD Sustainable Freight Transport Framework provides a modular step-by-step process that details how to plan, design, develop and implement tailored sustainable freight transport strategies. Applicable to different stakeholders, within and across modes of transport and in various geographical areas, the methodology is flexible and can be modulated to allow for some steps to be carried out in parallel. Substeps and related activities can also be adapted to reflect stakeholders’ varying needs, resources and priorities. In addition, the SFT Framework allows for a circular process in which a monitoring and evaluation exercise is undertaken at the end of the cycle after having implemented the sustainable freight transport strategy. The figures below provide a graphical illustration. The aim is to help determine how the sector is performing in terms of the economic, social, and environmental sustainability objectives. Once this performance measurement is established, adequate adjustment measures to improve the strategy can be envisaged. Incorporating sustainable freight transport considerations into existing public and private sector planning processes may require additional work and resources. Depending on the context, however, some steps are likely to be more critical than others, and may require more attention and resources. Overall efforts involved during each step can vary depending on local priorities and resources. An effective sustainable freight transport strategy does not stop at the question “what do we want to do?” i.e. outlining the overall vision. The strategy needs to support the vision with an action plan to deliver the desired outcomes through the appropriate instruments, including policy-related instruments. The main question is therefore, how do we do it and how do we get the resources (institutional and financial) to deliver the strategy? Other related considerations include the following: 1 Which issues in the freight transport sector should be considered? 2 Who are the stakeholders? 3 What determines the performance of the freight transport sector? 4 What are the broad and bold aspirations associated with the freight transport sector? 5 What is the ultimate objective that the sustainable freight transport strategy aims to achieve? 6 What are the best options for developing and implementing a sustainable freight transport strategy? 7 How to balance the varied perspectives and move the planning process forward? 8 How can the strategy be made into a reality? 9 How can we learn and adapt when things are not happening as planned? UNCTAD Framework for Sustainable Freight Transport Where to start? The steps of the Framework can be carried out in sequence or partially in parallel , depending on the local requirements, timelines and resources You can start by having a look at our tools: Sustainable Freight Transport Measures Key Performance Indicators Or You can begin with the first step of the methodology Go to: step 1 Diagnosis Who are we?   UNCTAD is part of the UN Secretariat. We report to the UN General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council but have our own membership, leadership, and budget. We are also part of the United Nations Development Group. We support developing countries to access the benefits of a globalized economy more fairly and effectively. And we help equip them to deal with the potential drawbacks of greater economic integration. To do this, we provide analysis, facilitate consensus-building, and offer technical assistance. More information about UNCTAD's work in transport is available at the UNCTAD site . It features a modular step-by-step methodology that details how to plan, design, develop and implement tailored sustainable freight transport strategies. In addition, the UNCTAD SFT Framework offers guidance and practical tools to help relevant stakeholders and decision makers, from both the public and the private sector, take adequate response measures that promote sustainable freight transport systems. SFT steps » Step 1: Diagnosis Step 2: Visioning Step 3: Targets and indicators Step 4: Implementation Step 5: Partnerships and programmes Step 6: Monitoring and evaluation Enabling factors SFT tools » Key performance indicators SFT measures SFT assessment reports SFT index » About the SFT index Interactive charts Methodology Land freight emissions model Contact About the SFT index UNTAD SFT index measures and visualizes countries’ performance in sustainable freight transport (SFT) in an internationally comparable manner, covering around 160 economies. Aligned with the UNCTAD SFT framework , the index comprises the overall score, scores for the three pillars of SFT (i.e., economic score, social score, and environmental score), and scores for the SFT elements.   SFT pillars and elements that are included in the SFT index: Economic pillar: Infrastructure Productivity Quality and reliability Transport cost Connectivity Social pillar: Safety Accessibility Labor condition Gender Noise Environmental pillar: Climate mitigation Air pollution   These scores offer insights into an economy’s relative standing in SFT performance worldwide. A score of 0 indicates that the economy has the worst performance in the world for all underlying SFT indicators, while a score of 100 indicates the best performance in the world for all indicators. By offering comprehensive visualizations , the UNTAD SFT index facilitates a deeper understanding of economies’ performances in sustainable freight transport and enables meaningful comparisons on a global scale. Economies' performances can be visualized by pillars or elements and users are allowed to select and compare different economies and/or economy groups.   Connect with us UNCTAD - Palais des Nations, 8-14, Av. de la Paix, 1211 Geneva 10, Switzerland © Copyright | Privacy notice | Terms of use

Featured programmes Automated System for Customs Data (ASYCUDA) Debt Management and Financial Analysis System (DMFAS) Search for a project In focus Impact stories Map of UN Development Account projects Project requests Sources of funding Technical assistance toolbox Media For registered journalists Newsroom (password required) Latest Brand assets News Press releases Secretary-General statements The Weekly Tradecast episodes Videos User account menu Home Angola sustainable freight transport assessment Angola sustainable freight transport assessment Highlight Downloads Freight transport systems are essential for economic growth, trade competitiveness, and sustainable development. Demand for freight transport infrastructure and services expands in tandem with growth in population, urbanization, international trade, and economic development. Despite the strategic economic importance of freight transport for trade and development, increased freight transport activity can, nevertheless, generate negative externalities and sustainability challenges. These include increased noise pollution, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, traffic congestion, road safety concerns, and environmental degradation. If left unchecked, future freight transport growth can potentially undermine the effective achievement of the objectives set in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and the Paris Agreement under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Recognizing the strong linkages between sustainable development and freight transport and logistics, UNCTAD launched the Sustainable Freight Transport (SFT) Assessment tool . The SFT Assessment enables the conduct of qualitative and quantitative analyses to generate a comprehensive assessment of the state of the freight transport sector. It assesses the sector’s performance as regards the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of sustainable development. This report sets out the main findings of the SFT Assessment in Angola . Angola’s SFT Assessment is carried out across the three pillars of sustainability, i.e., economic, social, and environmental. Making use of the SFT Assessment, the current situation and performance of Angola's freight transport and ability to meet relevant sustainability objectives are analysed. Assessing the state of play has helped to identify the main challenges and obstacles undermining the sustainability of Angola's freight transport sector and clarify their underlying causes. Special attention is also given to the role of freight transport and logistics in supporting the agribusiness and value chains as well as corridor development in Angola. The report is structured as follows: Chapters II and III establish Angola's profile, including as regards its freight transport sector. An overview of existing national and transport policies is presented highlighting the broader context and underscoring the important role of sustainable freight transport for Angola. Chapter IV sets out the main findings of Angola's SFT Assessment based on UNCTAD methodology supported by quantitative and qualitative analyses. Chapter V features a number of policy recommendations put forward together with an action matrix. Chapter VI summarizes the findings and identified recommendations and concludes with UNCTAD's role in improving Angola's freight transport sustainability. The Annexes provide more details about the methodology behind the UNCTAD SFT Assessment. The assessment was conducted under the EU-UNCTAD Joint Programme for Angola: Train for Trade II, with funding by the European Union, under the Transport and Logistics Component. Location Online, Fiji Add to calendar Add to Calendar Key Issues Documents Body UNCTAD is currently conducting a Sustainable Freight Transport (SFT) assessment for Fiji, as part of the United Nations Development Account (UNDA) project (Tranche 12) "Promoting a shift towards sustainable freight transport in the Asia-Pacific region" implemented by the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP). The UNCTAD SFT assessment aims to conduct a rapid analysis of Fiji's freight transport sector, encompassing maritime and road transport. This assessment seeks to achieve the following objectives: 1) investigate the current situation and performance of Fiji’s freight transport sector; 2) identify challenges and opportunities for transitioning to sustainable freight transport systems; 3) promote SFT systems that are economically viable, environmentally friendly, and socially equitable/inclusive; and 4) optimize the role of SFT in value chain development and regional integration. Underpinned by qualitative and quantitative analyses of the sector’s present status, performance, and the opportunities and challenges for fostering more sustainable, efficient, and socially inclusive freight systems, the outcome of the assessment is a comprehensive report featuring policy recommendations and an action matrix. The preliminary findings present the quantitative results of the SFT assessment, utilizing the UNCTAD SFT Index methodology that assesses the sustainability of Fiji’s freight transport in an internationally comparable manner, as well as the SFT survey drawing upon information and input received in response to the stakeholders’ survey questionnaires. Following consultation and validation, the final report of the SFT assessment for Fiji will be made available online. sections.md:
**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- Brazil's transport ministry is actively restructuring both road and rail concessions in 2025–2026, with road corridor upgrades on key North-South routes and a new public call rail model targeting 10,000 kilometres of idle lines. These changes will affect transit times and toll economics on specific corridors.
- Brazil launched the MOVER programme in 2024 as the first national framework regulating heavy-duty vehicle emissions, with specific vehicle regulations expected in 2027/8.
- The e-FAST Brasil platform, launched July 2025, is the first national multi-sector coalition specifically targeting road freight electrification and is backed by the Ministry of Transport and Ministry of Environment.
- Zero-emission commercial vehicle sales in Brazil grew 141% in the first half of 2025, but heavy-truck zero-emission capacity remains limited; São Paulo is the most developed market.

**What to avoid claiming:**

- Do not claim that zero-emission road freight is available at scale across Brazil's national network; the evidence supports São Paulo metropolitan availability only.
- Do not cite EZVolt's "80% lower operating costs" as an independently verified industry benchmark; it is a single-operator claim.
- Do not claim specific toll rates, diesel prices, or handling costs without real-time carrier data; none are grounded in the source blocks.
- Do not assert that the Brazilian Sustainable Taxonomy creates specific reporting obligations for freight forwarders without legal confirmation; the CNAE H integration is a governance framework development, not yet a compliance deadline.

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- Does your Brazil logistics contract have a carbon-reporting clause? If so, which standard (CSRD Scope 3, ISO 14083, GHG Protocol)? Brazilian carrier emissions data availability is variable and will need proactive sourcing.
- Are your Brazil-leg volumes concentrated on the BR-116/324 or Central-West corridors? If so, what tolerance do you have for transit-time variance during 2026–2027 construction phases?
- Is any portion of your Brazil freight government-tendered or government-adjacent? The Sustainability Taxonomy alignment for CNAE H may become a qualification criterion.

---

**Road — Diesel trucking: currently feasible, facing forward pressure**
Road freight trucking under the "Transporte Rodoviário de Cargas - TRC" regulatory framework is an active, operating mode listed by the Ministry. *Source: Ministério dos Transportes official portal, gov.br, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br. MOVER (Programa Nacional de Mobilidade Verde e Inovação) was launched in 2024 as "the first of its kind to regulate emissions from the heavy-duty transportation sector (with specific regulations expected for 2027/8)." *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Analytical inference: workspaces procuring road freight in Brazil on multi-year contracts should include a clause review window aligned to 2027/8 when MOVER heavy-duty vehicle regulations are expected to formalise, as they may impose efficiency or emissions standards on carrier fleets.

**Road — Zero-emission trucking: emerging, not yet at commercial scale for general freight**
Brazil saw a 141% increase in new zero-emission bus sales in the first half of 2025. More than 1,380 commercial electric vehicles (vans, buses, and trucks) were sold between January and July 2025 according to ABVE. *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. The Volkswagen Truck & Bus e-Delivery is described as "the first 100% electric truck designed and built in Brazil." *Source: ibid.* Analytical inference: zero-emission heavy truck availability in Brazil remains limited to early-stage models and pilot-scale fleets; workspaces seeking to cite zero-emission road freight capacity in Brazil to clients should confirm availability with specific carriers rather than citing market-aggregate growth figures, which are dominated by bus and van segments.

**Road — Electric charging infrastructure: in early corridor-building phase**
e-FAST Brasil, launched in July 2025 and coordinated by WRI Brasil, with support from the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, Ministry of Transport, Shakti Foundation, and CALSTART/Drive to Zero, lists as one of its "top stated initiatives" the acceleration of "the first Global Green Road Corridor in Latin America." *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Analytical inference: corridor-level charging infrastructure for medium- and heavy-duty freight vehicles does not yet exist at operational scale in Brazil; feasibility of electric truck routing outside São Paulo metropolitan area for general freight is currently restricted by infrastructure gaps.

**Rail — New brownfield concession model: feasible for longer-term multimodal planning**
Brazil's public call model permits private operators to assume control of underutilised railway segments. "The first section to be offered is the Minas-Rio railway corridor (Central-Atlantic Railway). The selection process will begin between September and October 2025." The Central Atlantic Railway is currently operated by VLI Logística, which renewed its concession rights until 2056 by returning approximately 3,200 kilometres of lines to the Federal Government. *Source: U.S. International Trade Administration, Brazil Rail Transportation, trade.gov, September 3, 2025. https://www.trade.gov/market-intelligence/brazil-rail-transportation. Analytical inference: rail feasibility for cargo verticals operating in the Centre-West or Minas Gerais corridors is improving in policy terms, but actual operator entry under the new public call model depends on selection process outcomes and investment timelines; commercial freight services on reactivated lines are unlikely before 2026–2027 at the earliest.

**Sustainability compliance as a concession-embedded condition:**
The Ministry's Sustainability Sub-secretariat, consolidated under Decree nº 11.961/2024, holds transversal responsibility for "integração de critérios de sustentabilidade, gestão de riscos, adaptação à mudança do clima e classificação das atividades econômicas segundo a Taxonomia Sustentável Brasileira, especialmente no que se refere às atividades enquadradas na CNAE H – Transporte, Armazenagem e Correio." *Source: Ministério dos Transportes, Subsecretaria de Sustentabilidade – SUST, gov.br, updated February 26, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br/assuntos/sustentabilidade. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the Brazilian Sustainable Taxonomy classification for CNAE H (Transport, Storage and Courier) creates disclosure or reporting obligations for freight forwarders operating in Brazil, and at what threshold, requires counsel review.

*On-site solar, BESS, and specific equipment feasibility for freight terminal operations not addressed in any provided source block; omitted per integrity rule.*

---

*No named competitor freight forwarders and their specific Brazil operational positions are present in any provided source block. Named-competitor analysis is omitted per the integrity rule.*

The following structural competitive dynamics are grounded in sourced content:

**Early access to zero-emission carrier capacity:**
EZVolt is described as "the largest electromobility company in Brazil" and services "roughly 75% of the e-bus fleets from São Paulo city." *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Analytical inference: workspaces that establish early relationships with zero-emission logistics providers in São Paulo (where capacity is most developed) are positioned to offer a differentiated green-freight product on intra-metropolitan movements before competitors who wait for wider national availability.

**e-FAST Brasil as a coalition platform — early participation advantage:**
e-FAST Brasil connects "innovators and stakeholders from across the freight and logistics value chain, including industry, financial institutions, and government." *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Analytical inference: workspaces with Brazil operations that join e-FAST Brasil's platform gain visibility into the first Latin American Green Road Corridor design, pilot operator selection, and emerging financing structures before these are publicly tendered — a lead-time advantage on corridor-level service design.

**Rail concession process — U.S.-flagged opportunity window:**
The U.S. ITA explicitly notes that Brazil's public call model creates opportunities for introduction of "advanced U.S. freight rail technologies, including alternative energy sources, digital solutions, and specialized equipment." *Source: U.S. International Trade Administration, Brazil Rail Transportation, trade.gov, September 3, 2025. https://www.trade.gov/market-intelligence/brazil-rail-transportation. Operational implication: workspaces with rail-adjacent logistics products or multimodal consulting capabilities should assess whether participation in the Minas-Rio corridor selection process (September–October 2025 start) creates a gateway to longer-term rail freight service design in Brazil.

COMPETITIVE EDGE — for workspaces that move on e-FAST Brasil coalition participation and São Paulo EV carrier relationships before broader market access develops.

---

*No sourced cost comparison data (road vs. rail, diesel vs. electric, owned vs. leased infrastructure) is present in the provided source blocks at the time of this authoring pass. This section is omitted per the integrity rule. The operator-level claim of approximately 80% lower operating costs for electric vs. diesel vehicles (sourced from EZVolt/CALSTART) is noted in Section 1 but is a single-operator assertion rather than a comparative study; it cannot be used as a breakeven or payback figure without independent verification.*

The one directional signal grounded in sourced content:

- Electric vehicles compared with diesel-powered vehicles: "approximately 80% lower operating costs, 80% to over 100% higher energy efficiency" — operator claim by EZVolt CEO, cited for directional navigation only. *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Analytical inference: this figure is not an independently verified study result; workspaces using it in client conversations or commercial proposals should label it as a private-sector operator estimate.

MONITORING — Re-check window: Q1 2027 (MOVER heavy-duty emissions regulations expected 2027/8; PNL 2050 final plan expected within 12–18 months of July 2025 consultation close).

*Specific industrial electricity rates, diesel fuel retail prices, drayage costs, and port handling tariffs not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

The source blocks provided do not contain line-item cost data for road freight, port handling, or energy in Brazil. The following structural cost signals are grounded in sourced content:

**Road freight — concession tolls in active change:**
The Brazilian Ministry of Transportation portal lists "Concessões Rodoviárias 2026" as an active programme, and the Consórcio 116 Sertões consortium won the BR-116/324/BA/PE concession with an infrastructure commitment of R$8.53 billion. *Source: Ministério dos Transportes official portal, gov.br, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br. Operational implication: workspaces routing cargo over the BR-116/324 corridor (Feira de Santana, BA to Salgueiro, PE) should expect toll structures tied to this new concession rather than legacy rates; the "maior desconto na tarifa por quilômetro" (largest discount in tariff per kilometre) outcome of the auction may reduce per-km tolls on this leg relative to prior concession terms, but carrier-specific confirmation is required.

**Road investment — BR-319/AM and BR-080:**
The Ministry portal reports R$1.45 billion allocated to the BR-319/AM (339 km, four lots) and R$407.8 million to BR-080 duplication between Taguatinga and Brazlândia, with the latter at approximately 20% execution. *Source: Ministério dos Transportes official portal, gov.br, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br. Analytical inference: active road works on these corridors create transit-time risk for road-dependent cargo during construction phases, particularly for time-sensitive freight verticals.

**Rail — idle lines and tariff structure:**
Brazil holds around 10,000 kilometres of idle railway lines. The new public call model sets contracts of up to 99 years with free tariffs. *Source: U.S. International Trade Administration, Brazil Rail Transportation, trade.gov, September 3, 2025. https://www.trade.gov/market-intelligence/brazil-rail-transportation. Analytical inference: free-tariff rail contracts increase pricing variability for multimodal shippers; rates on reactivated corridors will depend on negotiated terms between private operators and shippers rather than regulated tariff schedules.

**Electromobility operating cost signal:**
EZVolt, reported as the largest electromobility company in Brazil and servicing roughly 75% of São Paulo's e-bus fleet, has stated that electric vehicles deliver "approximately 80% lower operating costs" compared with diesel-powered vehicles. *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, "Charging Up Change: Brazil Accelerating its Drive to Zero," November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Industry interpretation: this operator-level figure is cited as a private-sector endorser claim, not an independently audited average; it is directionally useful for fleet cost modelling but should not be used as a binding cost projection without carrier-specific data.

*Specific diesel retail prices, SAF availability pricing, port handling fees, and industrial electricity tariffs not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

---

MONITORING — multiple forward triggers active; re-check window Q4 2026 and Q1 2028.

**1. MOVER heavy-duty vehicle regulations — 2027/8 MONITORING**
Brazil's MOVER programme launched in 2024 "with specific regulations expected for 2027/8" for the heavy-duty transportation sector. *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. When finalised, these regulations will impose emissions or efficiency standards on carrier fleets operating road freight in Brazil. Analytical inference: workspaces on multi-year Brazil road freight contracts should begin discussing fleet-upgrade provisions and compliance cost pass-through mechanics with carriers now, ahead of the regulatory finalisation window.

**2. e-FAST Brasil — First Latin American Green Road Corridor — phase and timing**
e-FAST Brasil was launched in July 2025. One of its "top stated initiatives is to accelerate the first Global Green Road Corridor in Latin America." *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Participants include WRI Brasil, Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, Ministry of Transport, Shakti Foundation, and CALSTART/Drive to Zero. Phase: design and stakeholder convening, post-launch. No operational corridor date has been stated in the source blocks. Analytical inference: based on comparable green corridor programmes (e.g., Nordic and US corridors), corridor-level operational readiness typically follows platform launch by 3–5 years; a conservative estimate for initial corridor operation would be 2028–2030, though this depends on infrastructure financing and pilot operator selection. Re-check: monitor e-FAST Brasil programme outputs in Q1 2027 for pilot corridor announcement.

**3. Minas-Rio railway public call — selection process**
The selection process for the Minas-Rio public call (first section offered under the new model) was scheduled to begin between September and October 2025. *Source: U.S. International Trade Administration, Brazil Rail Transportation, trade.gov, September 3, 2025. https://www.trade.gov/market-intelligence/brazil-rail-transportation. Analytical inference: if the selection process launched on schedule, an operator announcement may be available by Q1 2026; actual service launch on this corridor would follow investment and operational ramp-up. Current status of the selection outcome is not confirmed in any available source block; a direct check of ANTT (Agência Nacional de Transportes Terrestres) announcements is the appropriate next step.

**4. Electromobility Secretariat under Ministry of Mines and Energy — early stage**
Brazil's national government "recently announced the creation of an electromobility secretary under the Ministry of Mines and Energy." The secretariat is expected to "consolidate public policies that promote the electrification of vehicles in the country and improve dialogue between government and industry." The ABVE president stated the secretariat "will begin work as soon as a new head is appointed." *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Analytical inference: once the secretariat is operational, it will produce coordinated EV policy affecting charging infrastructure deployment, incentive structures, and fleet electrification timelines — each of which directly affects road freight cost and feasibility. Re-check: Q2 2026 for secretariat appointment and first policy outputs.

**5. PNL 2050 — National Logistics Plan consultation**
The Instituto de Energia e Meio Ambiente (IEMA) submitted a technical contribution to the Ministry's PNL 2050 public consultation in July 2025, calling for detailed GHG emissions mapping and modal sustainability indicators. *Source: IEMA, "Contribuição Técnica ao PNL 2050," energiaeambiente.org.br, July 2025. https://energiaeambiente.org.br/emissoes-detalhadas-de-carbono-e-trechos-de-transportes-em-areas-de-conservacao-precisam-estar-no-plano-nacional-de-logistica-2050-indica-iema-20250701. Analytical inference: PNL 2050, once adopted, will set the 25-year modal investment and emissions framework for Brazilian transport; workspaces with long-term Brazil freight contracts should monitor its adoption for priority modal shifts and emissions-linked infrastructure incentives.

**6. São Paulo zero-emission bus fleet mandate — 2038 target, near-term purchasing ban**
The City of São Paulo has banned the purchase of new diesel buses and is aiming for a 100% zero-emission fleet by 2038. *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Operational implication: while this policy directly targets buses, the charging infrastructure build-out it drives in São Paulo will accelerate the feasibility of electric freight vehicles on intra-city and near-city logistics routes; workspaces with São Paulo distribution operations should monitor EZVolt and peer operator announcements for freight-vehicle charging availability.

**7. Road concessions 2026 programme**
The Ministry portal lists "Concessões Rodoviárias 2026" as an active programme with upcoming projects. *Source: Ministério dos Transportes official portal, gov.br, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br. Analytical inference: new 2026 road concession auctions will reset toll economics on additional corridors; workspaces should track auction results for corridors used in their Brazil supply chain, as new concessionaires typically reset tariff structures within the first contract year.

---

**Brazil's modal mix is road-heavy by design and policy investment:**
The Ministry of Transportation's social media post, sourced from the portal, states that cargo "representa cerca de 50% do PIB do país" and the road network is the primary carrier of that cargo. *Source: Ministério dos Transportes official portal, gov.br, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br. Analytical inference: for workspaces with multimodal operations across Latin America, Brazil's road-dominance means ground transport costs, toll structures, and road concession changes have outsized impact on total Brazil logistics cost relative to peers like Argentina or Chile where rail or intermodal plays a larger role on specific corridors.

**North-South road corridor upgrades are accelerating — relevance to regional routing:**
Active investments on BR-116/324 (Bahia–Pernambuco), BR-319/AM, and BR-080 (Central-West) signal the Ministry's intent to increase corridor reliability. The BR-116/324 concession is described as "estratégico para o abastecimento regional, o transporte de cargas e a mobilidade da população." *Source: Ministério dos Transportes official portal, gov.br, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br. Analytical inference: workspaces routing time-critical freight (events equipment, film and TV, high-value cargo) between São Paulo, the Northeast, and Amazonian points should re-evaluate transit-time assumptions on these corridors in 2026–2027 as construction phases progress and concession terms take effect.

**Rail reactivation creates a future alternative to road on Centre-West corridors:**
Brazil's approximately 10,000 kilometres of idle railway lines represent potential modal diversification once the public call model produces operational services. *Source: U.S. International Trade Administration, Brazil Rail Transportation, trade.gov, September 3, 2025. https://www.trade.gov/market-intelligence/brazil-rail-transportation. Analytical inference: for workspaces with high-volume, non-time-critical freight (e.g., large events infrastructure, exhibition equipment, automotive parts) on Minas Gerais or Centre-West corridors, rail reactivation timelines are worth monitoring as a cost-reduction pathway; however, no confirmed operational timeline for reactivated services is available from the source blocks.

**COP30 as a regional and reputational inflection point:**
Brazil hosts COP30. The Global Drive to Zero source frames Brazil's commercial vehicle decarbonisation effort explicitly in the context of COP30 hosting responsibilities. *Source: Global Drive to Zero / CALSTART, November 3, 2025. https://globaldrivetozero.org/2025/11/03/charging-up-change-brazil-accelerating-its-drive-to-zero/. Analytical inference: workspaces with multinational clients operating European sustainability reporting frameworks (CSRD, ISO 14083) may face heightened scrutiny of their Brazil-leg emissions data in 2025–2026; the absence of a mature Scope 3 data pipeline from Brazilian road carriers is a reporting gap worth addressing now.

**Sustainability taxonomy integration — CNAE H:**
The Sub-secretariat's mandate to integrate the Brazilian Sustainable Taxonomy for CNAE H (Transport, Storage, and Courier) into infrastructure decisions signals that sustainability classification will become embedded in Brazilian transport concession governance. *Source: Ministério dos Transportes, Subsecretaria de Sustentabilidade – SUST, gov.br, updated February 26, 2026. https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br/assuntos/sustentabilidade. Analytical inference: workspaces tendering for Brazilian government logistics contracts or operating in state-adjacent supply chains should monitor whether Taxonomy alignment becomes a qualification criterion.

---

área de transferência Publicado em 13/03/2020 13h41 Atualizado em 26/02/2026 09h40 As questões socioambientais e sua interface com o setor de transportes assumem caráter estruturante no âmbito do Ministério dos Transportes, cujo planejamento institucional estabelece a sustentabilidade como premissa transversal das políticas, planos e programas do setor. Essa diretriz orienta a formulação e a implementação da infraestrutura de transportes sob a perspectiva da responsabilidade socioambiental, da resiliência e da adaptação à mudança do clima. Com a recriação do Ministério dos Transportes, por meio do Decreto nº 11.531/2023, e sua posterior reestruturação pelo Decreto nº 11.961/2024, consolidou-se a Subsecretaria de Sustentabilidade, no âmbito da Secretaria-Executiva, como unidade responsável pela coordenação transversal da agenda socioambiental e climática do setor de transportes terrestres. Criada em 2019, a Subsecretaria de Sustentabilidade tem entre suas atribuições estabelecer diretrizes, planejar, coordenar e supervisionar as atividades socioambientais relacionadas à infraestrutura de transportes, incluindo o enfrentamento à mudança do clima, o licenciamento ambiental, gestão de condicionantes, remoção involuntária, desapropriações, declaração de utilidade pública e gestão de áreas afetadas por empreendimentos federais. Nos termos do Decreto nº 11.961/2024, compete à Subsecretaria de Sustentabilidade: I – Coordenar e monitorar atividades relacionadas ao equacionamento de questões socioambientais necessárias à execução dos empreendimentos de infraestrutura de transportes no âmbito das competências do Ministério; II – Promover a articulação institucional com órgãos ambientais e representar o Ministério em fóruns, colegiados e agendas relacionadas à sustentabilidade; III – Coordenar o estabelecimento de diretrizes e a padronização de procedimentos para declaração de utilidade pública, remoção de interferências, desapropriações e deslocamento compulsório em obras de infraestrutura; e V – Apoiar as Secretarias finalísticas nas atividades relativas às dimensões socioambientais dos empreendimentos. No âmbito da Subsecretaria de Sustentabilidade, encontra-se a Assessoria de Participação Social e Diversidade (ASPAD), cuja competência está igualmente definida no Decreto nº 11.961/2024. À ASPAD compete assessorar na formulação, coordenação e acompanhamento de políticas, programas e ações relacionadas à participação social e à promoção da diversidade no setor de transportes, promover o diálogo institucional com a sociedade civil e apoiar a incorporação de diretrizes de equidade, inclusão e justiça social nos processos de planejamento e implementação das políticas públicas sob a responsabilidade do Ministério. Além das competências regimentais, a Subsecretaria exerce papel estratégico na articulação das Diretrizes Interministeriais de Sustentabilidade, na incorporação da agenda de mitigação e adaptação à mudança do clima no setor de transportes, do Plano Clima – Setorial de Transportes, e na integração de critérios de sustentabilidade, gestão de riscos, adaptação à mudança do clima e classificação das atividades econômicas segundo a Taxonomia Sustentável Brasileira, especialmente no que se refere às atividades enquadradas na CNAE H – Transporte, Armazenagem e Correio. Dessa forma, a Subsecretaria de Sustentabilidade consolida-se como instância de governança responsável por assegurar que a expansão e a modernização da infraestrutura de transportes ocorram de forma ambientalmente responsável, socialmente justa e alinhada aos compromissos nacionais e internacionais do Brasil.
