The terminal has already cut its Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 87% in 2024 compared to 2021, with these reductions independently assured by LRQA. A major milestone was reached in 2022 when the port became the first in the UK to eliminate fossil diesel from its operations entirely, switching to Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO), a renewable biodiesel that has slashed net carbon dioxide emissions by over 80% and significantly improved local air quality. Now, the terminal is set to hit its biggest landmark to date, with it on track to be operational net zero this year. Based on verified data from 2021-2024 and the implemented and future decarbonisation projects, DP World Southampton is on track to become Operational Net Zero for the 2025 Reporting Period. This will be a direct result of the continued efforts to reduce carbon emissions from our operations. Once the emissions have been reduced beyond this 10% of the baseline value, the appropriate amount of carbon credits will be retired to offset the final unabated and residual emissions. Combining innovation with strategic offsetting Operational Net Zero is defined as achieving and maintaining a balance between the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions produced through its Scope 1 and Scope 2 operations, and the measures taken to remove or offset emissions for them to equal zero. This aligns with the DP World global GHG emissions reduction targets as well as the Paris Agreement, GHG Protocol and SBTi Guidance. The container terminal operator, which plays a crucial role in the UK's supply chain infrastructure, has announced it is firmly on track to balance all greenhouse gas emissions from its operations through a comprehensive decarbonisation strategy that combines emissions reduction with high-quality carbon offsetting. This commitment represents more than just an environmental target – it's about reimagining how major port operations can contribute to a sustainable future. The initiative aligns with DP World's global science-based targets, validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), which call for a 42% reduction in direct emissions by 2030. Using 2021 as its baseline year – when the company first externally verified its carbon emissions against ISO 14064-1 standards – DP World Southampton has developed a robust five-year decarbonisation plan that focuses on three key pillars: Energy Efficiency Revolution: The terminal is adopting cutting-edge energy-efficient technologies and dramatically increasing its renewable energy usage, moving away from traditional fossil fuel dependencies. Operational Innovation: By utilising low-carbon fuels and promoting sustainable operational practices, the facility is fundamentally transforming how container handling can be conducted with minimal environmental impact. Strategic Offsetting: For remaining emissions that cannot be eliminated, the company will retire high-quality, verifiable carbon credits meeting strict ISO 14068 criteria. Aerial view of DP World Southampton port (Credit: DP World) The timing of this commitment is particularly significant for Southampton, as the city council has set an ambitious target to become net zero by 2035. DP World Southampton's 2025 achievement will provide crucial momentum for the broader regional decarbonisation effort. What sets this initiative apart is its commitment to rigorous verification and transparency. DP World Southampton will continue to have its emissions data independently verified annually against ISO 14064-1 standards, ensuring accountability and maintaining public trust in its environmental claims. The company has also committed to regularly reviewing and enhancing its decarbonisation plan to incorporate the latest scientific guidance and technological innovations, while carefully considering any potential unintended environmental or social consequences. Ambitious long-term targets Aerial view of container yard at Southampton port (Credit: DP World) While the 2025 operational net zero target represents a significant milestone, DP World Southampton's ambitions extend much further. The facility remains committed to supporting the global business target of reducing Scope 3 supply chain emissions by 28% by 2030 and achieving full net zero across all emission scopes by 2050. This includes innovative programmes such as the Modal Shift Programme and Carbon Inset Programme Trial, designed to reduce emissions throughout the entire supply chain ecosystem. John Trenchard, Vice President - Commercial & Supply Chain, DP World in the UK, says: "At DP World, we are committed to reducing our environmental impact and offering our customers lower carbon options for their supply chains. I'm incredibly proud of the achievements at our Southampton port, a true team effort. "Our sustainability strategy has fostered dedication across the business, and we will continue to invest in low-carbon technologies and business models to support our customers' sustainability goals. The sustainability journey continues." John Trenchard, Vice President, Commercial and Supply Chain UK at DP World DP World has also supported Southampton, with the introduction of items like the Green Charter, to support Southampton city's vision to create a cleaner, green, healthier and more sustainable city. DP World is the first port in the UK to introduce a 'green' charge on older trucks to pick up or drop off a container. It is part of a number of measures the company is taking to help cut emissions. DP World has also teamed up with Hampshire Wildlife Trust, through which it has funded the installation of two seabins helping the fight against plastic pollution in our local waterways. As well as launching an innovative Carbon Inset Programme Trial from 1 January 2025, providing importers into the UK the ability to reduce hard-to-abate Scope 3 carbon emissions from their containerised supply chains. The groundbreaking programme began issuing certificates in May following the registration of over 150,000 import containers since its January launch. Strong participation prompted an extension through year-end, expanding beyond the original six-month timeline to accommodate growing interest from cargo owners seeking carbon credits. In addition to the progress made in Southampton, DP World's site at London Gateway has invested heavily in electrification of its operations and has also made major progress to enable the energy transition. DP World's expansion project will add a further 400m-long all-electric berth and host Europe's tallest quay cranes, helping to enhance the decarbonisation of port operations and craft greener supply chains. Our commitment to decarbonization aims to achieve an ambitious target of more than 90% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 carbon emissions by 2030. If we would keep business as usual, our emissions for 2030 would be 2.3 times compared to 2022 emissions. The DP World Callao strategy for delivering on decarbonization is based on equipment electrification and efficiency, renewable energy, process efficiency and digitalization. Serving the strategy, and until 2030, more than US$72 million will be invested for the changeover to electric equipment (replacement and conversion) and renewable energy supply. We started by measuring our emissions and transforming our RTG cranes in 2019. In 2020, during the pandemic, we changed the entire lighting system of the operational area of the Port of Callao to LED lights. In 2021, we managed to stop emitting over a 1000 tons of CO2 by digitizing a large part of our processes and applying operational efficiency. In 2022, the Ministry of Environment recognized us with the third star of its Peru Carbon Footprint program, for managing and reducing our emissions for two consecutive years. We closed 2023 by stopping the emission of over 2680 tons of CO2 equivalents, through the acquisition of 100% of our electricity from renewable sources. In 2024, we have implemented a charging station for our 20 fully electric ITVs, and our first electric RTG yard cranes started operating. in the next years, we will make more efforts to achieve sustainable operations. In 2026, we will replace 30 diesel trucks with electric ones. In 2027, we will replace 6 additional RTG yard cranes with electric ones. In 2029, we will replace 11 trucks with electric ones. In 2030, we will convert 9 more cranes to electric to finally offset the remaining carbon. And thus, we aim to achieve our decarbonization targets for 2030. Renewable energy supply: 100% the electrical energy supply to the Terminal comes from power plants that generate energy from renewable sources since May 1st 2024 (I-REC certification). sections.md:
**Programme identity and structure**

Project JOLT — Joint Operator Logistics Trial — is a live, real-world eHGV trial programme led by The Centre for Sustainable Road Freight (SRF), a collaboration between Cambridge University, Heriot-Watt University, the University of Westminster, and industry and government partners. *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, "Operators unite in electric heavy goods vehicles trial," eng.cam.ac.uk, [2024]. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial.

The programme's stated objective is "to develop the knowledge and models needed to de-risk electric freight operations and inform investment decisions." *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, "Operators unite in electric heavy goods vehicles trial," eng.cam.ac.uk, [2024]. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial.

As of August 2025, Project JOLT is made up of 15 fleet operators, four manufacturers, a charge point operator, and three enablers. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial," Carol Millett, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article.

Named consortium partners include John Lewis Partnership, Volvo Trucks UK, and Flexible Power Systems — a software company specialising in fleet management optimisation software for electric vehicles. *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, "Operators unite in electric heavy goods vehicles trial," eng.cam.ac.uk, [2024]. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial.

Evyve, the charge point operator, is providing high-powered charging infrastructure and energy solutions for the initiative and subsequent roll-outs. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial," Carol Millett, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article.

**Trial design**

The trial pools operations and technical data from a fleet of rigid and articulated eHGVs across a wide range of 3PL, retailer, and manufacturer use cases. Project JOLT provides shared access to a fleet of electric vehicles and mobile chargers used by each partner for a pre-agreed sequence of trials. High-resolution operational data is collected during each trial period and then analysed, anonymised, and shared with all partners as part of a managed collective learning process. All shared data is subject to the provisions of a Data Confidentiality Agreement agreed between all partners before work starts. *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, "Operators unite in electric heavy goods vehicles trial," eng.cam.ac.uk, [2024]. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial.

Specialists at Cambridge University and Heriot-Watt University analyse and model data including vehicle and charger performance, operational efficiency, and costs across as many industry uses as possible. *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, "Operators unite in electric heavy goods vehicles trial," eng.cam.ac.uk, [2024]. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial.

**DP World trial results — the most recent published outcome (August 2025)**

DP World trialled three electric vehicles under Project JOLT, joining the initiative approximately three months before the August 2025 report. The three trucks were the Scania G230E and the Mercedes e-Actros 300, which was upgraded to the e-Actros 600 in the final three weeks. DP World's trial saw over 170 runs made, amounting to 24,000 kilometres, on daily shuttle routes of 115 kilometres between Swindon and Oxford. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial," Carol Millett, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article.

DP World Transport Controller Tim Mitchell devised simple metrics on battery charging to eliminate range anxiety and said he was "delighted" with the performance of the trucks. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial," Carol Millett, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article.

DP World and its customer carried out a strategic review on the commercial opportunity to permanently electrify the Swindon–Oxford route following the trial. The company stated that, although the cost of the electric truck is still high, the likely cost of electricity will create a favourable total cost of ownership compared to diesel. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial," Carol Millett, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article.

*Specific electricity cost figures and TCO modelling numbers not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*

Professor David Cebon stated: "Our research on battery performance is crucial to the ultimate findings on electrification and will help determine the residual value of electric trucks." *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial," Carol Millett, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article.

**Sector context**

HGVs account for 20% of CO₂ emissions from domestic transport in the UK. Freight contributed £13.6 billion to the UK economy in 2022. 98% of food and agricultural products are carried by road, mostly on HGVs. Electrifying the UK's HGV fleet would be the equivalent of removing 13 million cars from the roads. *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, "Operators unite in electric heavy goods vehicles trial," eng.cam.ac.uk, [2024]. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial.

---

**TCO at scale remains unquantified in published sources**

*Specific electricity cost figures and TCO modelling numbers not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.* While DP World states that the likely cost of electricity will create a favourable TCO compared to diesel, the modelling behind that claim is not in the published source material. The outcome of the post-trial strategic commercial review has not been published.

**Battery residual value — the key variable — is an open research question**

Professor Cebon explicitly states that battery performance research will "help determine the residual value of electric trucks," indicating this is a current research objective, not a resolved finding. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article. Analytical inference: Until residual value curves are published from JOLT's battery performance data, fleet procurement models carry an unquantified residual risk that may suppress full-cycle investment decisions.

**Applicability beyond fixed corridors**

The JOLT trial design covers rigid and articulated eHGVs "across a wide range of 3PL, retailer and manufacturer use cases," but the only published route result is a 115 km fixed shuttle. Analytical inference: Variable-route, long-haul, multi-drop, or cross-border road operations — which are common in live events, fine art logistics, and multi-modal high-value freight — are not addressed by the current published findings.

**44-tonne articulated eHGV viability**

Industry reporting from Motor Transport notes that battery payload loss affects eHGV economics at higher gross vehicle weights. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, "Battery payload loss and eHGV weight economics" [referenced in related articles navigation]. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article. Analytical inference: Full-articulated operations — typical for high-volume 3PL, automotive, and events equipment moves — face a payload economics constraint that JOLT's current published findings do not resolve.

**Regulatory linkage — pending, not resolved**

Analytical inference: The JOLT programme operates upstream of formal UK and EU regulatory compliance frameworks for HGV decarbonisation. The research findings will inform regulatory design and operator compliance pathways, but no binding compliance obligations derived from JOLT outputs have been published as of August 2025. The regulatory connection requires separate sourcing and monitoring.

**MONITORING — Re-check window: Q1 2026**

The programme is active and generating results on a rolling basis. The DP World commercial review outcome, broader fleet operator trial results from the other 14 operators in the consortium, and battery performance modelling outputs are all pending. The brief should be re-checked in Q1 2026 for: (a) publication of JOLT consolidated findings, (b) DP World permanent electrification decision, (c) expansion of the operator participant base, and (d) any regulatory referencing of JOLT data.

---

**What the workspace can credibly say**

- Project JOLT is a live, structured UK eHGV research programme, led by Cambridge and Heriot-Watt universities, now operating across 15 fleet operators, four OEM manufacturers, and a named charge point operator. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article.
- The most recent published results (DP World, August 2025) cover substantial mileage across many runs on a daily shuttle route, with the operator reporting favourable TCO expectations for electricity versus diesel on that corridor. *Source: Motor Transport / FreightCarbonZero, 12 August 2025.*
- The programme's design specifically targets the data gaps — battery performance, residual value, charging infrastructure integration — that prevent large-scale fleet commitment decisions.
- Analytical inference: For clients asking about road decarbonisation credibility, the workspace can reference the JOLT consortium structure and its own monitoring of trial outputs as evidence of grounded, not aspirational, engagement with eHGV transition.

**Questions to pose to clients**

- Analytical inference: "Which of your road freight lanes are fixed-corridor and depot-anchored? Those are the routes where eHGV feasibility is most supported by current trial evidence."
- Analytical inference: "What is your current Scope 3 Category 4 baseline on road freight? We can map emerging eHGV route options against that baseline."

**Pitfalls to avoid**

- Do not cite specific cost-per-kilometre or TCO figures for eHGVs — these are not publicly available from the JOLT source material as of August 2025, and the programme's own research is noted as ongoing. *Specific electricity cost figures and TCO modelling numbers not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.*
- Analytical inference: Do not represent JOLT results as proof that eHGVs are commercially viable at scale — the programme's stated purpose is to develop that understanding, not to confirm it. Overclaiming the state of readiness undermines credibility with sophisticated logistics clients.
- Do not represent the DP World result as applicable to variable-route, multi-drop, or long-haul operations — the trial covers a specific 115 km fixed shuttle and the research team has explicitly described understanding whole-fleet and industry transition as still "a long way to go." *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial.

---

**For road-primary and road-secondary freight operators**

Analytical inference: The DP World results — a substantial mileage across many runs on a high-frequency daily shuttle — are the most operationally specific published data point from Project JOLT to date, and they apply directly to the kind of depot-to-depot or port-to-inland drayage routes that characterise heavy-lift, live events, automotive, and time-critical road moves. The finding that range anxiety was manageable through simple battery-charging metrics is operationally significant: it reduces the perceived complexity barrier for operators on fixed-corridor runs of comparable length.

Analytical inference: The DP World post-trial commercial review — assessing permanent route electrification — signals the programme is moving from data collection to investment decision support, which is the transition from research value to commercial relevance for operators considering fleet commitment.

**Battery residual value as the commercial unlock**

Analytical inference: Professor Cebon's specific emphasis on battery performance research as the determinant of residual value identifies the key financial variable that currently prevents large-scale eHGV fleet commitment. Until residual value is predictable, total cost of ownership modelling remains incomplete, and capital allocation decisions on eHGV procurement carry unquantified downside. Project JOLT's ongoing battery data collection is therefore directly upstream of the TCO confidence that operators need before committing at scale.

**Digital fleet management as an enabling layer**

Analytical inference: Flexible Power Systems' role as a named JOLT partner — providing fleet management optimisation software for electric vehicles — positions digital fleet tools as a first-order operational requirement, not a secondary enhancement. The structured data collection and anonymised sharing model JOLT uses (Data Confidentiality Agreement across all partners) demonstrates that data governance is a prerequisite for pre-competitive collaboration in eHGV transition.

**Road freight decarbonisation regulatory pressure**

Analytical inference: The JOLT programme's urgency aligns with UK and EU regulatory trajectories for road freight decarbonisation, including the EU HGV CO₂ standards and UK Zero Emission HGV Infrastructure Demonstrator programmes. Operators generating real-world eHGV operational data through JOLT are building the evidence base that regulators are drawing on for compliance pathway design — creating an asymmetry between participating operators and those without data.

*Specific regulatory deadlines and penalty provisions for UK or EU HGV CO₂ standards not grounded in the source blocks provided; those items require separate sourcing.*

---

**Fleet electrification feasibility assessment — now possible for fixed-corridor road operations**

Analytical inference: The JOLT data model — high-resolution operational data pooled across 3PL, retailer, and manufacturer use cases — enables operators on comparable fixed routes (115 km or below, depot-anchored, daily shuttle pattern) to benchmark their own route feasibility against published trial outcomes rather than relying on OEM specifications alone. For workspaces operating road-primary delivery of time-sensitive or high-value cargo on repeatable UK corridors, this changes the feasibility conversation from theoretical to evidenced.

**Participation decision — JOLT is still open**

The trial is described as open to all HGV operators, who can participate either by accessing a shared vehicle fleet supplied by OEMs or by sharing data from their own vehicles. *Source: Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, "Operators unite in electric heavy goods vehicles trial," eng.cam.ac.uk, [2024]. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial. Analytical inference: For a workspace operating road freight in the UK, the participation option is a concrete near-term decision point: joining JOLT would provide access to research data, shared vehicle access, and the pre-competitive learning environment without requiring full fleet commitment. The cost of non-participation is measured in data asymmetry relative to the 15 fleet operators now inside the consortium.

**Charging infrastructure procurement**

Analytical inference: Evyve's role as charge point operator and provider of high-powered charging for subsequent roll-outs, named explicitly in the programme, signals that infrastructure procurement decisions are inseparable from vehicle decisions. Workspaces evaluating eHGV fleet moves in the UK should assess depot charging capability and infrastructure partnership options concurrently with vehicle procurement, not sequentially.

**Cargo vertical differentiation**

Analytical inference: The 115 km shuttle with fixed origin and destination is a proxy for port-drayage or venue-to-depot delivery patterns common in live events logistics and automotive finished-vehicle transport. These verticals are among those most amenable to early electrification due to route predictability and depot control. High-value fine art and luxury cargo, which typically uses dedicated road services on longer or more variable routes, faces a different feasibility profile — the JOLT findings do not yet resolve those cases.

**Scope 3 reporting**

Analytical inference: Road freight emissions from HGVs are a Scope 3 Category 4 source for cargo owners. Operators who can demonstrate eHGV fleet deployment on named routes are already in a position to offer verifiable Scope 3 emissions reductions to clients. The JOLT data-sharing model — anonymised, structured, DCA-governed — is a template for the kind of supplier-level data workspaces will need to substantiate Scope 3 claims under emerging disclosure frameworks.

electric heavy goods vehicles trial Electric heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) are to be trialled across the UK in a new programme to help freight operators decarbonise their fleet. The urgency of the climate crisis is driving adoption of electric heavy goods vehicles at a rate that few in the industry would have expected five years ago. Operators are purchasing and running these vehicles today in fleets of all sizes. But there’s still a long way to go to understand how whole fleets and industries can transition to electric heavy goods vehicles in a technically feasible way. David Cebon, Professor of Mechanical Engineering and director of The Centre for Sustainable Road Freight Called Project JOLT – standing for Joint Operator Logistics Trial – the programme is led by The Centre for Sustainable Road Freight (SRF) and involves partners including John Lewis Partnership, Volvo Trucks UK, and Flexible Power Systems, a software company specialising in fleet management optimisation software for electric vehicles.  The trial will pool operations and technical data from a fleet of rigid and articulated eHGVs being used across a wide range of 3PL, retailer and manufacturer use cases. Project JOLT will provide shared access to a fleet of electric vehicles and mobile chargers which can be used by each partner for the purpose of carrying out a pre-agreed sequence of partner trials. High resolution operational data will be collected during each trial period and then analysed, anonymised, and shared with all partners as part of a managed collective learning process. All shared data will be subject to the provisions of a Data Confidentiality Agreement which will be agreed between all partners before the work starts. The objective is to develop the knowledge and models needed to de-risk electric freight operations and inform investment decisions. The participating fleet operators will share their learning experiences in a pre-competitive environment to develop a clear understanding of how electric vehicles and charging infrastructure can be deployed most effectively to serve their business needs. The trial is open to all HGV operators becoming involved by accessing a shared vehicle fleet supplied by OEMs or sharing data from their own vehicles. The electrification of the UK’s commercial fleets needs to happen urgently. Freight is hugely important; it contributed £13.6 billion to the economy in 2022*. 98% of our food and agricultural products are carried by road, mostly on HGVs. However, HGVs also account for 20% of CO 2 emissions from domestic transport.  Electrifying the UK’s HGV fleet would be the same as removing 13 million cars from our roads.  Ensuring a smooth transition to electrification is a multi-faceted and onerous challenge: data driven insights are key to ensuring the confidence for companies involved in logistics to begin or continue their journey towards Net Zero.  SRF was founded to help industry and government minimise carbon emissions from the road freight sector and is a collaboration between Cambridge University, Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, the University of Westminster, and industry and government partners.  Professor David Cebon, Professor of Mechanical Engineering at Cambridge University and director of The Centre for Sustainable Road Freight, established Project JOLT. He said: “The urgency of the climate crisis is driving adoption of electric heavy goods vehicles at a rate that few in the industry would have expected five years ago.  “Operators are purchasing and running these vehicles today in fleets of all sizes. But there’s still a long way to go to understand how whole fleets and industries can transition to electric heavy goods vehicles in a technically feasible way.”  The JOLT partners will pool data and learning from their experiences with eHGVs in retail, delivery, and manufacturing operations to help develop transition plans for their own businesses and for the wider logistics industry.  Specialists at Cambridge University and Heriot-Watt University will analyse and model data including vehicle and charger performance, operational efficiency, and costs across as many industry uses as possible.  Professor Philip Greening is an expert in sustainable transport and logistics at Heriot-Watt University and co-director of The Centre for Sustainable Road Freight. He said: “A key feature of this project is understanding how the different range and load capabilities of electric heavy goods vehicles – as well as downtime for charging – will affect the efficiency of operators and supply chains. We’ll do this by analysing logistics data and technical information collected through sophisticated computer simulations known as digital twins, to help us understand operations at scale.”  John Lewis Partnership, one of the UK’s best-known retailers, has joined Project JOLT and will use an eHGV from Volvo Trucks UK in their logistics operation. The vehicle, a Volvo FM 4x2 tractor unit, is a heavy-duty truck that can carry up to 42 tonnes and can cover up to 300km on a single charge.  Justin Laney, Partner and General Manager of Central Transport for John Lewis Partnership said: “We are delighted to be kick starting this important initiative, which will inform our journey beyond eliminating fossil fuel from our fleet by 2030 to achieving a zero-carbon fleet by 2035.”  Volvo Trucks delivered around 145,000 Volvo trucks worldwide in 2023 and offers a range of electric trucks in the UK and Ireland.  Amy Stokes, Head of Electromobility at Volvo Trucks UK and Ireland, said: “At Volvo Trucks, we are committed to the environment, innovation, and safety in maintaining our position as market leaders in a changing world. We want to ensure our customers can take their next steps to zero-emission vehicles for their fleets with confidence.”  Project JOLT partners will use electric vehicle fleet management software FPS Operate, provided by Flexible Power Systems. Its platform is a remote, cloud-based system that connects to electric vehicle chargers, vehicles, building metering systems, and operational software. The three electric trucks were the Scania G230E truck and the Mercedes e-Actros 300, which was upgraded to the e-Actros 600 in the final 3 weeks. Project Jolt is a research project looking at the commercial viability of electric trucks. It is driven by the Centre for Sustainable Road Freight and is made up of 15 fleet operators, four manufacturers, a charge point operator and three enablers. DP World trial saw over 170 runs made, amounting to 24,000 kilometres. Tim Mitchell, DP World transport controller, devised some simple metrics on battery charging to eliminate range anxiety. He said he was “delighted” with the performance of the trucks as they made daily shuttles of 115 kilometres from Swindon to Oxford and back. Following the trial, DP World and its customer have carried out a strategic review on the commercial opportunity to permanently electrify this route. The company said that, although the cost of the electric truck is still high, the likely cost of electricity will create a favourable total cost of ownership compared to diesel and then of course there are the huge environmental gains. Dave Munday, DP World transport operations manager, said: “Project Jolt has provided us with the intelligence, knowledge and confidence in our 12 week trial to be comfortable in operating an electric fleet”. Professor David Cebon of the University of Cambridge and Project Jolt project director, said: “Our research on battery performance is crucial to the ultimate findings on electrification and will help determine the residual value of electric trucks.” Evyve, the charge point operator, is providing high powered charging infrastructure and energy solutions for the initiative and subsequent roll outs. Chief executive James Moat, said:“This is an exciting time in terms of all parties being able to evaluate how charging infrastructure and eHGVs perform in an operational environment. Evyve is pleased to be collaborating with Project Jolt to find practical solutions to these issues.” DP World initiative leader, Francis Dawson, added: “The benefits of testing the trucks live have been enormous. “We have given all our drivers on this route the chance to experience electric and the comments have all been highly complimentary. “However, the real boost is the knowledge that we can move forward with our net zero targets.” Carol Millett Follow Carol Millett is an award-winning freelance journalist with over 30 years’ of experience writing across a broad range of sectors, including road transport, construction and civil engineering, project management, private finance, technology, HR, and travel and tourism. ---

**MONITORING — FHWA Flexibility Certification Guidance**

FACT: The FHWA CRP fact sheet states: "Note: FHWA will issue guidance on how the Secretary will make such certifications" regarding the 23 U.S.C. 175(c)(2) flexibility provision allowing STBG-eligible projects when a State demonstrates transportation emissions reductions. *Source: Carbon Reduction Program (CRP) Fact Sheet, FHWA. https://highways.dot.gov/iija/fact-sheets/carbon-reduction-program-crp

Specific publication date for this FHWA flexibility certification guidance not available from primary sources as of June 5, 2026. *Analytical inference:* Given the FY2022–2026 program authorization window, any flexibility certification guidance published after FY2026 would have diminished practical effect unless CRP is reauthorized in a successor transportation bill. The workspace should monitor the status of surface transportation reauthorization (the current IIJA authorization expires September 30, 2026).

**Re-check window:** Surface transportation reauthorization deadline: September 30, 2026. The workspace should re-assess CRP continuity and any successor program structure by Q3 2026.

**MONITORING — IIJA Reauthorization / CRP Successor Program**

*Analytical inference:* The IIJA authorizes CRP contract authority through FY2026. Congressional reauthorization of surface transportation programs — including CRP or a successor — is due by October 1, 2026. Changes to eligible project categories, State strategy requirements, or suballocation formulas in any reauthorization would directly affect South Dakota corridor investment priorities.

Specific congressional schedule for surface transportation reauthorization not available from primary sources as of June 5, 2026.

---

**For State DOTs (not the workspace directly):**
*Legal Confirmation Required:* Registration and reporting obligations under 23 U.S.C. 175 run to State DOTs and FHWA. The workspace holds no direct registration or reporting obligation under the statute as written.

FACT: FHWA is required to "review the State's process for developing its carbon reduction strategy and certify that the strategy meets statutory requirements" within 90 days of State submission. *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(4); Carbon Reduction Program (CRP) Fact Sheet, FHWA. https://highways.dot.gov/iija/fact-sheets/carbon-reduction-program-crp

**For the workspace — indirect reporting context:**
*Operational implication:* Workspaces operating as freight forwarders on South Dakota corridors may face Scope 3 emissions reporting requests from clients that reference state-level CRP-funded emissions metrics. Understanding the basis of South Dakota's CRP strategy (energy efficiency focus, not VMT-based metrics) is relevant when responding to such data requests. SDDOT's strategy does not appear to produce route-level emissions intensity data that the workspace could directly cite in emissions reporting.

FACT: South Dakota's CRP strategy is described as quantifying, at SDDOT's discretion, "the total carbon emissions from the production, transport, and use of materials used in the construction of transportation facilities within the State," per 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2)(D). *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2)(D). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

Whether SDDOT has exercised this discretion and published embodied carbon data is not confirmed from the corpus as of June 5, 2026. Specific embodied carbon quantification status for SDDOT not available from primary sources as of June 5, 2026.

---

### 8.1 Carbon Reduction Strategy — Development Obligation

FACT: "Not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of the Surface Transportation Reauthorization Act of 2021, a State, in consultation with any metropolitan planning organization designated within the State, shall develop a carbon reduction strategy in accordance with this subsection." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(1). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

**Qualification — consultation requirement:** The development obligation is conditioned on consultation with "any metropolitan planning organization designated within the State." It is not a unilateral State obligation; MPO input is built into the process.

### 8.2 Carbon Reduction Strategy — Five Substantive Requirements (23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2))

FACT: The carbon reduction strategy "shall—
(A) support efforts to reduce transportation emissions;
(B) identify projects and strategies to reduce transportation emissions, which may include projects and strategies for safe, reliable, and cost-effective options—
(i) to reduce traffic congestion by facilitating the use of alternatives to single-occupant vehicle trips …
(ii) to facilitate the use of vehicles or modes of travel that result in lower transportation emissions per person-mile traveled …
(iii) to facilitate approaches to the construction of transportation assets that result in lower transportation emissions …
(C) support the reduction of transportation emissions of the State;
(D) at the discretion of the State, quantify the total carbon emissions from the production, transport, and use of materials used in the construction of transportation facilities within the State; and
(E) be appropriate to the population density and context of the State, including any metropolitan planning organization designated within the State." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

**Key qualifications:**
- Requirement (B)(i)–(iii) are permissive ("may include"), not mandatory components. The five lettered requirements (A)–(E) are mandatory.
- Requirement (D) is expressly "at the discretion of the State" — embodied carbon quantification is optional.
- Requirement (E) introduces a context-sensitivity qualifier that modulates all other requirements: the strategy need only be "appropriate to the population density and context."

FACT: SDDOT states its strategy "meets all five major requirements of 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2)." *Source: SDDOT Carbon Reduction Strategy page. https://dot.sd.gov/projects-studies/planning/carbon-reduction-strategy

*Operational implication:* For freight-vertical workspaces, requirement (B)(iii) — facilitating lower-emissions construction approaches — is potentially relevant if CRP funds are directed toward construction of new freight infrastructure. Requirement (D)'s optional embodied carbon quantification is a data gap that, if SDDOT exercises discretion to omit it, means no state-level carbon accounting baseline for construction materials will be available from the CRP strategy.

### 8.3 Update Obligation

FACT: The carbon reduction strategy "shall be updated not less frequently than once every 4 years." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(3). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

**Qualification:** The statute sets a floor ("not less frequently") — states may update more often. The four-year cycle is a minimum, not a fixed interval.

### 8.4 FHWA Review and Certification Obligation

FACT: "Not later than 90 days after the date on which a State submits a request for the approval of a carbon reduction strategy … the Secretary shall— (A) review the process used to develop the carbon reduction strategy; and (B)(i) certify that the carbon reduction strategy meets the requirements of paragraph (2); or (ii) deny certification of the carbon reduction strategy and specify the actions necessary for the State to take to correct the deficiencies in the process of the State in developing the carbon reduction strategy." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(4). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

**Key qualification:** FHWA reviews "the process used to develop the carbon reduction strategy" — not the substantive policy choices within the strategy. A denial specifies process deficiencies, not content mandates.

*Analytical inference:* This process-review (rather than content-review) structure gives States wide latitude in the substance of their strategies, provided procedural consultation requirements are met. SDDOT's FHWA-approved strategy accordingly reflects South Dakota's rural context and energy-efficiency focus without FHWA overriding those substantive choices.

### 8.5 Suballocation Obligations

FACT: "For each fiscal year, of the funds apportioned to the State under section 104(b)(7)— (A) 65 percent shall be obligated, in proportion to their relative shares of the population of the State— (i) in urbanized areas of the State with an urbanized area population of more than 200,000; (ii) in urbanized areas of the State with an urbanized population of not less than 50,000 and not more than 200,000; (iii) in urban areas of the State with a population of not less than 5,000 and not more than 49,999; and (iv) in other areas of the State with a population of less than 5,000; and (B) the remainder may be obligated in any area of the State." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(e)(1). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

**Key qualification — metropolitan area attribution:**
FACT: "Funds attributed to an urbanized area under paragraph (1)(A)(i) may be obligated in the metropolitan area established under section 134 that encompasses the urbanized area." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(e)(2). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

**Key qualification — alternative factor basis:**
FACT: "The State may obligate the funds described in subparagraph (A) based on other factors if— (i) the State and the relevant metropolitan planning organizations jointly apply to the Secretary for the permission to base the obligation on other factors; and (ii) the Secretary grants the request." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(e)(3)(B). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

### 8.6 Coordination and Consultation Obligations

FACT: "Before obligating funds for an eligible project under subsection (c) in an urbanized area that is not a transportation management area, a State shall coordinate with any metropolitan planning organization that represents the urbanized area prior to determining which activities should be carried out under the project." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(e)(4). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

FACT: "Before obligating funds for an eligible project under subsection (c) in a rural area, a State shall consult with any regional transportation planning organization or metropolitan planning organization that represents the rural area prior to determining which activities should be carried out under the project." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(e)(5). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

### 8.7 Federal Share

FACT: "The Federal share of the cost of a project carried out using funds apportioned to a State under section 104(b)(7) shall be determined in accordance with section 120." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(f). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

### 8.8 Treatment of Projects

FACT: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a project assisted under this section shall be treated as a project on a Federal-aid highway under this chapter." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(g). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

FACT: The FHWA fact sheet notes this treatment "ensures applicability of Davis-Bacon wage requirements." *Source: Carbon Reduction Program (CRP) Fact Sheet, FHWA. https://highways.dot.gov/iija/fact-sheets/carbon-reduction-program-crp

*Operational implication:* For workspaces co-investing in or contracting for CRP-funded infrastructure construction, Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply to the federally assisted work, affecting labor cost assumptions.

**Direct obligations under 23 U.S.C. 175:**
The statute imposes direct obligations on: (a) the Secretary of Transportation (to establish the program, review strategies, provide technical assistance); (b) each State (to develop the carbon reduction strategy, update it, and coordinate with MPOs); and (c) each State and relevant MPOs jointly, to ensure suballocation obligation authority compliance.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether freight forwarding workspaces, carriers, or logistics operators bear any direct obligation under 23 U.S.C. 175 — as opposed to being eligible recipients of CRP-funded projects — requires legal review. The statute's direct compliance chain as written runs from Congress to FHWA to State DOTs.

**Indirect position — project eligibility:**
*Operational implication:* Workspaces operating as logistics or freight forwarding entities may appear in the CRP compliance chain as project sponsors, infrastructure co-investors, or users of CRP-funded facilities (e.g., publicly accessible EV charging, natural gas fueling infrastructure, truck stop electrification) rather than as obligated compliance actors. Project-level eligibility is determined by State DOT and MPO project selection processes.

FACT: Before obligating CRP funds for an eligible project in a rural area, "a State shall consult with any regional transportation planning organization or metropolitan planning organization that represents the rural area prior to determining which activities should be carried out under the project." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(e)(5). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

*Operational implication:* Given South Dakota's predominantly rural context, workspaces with freight operations on rural South Dakota corridors are in the consultation zone: the State is required to consult regional or metropolitan planning organizations before obligating rural CRP funds. Participation in MPO or regional planning organization consultation processes is the primary pathway by which logistics operators can influence CRP project prioritization on freight corridors.

*Operational implication:* South Dakota's population is predominantly rural. Workspaces routing freight through rural South Dakota should expect infrastructure investment to be concentrated in Sioux Falls and Rapid City urbanized areas.

*Analytical inference:* SDDOT's stated strategy of allocating resources to improve energy efficiency — rather than mode-shift, transit expansion, or demand reduction — reflects the rural context qualification expressly permitted in 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2)(E), which requires the strategy to "be appropriate to the population density and context of the State." For freight-oriented workspaces, this means the South Dakota CRP investment profile is more likely to favor vehicle efficiency and fuel infrastructure improvements than urban transit or cycling alternatives.

**SDDOT Freight Plan alignment:**
FACT: The SDDOT Freight Plan includes the objective to "Improve energy efficiency of freight movement and idle time to reduce greenhouse gas emission." *Source: SDDOT Freight Plan page. https://dot.sd.gov/projects-studies/planning/freight-plan/

*Analytical inference:* The explicit alignment between SDDOT's freight plan emissions objective and the CRP strategy's energy efficiency focus creates a policy coherence that increases the likelihood of CRP funds being directed toward freight-specific eligible projects (truck stop electrification, ITS for freight, idle reduction) on South Dakota corridors.

This document analyzes the federal Carbon Reduction Program (CRP) established under 23 U.S.C. 175, specifically the carbon reduction strategy requirements of 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2), as they govern state-level transportation planning and project funding obligations. The primary focus is the substantive requirements imposed on state departments of transportation (DOTs), the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) compliance posture, and the implications for workspaces operating in freight forwarding, logistics, and supply chain services whose infrastructure investments, project eligibility, or freight corridor planning intersects with state CRP allocations.

- Source URLs used in FACT citations are drawn exclusively from the reference corpus provided. Additional sources are flagged in the New Sources Identified table.

**For the workspace — indirect operational readiness:**

*Operational implication:* The workspace does not face direct system build requirements under 23 U.S.C. 175. However, three operational dimensions are relevant:

**1. Alternative Fuel Infrastructure Readiness — South Dakota Corridors**

FACT: CRP eligible projects include "the acquisition, installation, or operation of publicly accessible electric vehicle charging infrastructure or hydrogen, natural gas, or propane vehicle fueling infrastructure." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(c)(1)(J)(i). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

*Operational implication:* As CRP-funded alternative fuel infrastructure becomes available on South Dakota corridors, workspaces operating or contracting road freight through the state may need to update carrier qualification criteria, routing software, and fuel planning tools to reflect the availability (or absence) of EV charging or alternative fuel stations. SDDOT separately maintains a South Dakota EV Fast Charging Plan listed alongside its Carbon Reduction Strategy. *Source: SDDOT Carbon Reduction Strategy page (EV Fast Charging Plan listed). https://dot.sd.gov/projects-studies/planning/carbon-reduction-strategy

**2. Truck Stop Electrification and Idle Reduction — Freight Corridor Implications**

FACT: CRP eligible projects include "a project described in section 149(b)(4) to establish or operate a traffic monitoring, management, and control facility or program, including advanced truck stop electrification systems." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(c)(1)(A). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

Workspaces should factor projected infrastructure availability into carrier contract terms and emissions accounting for South Dakota corridor routing.

**3. Zero-Emission Equipment and Vehicle Procurement**

FACT: CRP eligible projects include "the purchase or lease of zero-emission construction equipment and vehicles, including the acquisition, construction, or leasing of required supporting facilities." *Source: 23 U.S.C. 175(c)(1)(J)(ii). https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title23-section175&num=0&edition=prelim

*Operational implication:* Carriers receiving CRP-funded zero-emission vehicle subsidies in South Dakota may update fleet configurations on state corridors. Workspaces should monitor carrier fleet transition timelines to anticipate changes in vehicle availability, payload capacity, and range constraints relevant to freight routing.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether Davis-Bacon wage requirements apply to a specific CRP-funded project involving private-sector co-investment or public-private partnership structures requires legal review of 23 U.S.C. 175(g) as applied to the specific project structure.

Planning / Carbon Reduction Strategy The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Carbon Reduction Strategy meets all five major requirements of 23 U.S.C. 175(d)(2) and the minor ones by identifying projects and strategies to limit emissions. One of the best ways to limit emissions is to not produce them. There is no need to reduce what isn’t produced. Emissions and energy consumption are directly related so focusing on energy efficiency is a great strategy to limit emissions. It is also wise investment in good government because it supports economic efficiency and environmental stewardship as well. There are many strategies, methods, approaches, activities, and tactics SDDOT can use to implement SDDOT’s main carbon reduction strategy, which is to “Allocate Resources to Improve Energy Efficiency.” An intelligent approach to limit emissions aligns with economic and market forces to improve energy efficiency in ways that are appropriate to South Dakota’s context or setting. Developing a strategy that is “context sensitive” helps craft an effective approach. SDDOT and South Dakota citizens understand that strategies and methods that will work in an urban setting will not produce a favorable outcome in South Dakota’s rural setting. SDDOT cannot, and does not want to, dictate to its customers how they will use the state’s transportation system. Trying to override the “invisible hand” guiding individual transportation choices hinders those complementary forces and does not nurture a harmonious and coordinated strategy that will limit emissions while supporting resilience and mobility. South Dakota’s strategy will be shaped by the extent and limits of what SDDOT can control and influence.
